Section 1.1

Language models, LLMs and scale

≈ 4 min · Slides: FT-I s5–7

What is a language model?

A language model (LM) is a probabilistic model of text. Given a sequence of words it estimates the probability of the next word, and it assigns a probability to every possible next word:

Next-word prediction

“The cat sat on the ___” → mat 62%, sofa 21%, roof 9%, …

  • Learned from data: trained on large text corpora, so it captures grammar, facts and style.
  • Why it matters: next-word prediction is the engine behind autocomplete, translation and chatbots.

What is a large language model?

An LLM is a language model scaled up massively in parameters, training data and compute, almost always built on the transformer.

Billions+parameters. GPT-3 has 175B; frontier models are larger still.
Trillionsof training tokens: web pages, books, code and articles.
Transformerself-attention layers stacked dozens to hundreds deep.

Why scale changes everything

Capabilities that emerge with scale:

Fluent generation

Coherent essays, summaries, dialogue.

In-context learning

Learns a new task from a few examples in the prompt, with no retraining.

Reasoning & knowledge

Multi-step problem solving, world knowledge, code and math.

Well-known LLM familyMakerPositioning on the slide
GPTOpenAIGPT-3 → GPT-4 and beyond
ClaudeAnthropicAssistant models focused on safety
GeminiGoogleMultimodal frontier models
LlamaMetaOpen-weight models for research and industry

Crisp summary

  • An LM estimates : a probability for every possible next token.
  • An LLM is the same idea scaled up: billions of parameters (GPT-3 = 175B), trillions of tokens, deep transformer stacks.
  • Scale brings emergent abilities: fluent generation, in-context learning (few-shot, no retraining), reasoning and knowledge.
  • Families to know: GPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic, safety-focused), Gemini (Google, multimodal), Llama (Meta, open weights).
Section 1.2

The three transformer families

≈ 4 min · Slides: FT-I s8–11 · REV s4

Every LLM is one of three transformer layouts. Each block repeats N times: self-attention → Add & Layer Norm → position-wise feed-forward network → Add & Layer Norm.

Encoder-onlyDecoder-onlyEncoder–decoder
AttentionFully bidirectional: each token sees all tokens left and right; no causal maskCausal (masked): a triangular mask blocks the future, so token t attends only to 1…tEncoder bidirectional over the input; decoder causal over the output so far plus cross-attention to the encoder's memory (keys and values)
Pre-trainingMasked language modeling: ~15% of tokens hidden and predicted from context (BERT also used next-sentence prediction)Next-token prediction over raw text; generation is autoregressive: sample, append, predict again (KV-caching makes it fast)Denoising / span corruption (T5, BART) or paired data such as translation; target tokens are shifted right
Input / outputToken + segment + position embeddings, e.g. [CLS] the [MASK] sat [SEP]; outputs a contextual embedding per token; head = P(masked token) or a classifierToken + position embeddings; linear projection + softmax gives P(next token), e.g. “mat”, which is fed back inSource tokens x₁…xₙ into the encoder; decoder generates conditioned on the fully encoded input
Best atDeep understanding: classification, NER, sentence similarity, embeddings for search, retrieval and reranking. Not built to generate free textOpen-ended generation: chat, code, reasoning, summarization, agents. Scales exceptionally well and dominates modern LLMsExplicit input → output transformations: translation, summarization, question answering, structured rewriting
ExamplesBERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT, ELECTRA, DeBERTaGPT series, Claude, LLaMA, Mistral, Gemini (nearly all frontier chat models)Original Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), T5 / Flan-T5, BART, mT5, Marian NMT

Exam cue: “bidirectional + masked tokens” → encoder-only (BERT). “Causal mask + next token” → decoder-only (GPT). “Cross-attention over an encoded input” → encoder–decoder (T5, BART).

Crisp summary

  • Encoder-only (BERT family): bidirectional attention, masked-LM pre-training (~15% masked), best for understanding and embeddings, not free generation.
  • Decoder-only (GPT, Claude, LLaMA, Mistral, Gemini): causal mask, next-token objective, autoregressive generation with KV-caching; the dominant LLM design.
  • Encoder–decoder (Transformer, T5, BART, mT5, Marian): bidirectional encoder + causal decoder joined by cross-attention; span-corruption or paired-data training; translation and summarization.
  • All three repeat the same block: attention → Add & Norm → FFN → Add & Norm, N times.
Section 1.3

Training stages and why fine-tune

≈ 4 min · Slides: FT-I s12–19 · REV s5–6

1 · Pre-training2 · Fine-tuning3 · Safety / Alignment
Pre-training
  • Starts with zero knowledge of the world; doesn't understand word meaning
  • Task: next-token prediction (BERT: masked token, e.g. “what [MASK] you doing”)
  • Data: a giant unlabeled web corpus
  • Training: self-supervised
  • Result: learns language and knowledge
Fine-tuning
  • Take a pre-trained, general-purpose model and train some of its weights
  • General base model → specialized model for a particular use case
Safety / Alignment
  • Goal: outputs are safe and match human preference
  • How: further fine-tuning using a feedback mechanism on model outputs
  • Outcome: safer, less biased, aligned with human judgment

Why is fine-tuning necessary?

Domain expertise

Base models are generalists; they miss the jargon and conventions of medicine, law or finance.

Consistent behavior

Enforce a tone, output format or company policy that prompting alone can't guarantee.

Higher accuracy

A small fine-tuned model often beats a much larger general model on a narrow task.

Lower cost & latency

Shorter prompts and smaller specialized models cut inference cost and response time.

Domain specialists

ModelHow it was builtResult
BloombergGPT (finance)Trained on decades of financial documents, filings and news; specialized for sentiment analysis, entity recognition and financial Q&ADomain adaptation beat general models of similar size on finance tasks
Med-PaLM (Google)Base model PaLM (a general LLM), fine-tuned on medical Q&A datasets and clinician-written answersMed-PaLM 2 reached expert level, about 86% on USMLE-style questions

Base vs fine-tuned: two slide examples

Base model · “How to fine-tune a model?”

Continues with loosely related phrases: “control the complexity of a model · know when my model is done · test a model”.

Fine-tuned model · same query

Answers the task: choose a pre-trained model → prepare your new dataset → modify the top layers → train on new data → evaluate.

Base LLM · skin irritation, redness, itching

“Probably acne. Recommendation: visit cardiologist / dermatologist.”

LLM fine-tuned on dermatology data

“You have a mix of non-inflammatory and inflammatory acne. Recommendation: dermatologist.”

Crisp summary

  • Three stages: pre-training (self-supervised next-token on unlabeled web text) → fine-tuning (train some weights for a use case) → safety/alignment (feedback-driven tuning toward human preference).
  • Fine-tune for four reasons: domain expertise, consistent behavior/format, higher accuracy on narrow tasks, lower cost and latency.
  • Proof points: BloombergGPT (finance) and Med-PaLM 2 (≈86% on USMLE-style questions).
  • A fine-tuned model answers in the expected form and specialty; the base model rambles or stays generic.
Section 1.4

What fine-tuning actually updates

≈ 4 min · Slides: FT-I s20 · REV s4

Fine-tuning changes the trainable weight matrices inside each decoder block. The slide walks through multi-head self-attention with h = 2 heads.

Input : Per head: , : ; : Scaled dot-product attention per head → Concat heads → × () → :

The parameters a fine-tune can move are therefore in every layer, the feed-forward (MLP) weights, layer-norm parameters, the token/position embeddings and the LM head (linear + softmax over the vocabulary). Full fine-tuning moves all of them; PEFT (Module 3) freezes them and trains something small instead.

Crisp summary

  • Per head: ; attention = .
  • Shapes: : ; : ; concat of 2 heads is ; maps back to .
  • Trainable pieces: attention projections, FFN, layer norms, embeddings, LM head. Fine-tuning = changing some or all of these.
Section 1.5

Decision framework: prompt, RAG or fine-tune

≈ 4 min · Slides: FT-I s21–25 · REV s3

Three pathways to get things done with an LLM

Prompt engineering

Define what you want → write a clear prompt with context, instructions and examples → check the output against your goal → refine and iterate.

RAG

User query → search a vector DB built from your documents → top-k chunks → LLM → response.

Fine-tuning

Pre-trained LLM + domain-specific data → update weights → fine-tuned LLM.

The blueprint

PathwayBest forWhat you change
Prompt engineeringQuick prototyping, standard tasks, zero setupThe instructions, not the model or the data
RAGDynamic, massive or proprietary knowledge basesConnects the model to a database to fetch fresh facts before responding
Fine-tuningDeep customization, strict output formattingTeaches domain terminology at a foundational level (the weights)

Decision matrix

DimensionPrompt engineeringRAGFine-tuning
Primary goalDirecting behavior and task framingAccessing external / updated factsAdapting style, format and core behavior
External knowledgeVery low (limited by context window)Extremely highLow to medium
Style / format controlMediumLowExtremely high
Cost to set upMinimalMediumHigh (clean datasets + GPU time)
Latency impactLowMedium (adds a retrieval step)Very low (shorter prompts = faster inference)

When to choose what

ChooseWhenSlide example
Prompt engineeringYou are starting out, the task is fairly standard, and the model already knows how to do it“Summarize this email transcript into 5 bullet points.”
RAGData changes frequently or is private; a massive repository of information“Based on our Q3 internal HR policy updates, what is our maternity leave policy?”
Fine-tuningThe model must adapt to a new syntax or follow structured outputs“Translate the raw medical transcripts into structured ICD-10.”

Crisp summary

  • Prompting changes instructions; RAG changes the information the model sees; fine-tuning changes the weights.
  • Knowledge that is fresh, private or huge → RAG (external knowledge “extremely high”).
  • Strict style, format or new syntax (e.g. ICD-10 coding) → fine-tuning (format control “extremely high”, latency “very low”, setup cost high).
  • Standard task the model already knows → prompt engineering (minimal setup, low latency).
  • RAG adds medium latency because of the retrieval step.
Section 1.6

Fine-tuning approaches: the two axes

≈ 6 min · Slides: FT-I s26–38 · REV s7–11

Fine-tuning methods are classified along two independent axes (the slide notes this is not exhaustive):

By parameter-update strategy (what is trained)
  • Full fine-tuning
  • Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)
By task / style adaptation (what objective)
  • Unsupervised fine-tuning
  • Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
  • Safety / alignment fine-tuning

Unsupervised fine-tuning

Further training on raw, unlabeled domain text using the same self-supervised objective as pre-training (next-token or masked-token prediction). Same objective, new data; no annotations; the vocabulary, jargon, formats and facts of the domain get baked into the weights. Data is the cheapest to gather: internal wikis, filings, papers, tickets.

Slide example: building a medical LM

1 · Pretrained LM (Llama 2, Mistral, GPT-3.5)2 · Collect unlabeled medical text (papers, clinical notes, textbooks, forums)3 · Preprocess: clean, dedupe, tokenize, split4 · Self-supervised samples: context → next token (“Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disorder…”)5 · Continue training: next-token objective, AdamW, LR 2e-5, 1–3 epochs6 · Domain-adapted medical LM7 · Apps: chatbot, report summarization, clinical Q&A, literature search

Why no labels? The next word in the sentence itself is the target, so it is self-supervised. Optional next step: SFT / instruction tuning.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)

Learns from demonstrations: humans (or a stronger model) write the target outputs and the model imitates them token by token. SFT teaches behavior and format: instruction following, tone, structure (JSON, bullet lists) and task skills. Human-written demonstrations powered the SFT stage of InstructGPT. (Details in Section 1.7.)

Safety / alignment fine-tuning

  • Human feedback (RLHF): humans rank candidate answers; a reward model learns the ranking; PPO steers the policy toward it.
  • DPO: trains straight on (chosen, rejected) pairs, with no reward model.
  • Revision: the model critiques and revises its own outputs against written principles.

Full treatment in Module 4.

Full fine-tuning

Updates every parameter on the new data. Any recipe above (unsupervised, SFT, alignment) can be run as full fine-tuning: it describes what is trained, not the objective.

Maximum adaptation

All weights move, so it absorbs large domain shifts and deep behavior changes.

High cost

Adam training needs roughly 16 bytes of GPU memory per parameter, plus one full checkpoint per task.

Forgetting

Aggressive updates erase general skills (catastrophic forgetting, Module 2).

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)

Preserves most of the model's original weights. Three broad methods:

FamilyIdea
AdditiveAdd one or more trainable layers / a new set of parameters; only the new ones are changed
SelectiveSelect a subset of existing parameters to fine-tune
Re-parameterizationUse a new low-dimensional representation of the weight update and fine-tune that. Does not update all parameters, does not add separate physical adapter layers; uses low-dimensional matrix transformations during training. Prominent: LoRA and QLoRA

Full treatment in Module 3.

Crisp summary

  • Two axes: what is trained (full vs PEFT) and which objective (unsupervised, supervised, alignment).
  • Unsupervised FT = pre-training objective on unlabeled domain text; labels come free from the next token (medical example: AdamW, LR 2e-5, 1–3 epochs).
  • SFT = imitate demonstrations; teaches behavior and format (it powered InstructGPT's first stage).
  • Alignment FT = RLHF (rank → reward model → PPO), DPO (chosen/rejected pairs) or revision against written principles.
  • Full FT moves every weight: best adaptation, ~16 bytes/param with Adam, one checkpoint per task, risk of forgetting.
  • PEFT families: additive, selective, re-parameterization (LoRA, QLoRA).
Section 1.7

Supervised and instruction fine-tuning

≈ 7 min · Slides: FT-I s31, s39–50 · REV s10–14

Supervised fine-tuning

SFT takes a pretrained language model and teaches it a specific task by training on input–output pairs created by humans. Pre-training reads a huge portion of the internet and learns language patterns; SFT shows the model examples of correct answers and it learns to imitate them.

The analogy on the slide

You hire someone who already knows English well (they read millions of books during pre-training). For SFT you hand them a manual:

User asksCorrect response
“What are your business hours?”“We're open from 9 AM to 6 PM.”
“How do I reset my password?”“Click ‘Forgot Password’ on the login page.”

After thousands of examples they learn how you want them to answer.

The SFT loop

Pretrained modelTraining pair: input → correct outputPredict outputCompare with correct outputLoss (e.g. 0.234)Update weights (backprop + AdamW)Repeat: epochs 1…N, steps 1…millions

Slide example: medical SFT

  • Data: labeled instruction–response pairs, e.g. “What are common symptoms of diabetes?” → clinician answer; cleaned, put into one consistent template (### Instruction: … ### Response:), tokenized.
  • Training: next-token prediction with teacher forcing, cross-entropy against the labeled answer, AdamW, LR 1e-5 to 5e-5, 1–3 epochs, batch 8–32.
  • Evaluate on a held-out set with ROUGE, BLEU and AI-based evals.
  • Result: follows instructions, more accurate and safer, and ready for alignment (RLHF).

Instruction fine-tuning (IFT)

IFT is a specific type of SFT: the model is trained to follow natural-language instructions rather than to perform one fixed task. In SFT the model learns from input–output pairs; in IFT the input is explicitly written as an instruction and the model learns to execute it.

{ "instruction": "Translate the following sentence to French.",
  "input": "I love machine learning.",
  "output": "J'aime l'apprentissage automatique." }
{ "instruction": "Summarize the following article.",
  "input": "Large language models are pretrained on massive datasets...",
  "output": "LLMs are pretrained on large datasets before being specialized." }

Effect of IFT

PromptBefore IFTAfter IFT
Translate to French: Good morning“French is a Romance language spoken by millions of people…”“Bonjour”
Write a Python function to compute factorial.“Python is a programming language. A factorial is a mathematical function…”def factorial(n): return 1 if n <= 1 else n * factorial(n - 1)

IFT training pipeline

Instruction dataset (instruction, optional input, output)Prompt template: ### Instruction / ### Input / ### ResponseForward pass through the decoderPredicted tokens vs ground truthCross-entropy loss (on the response tokens)Backprop (AdamW) → update weightsRepeat for epochs → instruction-tuned LLM

SFT vs IFT

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)Instruction fine-tuning (IFT)
General training on labeled input–output pairsA specialized form of SFT using instruction–response pairs
May train on one task (e.g. sentiment classification)Trains on many tasks expressed as natural-language instructions
Input can be plain textInput includes an instruction (often with extra context)
Goal: improve task performanceGoal: improve instruction-following behavior

Crisp summary

  • SFT = training on human-made input → output pairs so the model imitates correct answers (loop: predict → compare → loss → AdamW update → repeat).
  • Typical SFT settings on the slide: teacher forcing, cross-entropy, AdamW, LR 1e-5–5e-5, 1–3 epochs, batch 8–32; evaluate with ROUGE/BLEU/AI evals.
  • IFT is SFT where the input is an explicit instruction; data = {instruction, input, output}; template ### Instruction / ### Input / ### Response.
  • Before IFT a base model continues text (“French is a Romance language…”); after IFT it executes the instruction (“Bonjour”).
  • SFT targets task performance (can be one task); IFT targets instruction-following across many tasks.
Section 1.8

Multi-task fine-tuning

≈ 4 min · Slides: FT-I s51–54 · REV s15–16

Multi-task fine-tuning fine-tunes a single model on multiple related tasks simultaneously instead of one task at a time.

  • Start from a pretrained model (e.g. BERT, T5, Llama).
  • The training set mixes examples from several tasks.
  • The model learns a shared representation while optimizing each task's objective.
InputTaskOutput
“I love this movie.”SentimentPositive
“Who discovered gravity?”QAIsaac Newton
Long articleSummarizationShort summary
“Google is in California.”NERGoogle (Organization), California (Location)

Instead of fine-tuning four separate models, you fine-tune one model on data from all four tasks.

Architecture: shared body, task-specific heads

An optional pretrained encoder (e.g. BERT) feeds an autoregressive decoder (masked multi-head self-attention, cross-attention, FFN; ×L) with a shared token embedding. On top sit task heads:

QA generative head

Linear → layer norm → vocabulary projection → softmax.

Classification head

Pooling → linear → ReLU → linear → softmax over C classes (e.g. “Technology” 0.78).

Summarization generative head

Generates the summary token by token.

MCQ head

Question and option representations → similarity scores → softmax over 4 options → predicted answer “C (Paris)”, p = 0.68.

Training several tasks sequentially instead of jointly leads to catastrophic forgetting; Module 3 shows how PEFT adapters solve this.

Crisp summary

  • One model, many tasks at once (sentiment, QA, summarization, NER), learning a shared representation.
  • Architecture: shared transformer body + separate heads (generative QA, classification with pooling + softmax over C classes, summarization, MCQ with softmax over options).
  • Replaces several single-task models with one; sequential multi-task training risks forgetting.
Section 1.9

Curriculum fine-tuning

≈ 5 min · Slides: FT-I s55–60

Curriculum learning presents training examples in a meaningful order, typically easy → hard, instead of uniformly at random.

Easy: short, commonMedium: longer, mixedHard: rare, complex
  • Inspired by human education: arithmetic before calculus.
  • Shapes the loss landscape: early easy examples guide optimization toward smoother regions before harder ones arrive.
  • Two core ingredients: a difficulty measure (what is “hard”?) and a schedule (when is it introduced?). Data difficulty follows model competence.

Why curriculum for LLMs?

Faster convergence

Easy examples give clean gradients early, so target loss is reached in fewer steps and less compute.

More stable training

Fewer loss spikes and divergences: noisy, hard or out-of-distribution samples arrive only once the model can absorb them.

Better generalization

Easy-to-hard ordering acts like a continuation method, steering optimization toward flatter minima that transfer better.

Data & compute efficiency

Good ordering squeezes more from limited fine-tuning data, critical when instruction data is scarce or expensive.

Pipeline

1 · Pool data: instructions, code, domain corpora2 · Score difficulty: length, loss, perplexity, labels3 · Order / bucket: easy → hard stages or a continuous ranking4 · Scheduled training: phases, expanding the pool as competence grows5 · Evaluate & adapt: track validation loss per stage; re-pace or re-score if progress stalls

Feedback loop: evaluation results update difficulty scores and pacing.

Three key design decisions

DecisionQuestionOptions
Difficulty measureHow do we quantify “hard”?Static heuristics (length, rarity, depth) · model-based (loss, perplexity, margin) · external (human labels, grade level)
Schedule (pacing)When does harder data arrive?Stage boundaries fixed vs adaptive · pacing function linear, root or exponential · trigger by step count or a competence signal
Data mixingWhat does each phase contain?Cumulative (keep easy data) · replacement (swap stages entirely) · replay easy samples to avoid forgetting

Scheduling strategies

StrategyHow it worksTrade-off
Baby StepsTrain on the easiest bucket, then add the next bucket while keeping earlier dataCumulative, robust to forgetting
One-Pass (staged)Train on each bucket once, in order, discarding previous stagesCheap, but risks catastrophic forgetting
Self-Paced LearningThe model picks its own curriculum: samples with loss below a rising threshold are included“Easy” is defined by the learner
Competence-BasedA pacing function grows over time; each step samples from the easiest fraction of dataSmooth, tunable pacing
Anti-curriculum / hard-firstStart with hard examplesOccasionally useful for robust features, or when easy data dominates and adds little signal

Crisp summary

  • Curriculum = ordered training (easy → hard) instead of random order; needs a difficulty measure and a pacing schedule.
  • Benefits: faster convergence, stability (fewer spikes), better generalization (flatter minima), data/compute efficiency.
  • Pipeline: pool → score difficulty → bucket → scheduled training → evaluate and re-pace (feedback loop).
  • Difficulty can be static (length, rarity), model-based (loss, perplexity, margin) or external (human labels, grade level).
  • Strategies: Baby Steps (cumulative), One-Pass (discard, forgetting risk), Self-Paced (loss threshold), Competence-Based (pacing c(t)), Anti-curriculum (hard first).
Section 1.10

Making full fine-tuning efficient

≈ 4 min · Slides: FT-I s61–68 · REV s17

Why full fine-tuning is expensive

Every parameter is updated. InstructGPT has 175 billion parameters; storing and updating them needs a lot of GPU memory, a lot of compute and therefore a lot of money. A slide fact: GPT-4 training used roughly 25,000 A100 GPUs for months at a cost of around US $100 million.

Memory for full-parameter instruction tuning of a 10B model

ItemPrecisionMemory (10B params)
ParametersFP16 (2 bytes each)20 GB
GradientsFP1620 GB
Adam optimizer states (momentum, variance, plus FP32 master weights)FP32120 GB
Total160 GB ≈ 16 bytes / parameter

160 GB does not fit on one card: the slide's answer is a “7 GPU pack” of 24 GB GPUs (7 × 24 = 168 GB). The ultimate reality: full fine-tuning is very expensive in both time and memory, but adaptation to the new task is better.

The PEFT lecture (Module 3) gives a second version of this sum for a 7B model: 14 GB weights + 14 GB gradients + 28 GB Adam momentum + 28 GB Adam variance + 8 GB activations ≈ 92 GB. Same idea, different accounting (no FP32 master copy, activations included).

Three heuristics to make full fine-tuning cheaper

One layer at a time

Fine-tune all layers, but only one layer is trainable at any moment (e.g. decoder 1…6 above the embedding), so gradients and optimizer state exist for one layer at a time.

Block-wise

Instead of individual layers, train contiguous blocks of layers (e.g. decoders 1–2, then 3–4, then 5–6).

Progressive layer-wise

Rather than training all selected layers from the start, progressively unfreeze deeper layers as training goes on.

Crisp summary

  • Full FT of a 10B model in FP16 with Adam: 20 GB weights + 20 GB grads + 120 GB optimizer states = 160 GB (~16 bytes/param) → seven 24 GB GPUs.
  • Scale of the problem: InstructGPT 175B parameters; GPT-4 training ≈ 25,000 A100s for months, ≈ $100M.
  • Full FT is expensive in time and memory but adapts best.
  • Cheaper variants: one layer at a time, block-wise (contiguous blocks), progressive layer-wise unfreezing.

Section 2.1

How LLMs learn: the training loop

≈ 8 min · Slides: FT-II s4–13

Training is one loop executed millions of times. Each pass over one mini-batch nudges every parameter slightly downhill on the loss.

1 · Raw text (corpus)2 · Tokenize: text → IDs3 · Mini-batch of B sequences4 · Forward pass: predictions5 · Loss: cross-entropy6 · Backward: gradients7 · Update: θ ← θ − η·g, then the next mini-batch

Tokenization: text becomes numbers

“The cat sat on” → sub-word tokens [The, _cat, _sat, _on] → vocabulary IDs [464, 3797, 7891, 319]. Vocabularies hold about 50k–250k entries. Training sees long ID sequences packed into fixed-length windows of T tokens (the context length).

Mini-batches

The shuffled training set is sliced into batches; each batch is a GPU tensor of shape [B × T] (e.g. 32 sequences × 2,048 tokens), all processed in parallel. Averaging over B examples gives a gradient that is less noisy than one example and far cheaper than the whole dataset.

Full-batch

Exact gradient, but one step needs the entire dataset: impossibly slow.

Stochastic (B = 1)

Cheap steps, but the gradient is wildly noisy.

Mini-batch ✓

The sweet spot: a stable averaged gradient plus full GPU parallelism.

Predict the next token at every position

Token IDs [B×T]Embedding: IDs → vectorsTransformer × L (attention + MLP)LM head (linear)Logits [B×T×V]

V is the vocabulary size. The targets are the same tokens shifted by one: input “The cat sat” → targets “cat sat on”.

Softmax: logits → probabilities

Candidatematrugdogtherun
Logit z2.11.30.4−0.5−1.2
Probability0.400.230.100.050.03

The true next token is “mat”. The five values shown are the top of a distribution over the whole vocabulary.

Cross-entropy: score every prediction, then average

Per-token loss ; the batch loss is the mean over all B×T positions.

ContextTrue next tokenp assigned−log p
“The”cat0.620.48
“The cat”sat0.311.17
“The cat sat”on0.400.92
Batch loss L(0.48 + 1.17 + 0.92) / 3 = 0.86

This single scalar L is what gradient descent minimizes. Lower loss ⇔ the model assigns higher probability to the actual text.

Backpropagation and the update

Gradients flow right to left: loss → LM head () → every transformer layer () → embedding (). Each gradient answers: if I nudge this weight up, does the batch loss go up or down, and how fast?

  • η, the learning rate: too large diverges, too small crawls; typically ~1e-4 with warmup + decay.
  • Adaptive SGD in practice: plain SGD is rarely used for LLMs. Adam rescales each parameter's step using running averages of its gradients.
  • The loss surface has many local minima and one global minimum; the annotated slide stresses that the initial point matters (fine-tuning starts from the pretrained weights).

Watching the loss fall

StepOne mini-batch → one parameter update
EpochOne full pass over the training set (frontier LLMs often train for ~1 epoch on huge corpora)
When to stopWhen loss on held-out validation data flattens; training further risks memorizing

The wiggle in the loss curve is not a bug: each mini-batch is a random sample, so its loss is a noisy estimate of the true loss around a smooth downward trend.

Crisp summary

  • Loop: tokenize → mini-batch [B×T] → forward → cross-entropy → backward → θ ← θ − η·∂L/∂θ → repeat millions of times.
  • Vocabularies are ~50k–250k tokens; sequences are packed into context windows of T tokens; logits have shape [B×T×V]; targets are inputs shifted by one.
  • Mini-batches beat full-batch (too slow) and B = 1 (too noisy).
  • Softmax turns logits into probabilities; per-token loss is −log p(true token); worked batch loss = 0.86.
  • LR ~1e-4 with warmup + decay; Adam (adaptive per-parameter steps) instead of plain SGD.
  • Step = one update; epoch = one pass; stop when validation loss flattens. Noisy per-batch loss is normal.
Section 2.2

Training instability and how to tame it

≈ 8 min · Slides: FT-II s14–21

Why fine-tuning becomes unstable

One oversized update damages the weights, which produces worse predictions, larger losses and even bigger gradients on the next step: a feedback loop.

Sharp loss landscapes

Pretrained optima sit in narrow valleys; a big step overshoots the walls.

Low-precision arithmetic

fp16 overflows above ~65,504: one large activation becomes Inf and poisons the gradient.

Heterogeneous batches

One outlier batch (extreme length, corrupted text, unusual tokens) can produce a gradient 10–100× the typical norm.

Scale amplifies everything

Deeper networks multiply perturbations layer by layer (the update is a product of many factors).

Three symptoms

SymptomWhat you seeWhat is happening
Loss spikeSudden jumps with slow recovery (in the slide's run, ~1.6 → 3.8 at 35% of training and ~1.2 → 2.9 at 65%)One batch produced an outsized gradient and knocked the weights off the low-loss valley. Later steps repair the damage, but each spike wastes hundreds of steps. Spikes cluster where LR is highest, just after warmup
Gradient explosionGradient norm stable (~1–2), then exponential runaway (to ~95)The feedback loop: bad update → worse loss → bigger gradient → worse update. Norms grow exponentially over tens of steps; this is the phase before the loss visibly diverges. In fp16 it ends in overflow: Inf, then NaN
DivergenceLoss falls normally, then climbs without recovery (~1.5 → ~19.5)The terminal state: the weights have left every good region and updates no longer point downhill. Unlike a spike there is no self-repair (or loss flatlines at random-guess level). Outputs degenerate into gibberish, repetition or empty strings

Mitigation 1: gradient clipping

Clipping rescales any gradient whose norm exceeds a cap c. The direction is preserved and the magnitude is bounded, so outlier batches can't knock the model off course.

# manual training loop
loss.backward()
torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
optimizer.step()

# Hugging Face Trainer: one argument
TrainingArguments(max_grad_norm=1.0)   # the default, keep it
  • 1.0 is the standard cap for LLM fine-tuning. In the slide's comparison, the same run without clipping spiked twice and diverged late; clipped at 1.0 it stayed smooth to ~1.05.
  • Log the pre-clip norm. If more than 20% of steps clip, the learning rate is too high. Clipping is a seatbelt, not a steering wheel.

Mitigation 2: learning-rate scheduling

A constant LR (e.g. 2e-5 throughout) is risky. Warm up to the peak (~10% of the run in the chart), then decay with a cosine or linear curve to ~0.

TrainingArguments(learning_rate=2e-5, lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
                  warmup_ratio=0.03, num_train_epochs=2)
# cosine: smooth decay to ~0 at run end · linear: same idea, straight line
# constant: only for short LoRA runs

Example: the late-run spike

A legal-domain SFT at a constant 2e-5 spiked repeatedly in the last 20% of training. Switching to cosine with the identical peak LR removed every late spike and improved final validation loss by 4%.

A stability checklist that compounds

LayerSettingWhat it prevents
Clippingmax_grad_norm=1.0Loss spikes; starves the explosion loop
Schedulelr_scheduler_type="cosine"Late-run spikes as the valley narrows
Warmupwarmup_ratio=0.03Step-zero spikes and instant divergence
Precisionbf16=True (not fp16)Overflow → Inf/NaN cascade
Peak LR1e-5 – 2e-5 full FT; 1e-4 – 2e-4 LoRAOvershooting sharp valley walls
MonitoringLog grad-norm; alert at 5–10× the medianCatching explosion before divergence
CheckpointsSave every N steps; keep the last 3Losing the run when divergence strikes

Crisp summary

  • Instability is a feedback loop: oversized update → worse loss → bigger gradient → worse update.
  • Causes: sharp valleys, fp16 overflow (> ~65,504 → Inf), outlier batches (10–100× gradient norm), depth amplifying perturbations.
  • Symptoms: loss spike (recovers, wastes steps, clusters after warmup) → gradient explosion (norm grows exponentially, precedes divergence) → divergence (no recovery, gibberish output).
  • Gradient clipping at max_grad_norm = 1.0 keeps direction, bounds magnitude; >20% of steps clipping means the LR is too high.
  • Use warmup + cosine instead of a constant LR (legal SFT example: late spikes gone, val loss −4%).
  • Checklist: clip 1.0 · cosine · warmup 3% · bf16 not fp16 · peak LR 1e-5–2e-5 (full) / 1e-4–2e-4 (LoRA) · alert at 5–10× median grad-norm · keep last 3 checkpoints.
Section 2.3

Catastrophic forgetting

≈ 10 min · Slides: FT-II s22–31

When a pretrained LLM is fine-tuned on a narrow task, gradient updates overwrite the weights that encode its broad, general-purpose knowledge. The model gets better at the new task and quietly worse at almost everything else.

The classic failure

Base LLM with broad skills (math, code, languages, facts) → full fine-tune on medical Q&A only → a specialist that is great at medical Q&A but forgot how to write Python, follow instructions, speak French and do arithmetic.

  • Skill regression: reasoning, coding, multilinguality and instruction-following degrade after domain fine-tuning.
  • Silent failure: task metrics improve while general benchmarks collapse, invisible unless you measure both.
  • Worst in full fine-tuning: updating all weights at a high LR on narrow data erases prior knowledge fastest.

Why fine-tuning erases knowledge

Shared, distributed weights

Knowledge is superimposed across the same parameters.

Narrow gradient signal

Fine-tuning data covers a tiny slice of the pretraining distribution.

Weight drift from the initial model

The further parameters move from the pretrained optimum, the more prior-task loss rises.

No replay, no anchor

Vanilla AdamW has no memory of old tasks unless you re-expose old data or penalize drift.

Measure it: benchmarks before vs after

Benchmark (7B model, full FT, 3 epochs on legal contracts)BeforeAfter
Legal task (target)4188
GSM8K (math)6239
HumanEval (code)4830
MMLU6455
IFEval (instruction following)7147

Illustrative accuracy (%). Rule: always run a fixed general eval suite (“canary evals”) before and after every fine-tune.

Five mitigations

1. Rehearsal: mix in general data

Interleave 1–10% general instruction / pretraining-style data into every batch so gradients keep defending old skills; the optimizer can no longer trade general ability for task gains for free.

train_ds = interleave_datasets([domain, general],     # general = OpenHermes-2.5
                               probabilities=[0.95, 0.05], seed=42,
                               stopping_strategy="all_exhausted")

Replay whatever you most fear losing: diverse instructions, code, math, multilingual samples. Cost: slightly slower target-task convergence, and you need access to (or a proxy of) general data.

2. Regularize toward the pretrained weights

Add a penalty for drifting from initialization. L2-SP pulls every weight back uniformly: penalty , one hyperparameter λ. EWC (Elastic Weight Consolidation) weights the penalty by Fisher information , so parameters important to old tasks are held tighter:

Trade-off: λ too high → underfits the new task; λ too low → forgets. Tune λ against the canary evals.

3. Conservative hyperparameters (the cheapest fix)

Make the update small; most forgetting horror stories are just aggressive schedules.

TrainingArguments(learning_rate=1e-5,          # not 1e-4
                  num_train_epochs=1,          # not 5
                  warmup_ratio=0.03, lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
                  per_device_train_batch_size=8, gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
                  eval_strategy="steps", eval_steps=200,   # canary suite
                  load_best_model_at_end=True)
  • LR 1e-5 – 2e-5 for full FT: LR is the single biggest lever on drift.
  • 1–2 epochs is usually enough; loss keeps falling long after generalization stops improving, so train less than feels safe.
  • Warmup + cosine; early-stop on canary evals, not on training loss.

4. Weight averaging (WiSE-FT / merging)

Fine-tune freely, then interpolate the result with the original weights to recover generality after the fact:

α = 0 is the base model, α = 1 the fine-tuned one (the code example uses α = 0.6). It works because the base and fine-tuned models sit in a connected low-loss region, so the interpolation keeps most of both behaviors. Choose α by sweeping 0.3…0.9 and picking the knee of the target-vs-general trade-off; no retraining per point.

5. Freeze layers, tune selectively

Freeze the embeddings and lower blocks (where broad linguistic and world knowledge concentrates) and tune only the top N blocks or task-closest modules. Example: a 32-layer model with the top 8 blocks (24–31) trainable ≈ 25% of weights. Rules of thumb: tuning the top 25–50% of blocks captures most task gains; freezing the embeddings and LM head is a cheap stability win.

Choosing your mitigation stack

StrategyAttacks causeExtra costWhen to reach for it
Conservative hyperparametersWeight driftNoneAlways: the default baseline
Rehearsal / data mixingNarrow gradientsData curationYou have (proxy) general data
L2-SP / EWCWeight driftMemory for θ₀ (+ Fisher)Full FT required, no general data available
Weight averaging (WiSE-FT)Lost directionsOne merge passModel already fine-tuned and degraded
Layer freezingUpdate sizeNoneTight compute or very small datasets

Crisp summary

  • Catastrophic forgetting: narrow fine-tuning overwrites general knowledge; it is silent unless you track general benchmarks (legal FT example: target 41→88 while GSM8K 62→39, IFEval 71→47).
  • Causes: shared distributed weights, narrow gradient signal, drift from θ₀, no replay/anchor in AdamW.
  • Rehearsal: 1–10% general data in every batch (95/5 interleave).
  • L2-SP: uniform ‖θ−θ₀‖² pull; EWC: Fisher-weighted pull; λ trades underfitting vs forgetting.
  • Conservative settings first: LR 1e-5–2e-5, 1–2 epochs, cosine + warmup, early-stop on canary evals.
  • WiSE-FT: θ = (1−α)θ_base + αθ_ft, sweep α 0.3–0.9, works because both sit in one connected low-loss region.
  • Freeze embeddings + lower blocks; tuning the top 25–50% captures most gains.
Section 2.4

Learning-rate scheduling

≈ 8 min · Slides: FT-II s32–45

No single learning rate is right for the whole run

Constant, too high

Learns fast early but bounces around the minimum forever: a noisy, spike-prone plateau.

Constant, too low

Perfectly stable but still far from converged when the budget runs out (val loss ~2.0 vs ~1.05).

Scheduled (warmup + decay)

Big steps early, small steps later: the best validation loss.

The annotated slide sketches the update on a valley: small η = slow, steady descent; large η = overshoot, bouncing across the valley walls; very large η = jumps out of the basin (diverges).

Training has phases, and the LR should track them

PhaseStepsWhat happensLR job
1 · Fragile start0 – ~3%A new data distribution shocks the pretrained weights; full-size steps cause instant spikesRamp up from zero (warmup)
2 · Rapid learning~3% – ~60%Gradients are large, consistent and informative; most of the task is learned hereEarns the peak LR
3 · Convergence~60% – 100%The model sits in a narrowing valley; safe step size shrinksDecay

Four numbers define any schedule

Warmup length

How long LR ramps 0 → peak. Default 3% of steps; raise to 5–10% for short or unstable runs.

Peak LR

The single most important fine-tuning hyperparameter: 1e-5–2e-5 full FT, 1e-4–2e-4 LoRA.

Decay shape

The path down from the peak: linear, cosine, steps or restarts.

Floor (min LR)

Where decay ends: 0, or ~10% of peak to keep learning alive for continual training.

The schedule shapes

Warmup (linear ramp for the first steps):

Linear decay (straight line to zero at the final step):

Cosine decay (t = current decay step, T = total decay steps):

ShapeBehaviorHF / PyTorch setting on the slideUse
Constant (± warmup)One LR for the whole run; no decay means full-size steps even at convergenceconstant_with_warmup, lr 1e-4, warmup_ratio 0.03; plain constant skips warmupShort runs only; spike-prone in long ones
LinearAfter warmup, straight line to zero at the last steplinear, lr 2e-5, warmup 0.03, 2 epochsThe no-surprises default
CosineHalf-cosine: lingers near the peak early (more time at productive step sizes), glides gently into the floorcosine, lr 2e-5, warmup 0.03; cosine_with_min_lr adds a floorThe modern default for LLM pre-training and fine-tuning
Step decayA staircase: flat, then drop by a factor (e.g. ×0.5) at milestonesMultiStepLR(milestones=[2000, 3500], gamma=0.5); reactive ReduceLROnPlateau(factor=0.5, patience=3)Inherited from computer vision; modern LLM form is reactive: drop when val loss plateaus
Cosine with restarts (cyclical)Cosine decay that periodically snaps back to the peak; each restart kicks the model out of its basincosine_with_restarts, lr 2e-5, warmup 0.02, lr_scheduler_kwargs={"num_cycles": 3}A cheap way to explore several solutions (multi-solution runs)
Warmup–Stable–Decay (WSD)A trapezoid: warm up, hold the peak for most of the run, decay sharply in the final ~10–20%warmup_stable_decay, lr 2e-5, warmup 0.03, {"num_decay_steps": 500}Open-ended budgets

Match the schedule to the run

Your situationScheduleWhy
Standard SFT, known lengthCosine (or linear) + 3% warmupBest default; the tail stabilizes convergence
Run length unknown / continual trainingWSDDecay on demand from any point in the stable phase
Data arrives in waves; validation-driven controlStep decay (ReduceLROnPlateau)Drops react to plateaus instead of the calendar
Want several candidate models in one budgetCosine with restartsEach cycle yields a checkpoint at an LR minimum
Instability at any pointLengthen warmup, then lower the peakShape tweaks beat shape swaps for stability

Crisp summary

  • You need big steps early and small steps late: constant-high is noisy, constant-low never converges, warmup + decay wins.
  • Phases: fragile start (0–3%, warm up), rapid learning (3–60%, peak LR), convergence (60–100%, decay).
  • Four knobs: warmup (default 3%, 5–10% if unstable), peak LR (most important: 1e-5–2e-5 full, 1e-4–2e-4 LoRA), decay shape, floor (0 or ~10% of peak).
  • Formulas: warmup η_max·t/T_w; linear to zero; cosine η_min + ½(η_max−η_min)(1+cos(πt/T)).
  • Shapes: constant (short runs), linear (no-surprises), cosine (modern default), step decay (val-driven, ReduceLROnPlateau), cosine restarts (several candidates), WSD (unknown length, decay in last 10–20%).
  • For instability: lengthen warmup first, then lower the peak.
Section 2.5

Choosing the batch size

≈ 5 min · Slides: FT-II s46–53

Four factors drive the choice: GPU memory, training stability, throughput and generalization. Goal: maximize hardware utilization while keeping good convergence.

Effective batch size

  • Micro-batch size (per GPU): samples processed in one forward/backward pass.
  • Gradient accumulation steps: micro-batches whose gradients are summed before one optimizer update.
  • Number of GPUs: each GPU's gradients are combined.

Step-by-step strategy

1 · Decide the maximum sequence length2 · Raise the micro-batch until GPU memory is nearly full3 · Use gradient accumulation to reach the desired effective batch

Trade-off

Smaller batch

+ better generalization, more frequent updates
− noisy gradients, slower convergence

Larger batch

+ stable gradients, faster throughput, better GPU utilization
− can reduce generalization, fewer optimizer updates, may need a higher LR

Batch size and learning rate: the linear scaling rule

Increasing the batch usually requires increasing the LR. If the effective batch doubles, the LR roughly doubles: 32 → 2e-5; 64 → 4e-5.

Practical recommendations

GPU memoryMicro-batchGradient accumulationEffective batch
24 GB1–48–3216–64
40 GB4–84–1632–128
80 GB8–321–864–256

Let the loss curves judge your batch size

DiagnosisCurveAction
Batch is fineTraining loss falls smoothly; curve noise shrinks over timeKeep it
Batch too smallPersistent jitter that never shrinks (or the LR is too high): noisy gradientsRaise the effective batch: increase gradient_accumulation_steps (or lower the LR) until the trend, not the noise, dominates
Batch too largeTrain and val losses both plateau high; dataset ÷ batch left only a handful of updates (~8 in the example), so the model underfitsShrink the effective batch until the run gets ≥ 500–1,000 optimizer steps

Crisp summary

  • Effective batch = micro-batch × gradient-accumulation steps × GPUs (2 × 16 × 4 = 128).
  • Recipe: fix max sequence length → fill GPU memory with micro-batch → reach the target with gradient accumulation.
  • Small batch: generalizes better, noisy, slower. Large batch: stable and fast, fewer updates, may need higher LR and generalize worse.
  • Linear scaling rule: double the batch → roughly double the LR (32 → 2e-5, 64 → 4e-5).
  • Guide: 24 GB → eff. 16–64; 40 GB → 32–128; 80 GB → 64–256.
  • Jitter that never shrinks → batch too small; both losses plateau high with few steps → batch too large (aim ≥ 500–1,000 optimizer steps).
Section 2.6

Data quality problems

≈ 4 min · Slides: FT-II s54–60

Five data challenges that quietly break models

#ChallengeIncludes
1Data quality issuesNoisy data, incorrect labels, duplicates, inconsistent formatting, outdated information
2Insufficient training dataSmall datasets, limited edge-case coverage, lack of diversity
3Imbalanced datasetsSkewed class distributions and the accuracy paradox
4Data splittingTrain / validation / test design and avoiding leakage
5Domain & distribution shiftWhen production data stops looking like training data

This section covers challenge 1; the next two cover 2–5.

Noisy data

Raw Common Crawl is mostly not clean prose.

  • Boilerplate & artifacts: menus, cookie banners, ads, broken HTML
  • SEO spam & machine text: keyword stuffing, content farms
  • OCR errors: character garbage, broken hyphenation in scanned books
  • Gibberish & lists: code fragments, lorem ipsum, word salad
  • AI-generated slop: LLM output on the web risks degenerative feedback loops
Incorrect “labels”
  • Wrong content learned as truth: misinformation, conspiracy sites, confidently wrong forum answers
  • Buggy code from Q&A sites teaching broken patterns
  • Language-ID errors: audits found some low-resource “languages” were mostly wrong-language or unusable text
  • Mislabeled quality scores: noisy classifiers silently decide what enters the corpus
Duplicate samples

Duplication wastes compute, amplifies memorization and contaminates evaluations.

  • Crawl redundancy: the same article syndicated, mirrored, re-crawled thousands of times
  • Verbatim memorization: duplicated passages get regurgitated word for word (privacy and copyright risk)
  • Templated near-duplicates: product pages and licences differing by a few tokens
  • Benchmark contamination: MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval inside the crawl inflate reported scores
Inconsistent formatting

The same content arrives as HTML, Markdown, LaTeX, PDF text and plain text.

  • Lost structure: tables, math, code flattened by naive extraction
  • Encoding chaos: mixed Unicode forms, control characters
  • Whitespace & line breaks: PDF extraction splits sentences mid-line
  • Math & code variance: LaTeX vs MathML vs Unicode; mixed indentation
  • Tokenizer interactions: inconsistent digit grouping and punctuation inflate token counts and hurt arithmetic
Outdated information
  • Training cutoff: names a former officeholder as current, misses recent events
  • Deprecated APIs: suggests library versions and functions that no longer exist
  • Stale web pages: old prices, policies, superseded science
  • Conflicting snapshots: many crawl versions of one page teach contradictory “facts”

Crisp summary

  • Five challenges: quality, insufficient data, imbalance, splitting/leakage, distribution shift.
  • Noise: boilerplate, SEO spam, OCR errors, gibberish, AI-generated slop (feedback-loop risk).
  • Wrong labels: misinformation, buggy code, language-ID errors, noisy quality classifiers.
  • Duplicates: waste compute, cause verbatim memorization (privacy/copyright), and benchmark contamination inflates scores.
  • Formatting chaos (HTML/LaTeX/PDF, Unicode, digit grouping) and outdated facts (cutoff, deprecated APIs, conflicting snapshots) also degrade learning.
Section 2.7

Too little data, edge cases, diversity and imbalance

≈ 5 min · Slides: FT-II s61–64

Small datasets

Too few labeled samples to estimate parameters reliably: high variance and easy overfitting.

What it looks like
  • Medical: a rare-disease study with ~200 labeled scans for a deep model
  • Low-resource NLP: little digitized, annotated text
  • New products: weeks of user data trying to personalize
  • Costly labels: an expert hour per label (radiology, legal review)
Mitigations
  • Transfer learning (fine-tune pretrained models): the dominant strategy today
  • Data augmentation: rotations/crops; back-translation and paraphrasing for text
  • Synthetic data: simulation or generative models (validate carefully)
  • Right-sized models with strong regularization; cross-validation rather than a single split
  • Few-shot / zero-shot with foundation models

Limited coverage of edge cases

The long tail of rare but important scenarios is missing, so the model fails exactly where failure matters most.

What it looks like
  • Autonomous driving trained in clear daylight struggles with snow, glare, unusual obstacles
  • Fraud & abuse: novel attack patterns absent from history
  • Chatbots: ambiguous, adversarial or out-of-scope queries
  • Manufacturing QC: defects that occur once per 100k units
Mitigations
  • Targeted collection for known gaps (not more of the same)
  • Simulation of rare scenarios (standard in autonomous-vehicle programs)
  • Active learning: mine production traffic for high-uncertainty samples and label those first

Lack of diversity

Data over-represents a narrow slice of the population, so the model works well for some groups and poorly for others.

What it looks like
  • Speech recognition worse on regional and non-native accents
  • Clinical risk scores trained on one demographic transfer poorly
  • Geography bias: vision models trained on Western imagery misread objects from other regions
Mitigations
  • Stratified sourcing with explicit coverage targets (demographics, devices, conditions)
  • Disaggregated evaluation: metrics per subgroup, not one global average
  • Bias audits; document data in datasheets / model cards
  • Diverse annotation teams

Imbalanced datasets

99.8%of credit-card transactions are legitimate
0.2%are fraud: the class you actually care about
99.8%accuracy for a model that never flags fraud, and catches none

One class vastly outnumbers the others, so a model can look accurate while never detecting the class you care about. The accuracy paradox: predicting “never fraud” scores 99.8% accuracy and catches zero fraud. Similar skews: disease screening (~1:1000), defect detection, churn.

  • Use the right metrics: precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC; never plain accuracy on skewed data.
  • Resampling: oversample the minority (SMOTE and variants) or undersample the majority.
  • Cost-sensitive learning: class weights or focal loss make minority errors expensive.

Crisp summary

  • Small data → high variance/overfitting; transfer learning is the dominant fix, plus augmentation, validated synthetic data, regularized right-sized models, cross-validation, few/zero-shot.
  • Edge cases (snow for self-driving, novel fraud, 1-in-100k defects) → targeted collection, simulation, active learning on uncertain production samples.
  • Low diversity (accents, demographics, geography) → stratified sourcing, per-subgroup metrics, bias audits, diverse annotators.
  • Imbalance (fraud 0.2%) → accuracy paradox; use precision/recall/F1/PR-AUC, SMOTE or undersampling, class weights or focal loss.
Section 2.8

Data splitting and distribution shift

≈ 5 min · Slides: FT-II s65–66

Splitting for training and testing

How you split decides whether your reported performance is an honest estimate of real-world performance.

TRAIN 70% · fit model parametersVALID 15% · tune hyper-parametersTEST 15% · touch once, at the end
Common pitfalls (leakage)
  • Preprocessing before splitting: scaling or imputing on the full dataset leaks test statistics into training
  • Duplicates across splits inflate scores
  • Random splits of time series: the model “sees the future” and collapses in production
  • Grouped data split randomly: the same patient / user / device in both train and test
Best practices
  • Split first; fit transforms on train only, then apply them to validation and test
  • Stratify to preserve class proportions (vital when imbalanced)
  • Time-based splits: train on the past, test on the future
  • Group-aware splits: each patient / user entirely in one split
  • k-fold cross-validation for small data; keep the test set sacred and use it once

Domain and distribution shift

The model is trained on scraped documents but deployed on live conversations, tools and a moving world.

ShiftChangeExample
Usage shiftDocuments → dialogue: web pages at training time; instructions, chats and agent loops at deploymentBase vs chat: a raw pretrained model continues your text instead of answering; the training task isn't the deployment task
Temporal shiftThe world moves on: new events, new APIs, even LLM-influenced writing styles after the cutoffCode drift: assistants suggest APIs from old library versions common in the crawl
Domain shiftGeneral → specialist: web-trained models deployed on clinical notes, contracts, proprietary codeEnterprise gap: weak on internal jargon, formats and private-domain text

Mitigation strategies

  • Post-training alignment: instruction tuning + RLHF bridge the document → dialogue gap (now standard).
  • Mid-training / annealing: shift the late-training mixture toward deployment-like data (chat, code, math).
  • Continual and domain-adaptive pre-training: refresh on recent and in-domain corpora, with replay.
  • Retrieval & tools: ground answers in current, in-domain sources at inference.
  • Monitor in production: track quality on live traffic; refresh models when drift shows.

Crisp summary

  • Split 70/15/15: train fits parameters, validation tunes hyper-parameters, test is touched once.
  • Leakage traps: preprocessing before the split, duplicates across splits, random splits of time series, the same patient/user in train and test.
  • Fixes: split first, stratify, time-based and group-aware splits, k-fold CV for small data.
  • Shifts: usage (documents → dialogue; base models continue text), temporal (cutoff, code drift), domain (general → specialist, enterprise gap).
  • Mitigate with alignment (IT + RLHF), mid-training/annealing, continual domain-adaptive pre-training with replay, retrieval/tools, production monitoring.
Section 2.9

Reading the loss curves

≈ 4 min · Slides: FT-II s67–69

Plotting training loss vs validation loss across fine-tuning steps tells you which failure mode you are in. These three curves are “your ultimate guide”.

DiagnosisSignalSlide numbers (train / val)
Underfitting (high bias)Both losses stay high and plateau early3.0 → 2.36 / 3.05 → 2.52 by step 1,400
Overfitting (high variance)Train loss → 0 while validation loss turns back upTrain 3.0 → 0.15; val bottoms ~1.45 at step 600, then rises to 2.2
No learning (flat curves)Both losses flat at their initial value: nothing updates~2.95 / ~3.0 throughout

What good learning looks like

Both losses fall together with a small, stable gap (healthy run: train 3.0 → 0.64, val 3.05 → 0.93 over 2,000 steps).

Curves move together

Validation loss follows training loss down: the model generalizes, not memorizes.

Small, stable gap

A modest train–val gap that stops widening is normal and healthy.

Diminishing returns

Loss flattens smoothly; no oscillation, spikes or divergence.

Stop at the validation minimum

Checkpoint where validation loss bottoms out; training longer buys nothing.

Crisp summary

  • Underfitting: both curves high and flat early (high bias).
  • Overfitting: train → 0 while validation turns back up (high variance); stop at the val minimum.
  • No learning: both flat at the starting value; nothing is updating.
  • Healthy: curves fall together, small stable gap, smooth diminishing returns, checkpoint at the lowest validation loss.

Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)
