Section 3.1

Why PEFT: post-training and the cost of scale

≈ 6 min · Slides: PEFT s3–14

Where PEFT sits

PEFT belongs to post-training, the stage after pre-training (Tie et al., A survey on post-training of large language models, 2025).

Fine-tuning: SFT ✓, reinforcement fine-tuningAlignment: RLHF ✓, DPO ✓, GRPOReasoning: self-refine, RL for reasoningEfficiency: model compression ✓, PEFT ✓, knowledge distillation

Evolution of post-trained language models (PoLMs). Ticks mark the topics this course covers.

PoLM scopeContents
TechniqueFine-tuning (SFT, adaptive FT, reinforcement FT) · Alignment (RLHF, RL from AI feedback, DPO) · Reasoning (self-refine, RL for reasoning) · Efficiency (model compression, PEFT, knowledge distillation) · Integration & adaptation (multi-modal integration, domain adaptation, model merging)
DataDialogue, reasoning, multilingual, code, question answering, text generation, instruction following
ApplicationProfessional domains (legal, healthcare, finance) · technical & logical reasoning (math, code generation) · understanding & interaction (recommendation, speech conversation, video understanding)

Emergence with scale

ScaleCan doCannot yet do
Small · 7BBasic completion, simple translation (“simple Q&A only”)Reasoning, arithmetic, code
Medium · 70BBetter completion, translation, basic reasoning, weak arithmeticComplex code
Large · 400B+All of the above plus chain-of-thought, complex math, code generation—

Emergent abilities appear abruptly, not gradually, once a critical scale threshold is passed. The catch: bigger models are far costlier to adapt.

When scale is a curse: full fine-tuning a 7B model

Assumptions on the slide: 7 × 10⁹ parameters, FP16 weights, Adam, batch 4, sequence 512, d = 4096, 32 layers.

Weights FP16Gradients FP16Adam momentum m (FP32)Adam variance v (FP32)Activations (FP32)Total
7B × 2 B = 14 GB7B × 2 B = 14 GB7B × 4 B = 28 GB7B × 4 B = 28 GB≈ 8 GB≈ 92 GB

Adam's states alone are 56 GB, 4× the weight memory. GPUs needed to hold 92 GB:

GPUVRAMGPUs needed
RTX 409024 GB5
A100 40GB40 GB3
A100 80GB80 GB2
H10080 GB2
H100 NVL188 GB1

Full fine-tuning is “astronomically costly”. A second problem: multi-task fine-tuning done sequentially (task 1, then 2, … then n) causes catastrophic forgetting of earlier tasks.

The PEFT promise

Why update 7 billion parameters when 4 million will do?
< 1%of parameters trained, without sacrificing accuracy
92 → 15 GBfull FT of 7B (multiple GPUs) vs PEFT (one GPU)
1 GPUthe full power of a billion-parameter model at a fraction of the time and cost

Crisp summary

  • PEFT is a post-training technique (PoLM taxonomy: fine-tuning → alignment → reasoning → efficiency).
  • Abilities emerge abruptly with scale (7B → 70B → 400B+), but adaptation cost grows with it.
  • Full FT of 7B ≈ 14 + 14 + 28 + 28 + 8 = 92 GB (Adam states = 56 GB = 4× weights) → 5× RTX 4090 or 2× A100-80GB.
  • Sequential multi-task fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting.
  • PEFT trains < 1% of parameters (≈4M of 7B) in ~15 GB on a single GPU with no accuracy loss.
Section 3.2

The PEFT family tree

≈ 4 min · Slides: PEFT s5, s15–17 · FT-I s34–38 · REV s18

FamilyIdeaMethods on the concept map
AdditiveFreeze the backbone; add small trainable modules (“+A”) and train only thoseAdapters, AdapterFusion
Soft promptingAdd trainable virtual tokens in the input/token spacePrefix tuning, SMoP
SelectiveTrain a chosen subset of existing parameters: bias terms, layer norms, some attention heads or the last layer; < 1% of parameters receive gradients; no new parameters, minimal memoryBitFit (bias terms only), Diff pruning (a sparse learned difference added to frozen weights)
Re-parameterizationRestructure the update during training and revert to the original form at inference; no extra physical layersLoRA, QLoRA

The 15 Aug revision deck groups the methods it teaches as soft prompting, prefix tuning and re-parameterization.

The pictures behind the families

Additive

Pre-trained model: all parameters frozen, no gradients. Small “+A” modules are inserted and trained: < 1% of parameters, ≈ 15 GB for LLaMA-7B.

Re-parameterized (LoRA)

Original weight (, e.g. 4096 × 4096 = 16M params) never changes. Train , , : with r = 8 that is ≈ 65K parameters instead of 16M. At inference merge : same shape, identical architecture, zero overhead.

Selective

Model frozen except bias terms, layer norms, some attention heads or the last layer.

Quantization PEFT

Compress the weights, keep training small. LLaMA-7B in FP16 = 14 GB → NF4/INT8 4-bit ≈ 3.5 GB (4× smaller). QLoRA = frozen NF4 base (3.5 GB) + BF16 adapters (~24 MB) → ≈ 15 GB total.

Multi-task PEFT: one backbone, many tasks

Naive: one full copy per task

3 tasks × 14 GB = 42 GB. Storage and serving scale linearly with the number of tasks.

PEFT: shared frozen backbone

One 14 GB backbone + ~24 MB adapter per task. A new task needs only a new adapter (< 1% of parameters).

Crisp summary

  • Four PEFT families: additive (adapters, AdapterFusion), soft prompting (prefix tuning, SMoP), selective (BitFit, diff pruning), re-parameterization (LoRA, QLoRA).
  • Additive adds modules; selective trains a subset of existing weights; re-parameterization trains a low-rank update and merges it away at inference.
  • LoRA numbers: a 4096 × 4096 weight = 16M params; rank 8 trains ≈ 65K.
  • Quantization: 7B FP16 14 GB → 4-bit 3.5 GB; QLoRA ≈ 15 GB total with ~24 MB adapters.
  • Multi-task: 3 full copies = 42 GB vs one 14 GB backbone + 24 MB per task.
Section 3.3

Adapters: setups, requirements, sequential adapters

≈ 6 min · Slides: PEFT s18–24

Four ways to organize adapters

Explicit task identification

Input arrives with a task ID; the matching adapter (Task 1 … Task N) is plugged in.

AdapterFusion

For a single target task, the outputs of all task adapters are combined, reusing knowledge from every task.

Adapter routing

A gate/router decides which adapters to use, and how much, for the input.

Multi-task adapter

One adapter shared by tasks 1, 2, …, N.

The general form of an adapter

Hidden state h (dim d)Down-project to m ≪ dNon-linearityUp-project back to dAdd to h (skip connection)

Houlsby's comparison: adapters stay within about 0% of full fine-tuning accuracy with only 10⁵–10⁷ trainable parameters per task, while “fine-tune the top layers” is roughly 10% worse at 10⁶ parameters and only catches up near 10⁸.

Two requirements of adapters

  1. Few parameters: the total model size grows slowly as tasks are added.
  2. Near-identity initialization: the adapter starts as (almost) a no-op, so training begins from the pretrained behavior: The projection weights are initialized near zero.

Sequential adapters (Houlsby et al., 2019)

Two adapters are inserted in series in every transformer layer: one after the multi-head attention block and one after the feed-forward block, each before the layer's Add & Norm and each with its own skip connection. Only the adapters (and layer norms) train; everything else is frozen. The slide's analogy: one simple building fitted out as a laboratory or an office.

Worked numbers (d = 768, m = 64)

Layer ≈ 9.5M parameters; one adapter ≈ 0.1M → about 1% of the layer. With two adapters per layer this is the “tune ~2%” figure.

GLUE (BERT-large)Total paramsTrained / taskAverage score
Full fine-tuning9.0×100%80.4
Adapters (size 8–256)1.3×3.6%80.0
Adapters (size 64)1.2×2.1%79.6

“9.0×” = nine separate full copies for nine tasks; adapters add only 20–30% on top of one model.

Limitations of sequential adapters

  • Inference latency overhead (extra layers on the critical path)
  • Parameter cost scales with depth
  • Cannot be parallelized with the existing computation (they sit in series)
  • Multi-task serving is expensive

Crisp summary

  • Setups: explicit task ID, AdapterFusion (combine all task adapters), adapter routing (gated), one multi-task adapter.
  • Adapter = down-project (d → m) → non-linearity → up-project (m → d) + skip.
  • Requirements: few parameters, and near-identity init (h' = h + f(h), f ≈ 0) so training starts from pretrained behavior.
  • Houlsby: two sequential adapters per layer (after attention, after FFN); 2dm + m + d params each vs 16d² + 19d per layer (≈1% at d = 768, m = 64).
  • GLUE: adapters 80.0 with 3.6% trained vs full FT 80.4 with 100%.
  • Weaknesses: added latency, cost grows with depth, sequential (not parallelisable), costly multi-task serving.
Section 3.4

Residual adapters and what adapters buy you

≈ 4 min · Slides: PEFT s25–32

Residual adapter (Lin et al., 2020, on GPT-2)

The residual adapter is parallel: inside each block the frozen FFN and the trainable adapter both read the same H, and their outputs are added together with the residual before layer norm: . Multi-head attention and FFN stay frozen.

One frozen GPT-2 hosts a separate adapter per task: conversational QA, natural-language generation, summarization, machine translation, dialogue. Each task also gets its own task / segment embeddings added to the word and position embeddings.

Task-specific tokens for QA

"qa": ["<bos_qa>", "<document>", "</document>", "<question>", "</question>", "<answer>", "</answer>", …, "<eos_qa>"]

Dialogue generation and summarization are formatted the same way with their own tokens.

Other ideas named on the slides: AdapterFusion and the Tiny-Attention Adapter.

In a nutshell

  • Fine-tuning adapts pre-trained models to specific tasks but has two major issues: it is costly, and it causes catastrophic forgetting in multi-task settings.
  • Adapters reach a similar level of performance by tuning only a tiny fraction (~2%) of the parameters.
  • Freeze the original model; update only the adapter parameters.
  • Task-specific adapters solve the catastrophic-forgetting issue: each task's knowledge lives in its own adapter and the backbone never changes.

Food for thought: why adapters instead of fine-tuning only the last few layers? The Houlsby curve answers it: top-layer tuning needs ~100× more trainable parameters to match full fine-tuning, whereas adapters reach parity with very few, because they add capacity inside every layer while leaving the backbone untouched and swappable per task.

Crisp summary

  • Residual adapter: Adapter(H) = ReLU(LN(H)·W^E)·W^D + H, with W^E (d×m) and W^D (m×d).
  • It runs in parallel with the frozen FFN (outputs summed with the residual), unlike Houlsby's sequential adapters.
  • Lin et al. use one GPT-2 with per-task adapters (CQA, NLG, SUM, NMT, DLG) plus task/segment embeddings and task tokens such as <bos_qa>, <document>, <question>, <answer>.
  • Adapters ≈ full fine-tuning quality at ~2% of parameters; task-specific adapters avoid catastrophic forgetting.
  • They beat top-layer tuning because they add capacity at every layer with far fewer parameters.
Section 3.5

Soft prompts: prompt tuning and prefix tuning

≈ 6 min · Slides: PEFT s33–39 · REV s19–20

The idea

Adapters

Add architectural elements vertically; adaptation happens in the architectural space.

Soft prompts

Adaptation in the token space: add and configure task-specific tokens. Conditioning on the right context can steer the LM without changing its parameters.

  • Discrete prompt: a sequence of real token embeddings (words you could type).
  • Continuous prompt: a sequence of virtual, trainable token embeddings.

Why continuous prompts? Manual prompts are fragile

Manual promptScoreWith prompt tuning
[X] is located in [Y].31.357.8
[X] is located in which country or state? [Y]19.857.8
[X] is located in which country? [Y]31.458.1
[X] is located in which country? In [Y]51.158.1

Small wording changes swing manual-prompt performance from 19.8 to 51.1; learned prompts land at ~58 regardless.

Prompt tuning (soft prompting at the input)

Prepend m learnable vectors (initialized e.g. from ) to the input embeddings. The LLM is frozen; the cross-entropy loss sends gradients only to the soft prompt; the learned prompt is reused at inference.

Prefix tuning (Li & Liang, 2021)

Fine-tuning keeps a separate full transformer copy per task (translation, summarization, table-to-text). Prefix tuning keeps one frozen transformer and learns a small task-specific prefix of virtual tokens for each task.

  • Autoregressive LM (GPT-2): . Encoder–decoder (BART): . = the prefix positions.
  • Activations at prefix positions are free parameters; everything else is computed by the frozen LM φ, which attends to the prefix:
  • Re-parameterization for stable training: , where is a smaller matrix (k-dim → d). Only the resulting prefix is kept after training.
  • In practice the prefix enters every layer as extra keys and values:
Prompt tuning (soft prompting)Prefix tuning
WherePrepended to the input embeddings onlyPrepended to the keys and values of every layer (not the input embeddings)
Trainablem prompt vectorsPrefix vectors (via a trainable prefix-encoder MLP during training)
Shared traitsLLM frozen; task-specific; m ≪ n (sequence length); works for any sequence length; low training cost and memory

Crisp summary

  • Adapters adapt in architectural space; soft prompts adapt in token space by learning virtual tokens while the LM stays frozen.
  • Manual prompts are brittle (19.8–51.1 for near-identical wordings); learned continuous prompts reach ~58.
  • Prompt tuning: m trainable vectors prepended to the input embeddings; gradients flow only into them.
  • Prefix tuning: z = [PREFIX; x; y] (GPT-2) or [PREFIX; x; PREFIX'; y] (BART); prefix activations are free parameters fed as extra K/V at every layer.
  • Prefix training is stabilized by re-parameterizing through an MLP from a smaller matrix P'.
  • One frozen model + one tiny prefix per task replaces a full model copy per task.
Section 3.6

Smarter soft prompts: SMoP, APT, IDPG, SPT

≈ 7 min · Slides: PEFT s40–54

The cost of prompt tuning

Good results often need many soft tokens (~100), and a longer prompt means more attention compute and more parameters. Are all prompt tokens effective for a given input? Three remedies: use short prompts; use multiple prompts to cover different parts of the data; use a gating mechanism to match a prompt to a data subset.

SMoP: Sparse Mixture-of-Prompts (Choi et al., 2023)

Keep k short soft prompts. A router reads the input and picks one (e.g. prompt 2 with probability 0.6), which is prepended to the input of the frozen PLM.

  • Input embeddings ; = their average.
  • Router with , k = number of soft-prompt units: .
  • The top prompt c is selected and scaled: objective .

APT: Adaptive Prefix Tuning (Zhang et al., 2023)

Standard prefix tuning gives every layer the same prefix length. But bottom layers capture concrete, shallow, phrase-level features (more information → longer prefix), while top layers carry abstract semantics (shorter prefix). APT learns a dynamic prefix length per layer with two gates:

  • Fine-grained (token-level): , a vector deciding how many pseudo-tokens layer i needs.
  • Coarse-grained (layer-level): a weight balancing prefix vs input in layer i.
  • Combined: .

Learned weights match the theory: CoNLL04 (entity–relation extraction) leans on the bottom, phrase-level layers; COPA (commonsense causal reasoning) leans on the higher, semantic layers.

IDPG: Instance-Dependent Prompt Generation (Wu et al., 2022)

Prompt-tuned soft prompts are instance-independent: every input of a task gets the same prompt. That contradicts the LM objective, since a pre-training corpus rarely shows many different sentences behind the same prefix. IDPG generates a prompt per input.

  • General framework: input (or a single sentence); task prompt : t soft tokens of hidden size d.
  • IDPG: . The frozen pre-trained model M encodes the input; a lightweight generator G (down-project → non-linearity → up-project ) emits t instance-dependent soft tokens. Only G is tuned.
  • Generator size: parameters.

Does every layer need a prompt? LPT and SPT

Soft prompts are usually added at the input layer. Late Prompt Tuning (LPT) showed prompts can be inserted at an intermediate layer instead. With a budget of at most K prompted layers, Selective Prompt Tuning (SPT, Zhu & Tan, 2023) learns where to inject prompts for the task at hand.

In a nutshell

MethodFixesHow
Prefix tuningFragile manual promptsLearnable virtual tokens enrich the input context
SMoPLong, costly prompts that don't suit all dataRouter picks one short prompt per input
APTSame prefix length at every layerLonger prefixes for bottom layers, shorter for top layers
IDPGOne prompt for all inputsGenerator makes input-dependent prompts
LPT / SPTPrompts only at the input layerInsert at intermediate layers; SPT learns which layers

Crisp summary

  • Prompt tuning often needs ~100 soft tokens; remedies are short prompts, multiple prompts and gating.
  • SMoP: k short prompts + a softmax router over the averaged input embedding; one prompt is active per input (sparse).
  • APT: per-layer prefix length via token-level gates α = sigmoid(hW) and layer-level weights λ; bottom layers get longer prefixes (CoNLL04 uses bottom layers, COPA uses top layers).
  • IDPG: a small generator G(M(x), T) produces instance-dependent prompts from a frozen encoder; params m(d+1) + td(m+1).
  • LPT inserts prompts mid-network; SPT learns where to insert them under a K-layer budget.

Lecture resources: general PEFT surveys by Wang et al. (2025) and Xu et al. (2023); additive PEFT: Houlsby et al. (2019), Lin et al. (2020); soft prompting: Li & Liang (2021, prefix tuning), Choi et al. (2023, SMoP), Zhang et al. (2023, APT), Wu et al. (2022, IDPG).

Section 3.7

LoRA: low-rank adaptation

≈ 4 min · Slides: REV s21–30 · PEFT s15

Start from gradient descent

Training updates a weight matrix by adding a change: , where . LoRA learns a compact version of that ΔW instead of touching W.

Key idea

  1. Freeze the original model parameters.
  2. Introduce a pair of low-rank matrices during fine-tuning.
  3. Update only these matrices.
  4. Merge them into the weights for inference.

Low-rank factorization

Any matrix of rank r can be written as a product with , , . The slide's rank-2 example: a 5 × 5 matrix (25 numbers) = (5 × 2)(2 × 5), only 20 numbers. At LLM scale the saving is dramatic: a 4096 × 4096 weight has ~16.8M entries (the slide rounds to 16M), while rank 8 needs 2 × 4096 × 8 ≈ 65K.

Decompose only the update

  • α is a scaling hyperparameter; r is the rank (r ≪ d).
  • Initialization: B = 0 (A random), so BA = 0 and the model starts exactly at the pretrained behavior.
  • During backpropagation, gradients flow only through the adapters A and B; W stays frozen.
  • After training, merge : same shape as W, identical architecture, no extra inference latency (unlike sequential adapters).

LoRA still has a memory problem

Fine-tuning (10B model)Optimizer stateBase modelAdapterMemory
Full parameterFP32FP16—160 GB
LoRAFP32 (adapters only)FP16FP1640 GB

40 GB is a big cut, but the frozen FP16 base still dominates memory. QLoRA attacks exactly that.

Crisp summary

  • LoRA freezes W and learns the update as a low-rank product: W + (α/r)·BA, with B (d×r), A (r×d), r ≪ d.
  • Forward pass: h = Wx + (α/r)BAx; B starts at 0 so the model starts as the pretrained one.
  • Only A and B receive gradients; at inference they merge into W, so there is zero added latency.
  • Savings: 4096 × 4096 (16.8M) vs rank 8 (≈65K) trainable parameters.
  • Memory for 10B: full FT 160 GB vs LoRA 40 GB; the FP16 base is the remaining bottleneck.
Section 3.8

QLoRA: quantized LoRA

≈ 6 min · Slides: REV s31–47 · PEFT s16

Key idea: quantize the frozen network parameters from high precision to low precision, and train LoRA adapters on top. Four concepts: quantization, 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), double quantization and paged optimizers.

1 · What is quantization?

Bucketing continuous values: numbers between 0 and 10 quantized with bucket width 1 give 10 buckets (0–1, 1–2, …, 9–10); width 2 gives 5 buckets (0–2, …, 8–10). Fewer buckets = fewer bits, less precision.

FP32 → INT8 (absmax quantization)

is the quantization constant, one per set (block) of values. For X = [1.5, 2.3, …, 10.2] it is 127 / 10.2 ≈ 12.45.

2 · 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)

4 bits represent 2⁴ = 16 values. Neural-network weights are roughly normally distributed, so NF4 uses equally-sized buckets (the same number of weights per bucket) rather than equally-spaced ones. That places more precision near the mean and less in the tails.

Index01234567
NF4 value−1.00−0.70−0.50−0.35−0.22−0.12−0.05−0.01
Index89101112131415
NF4 value0.010.050.120.220.350.500.701.00

The slide's NF4 codebook: values crowd together near 0 where most weights live.

Worked example

Weights W−0.82−0.30−0.070.020.180.61
÷ absmax 0.82−1.00−0.37−0.090.020.220.74
Nearest NF4−1.00−0.35−0.120.010.220.70
Stored index03581114

Dequantization: with scale 0.82, e.g. index 14 → 0.82 × 0.70 ≈ 0.57 (the original was 0.61). Only the 4-bit indices plus one scale per block are stored.

3 · Double quantization

Quantize each row/block, which leaves one quantization constant per block (e.g. 127/0.7, 127/1.7, 127/1.5, 127/1.7, 127/2.2). Those constants themselves take memory, so quantize the constants again with a second-level constant. Memory is saved twice.

4 · Paged optimizers

Background, gradient checkpointing: running out of memory is common because the forward pass stores the activations of every layer for the backward pass. Checkpointing keeps only a subset of activations and recomputes the rest during backward, trading compute for memory.

Paged optimizer: uses the CPU and GPU together. Pages are transferred automatically between them: active pages stay on the GPU, inactive ones move to CPU RAM, so memory spikes don't crash training.

Putting it together

Frozen base weights in NF4 (7B ≈ 3.5 GB)Double-quantized block constantsBF16 LoRA adapters (~24 MB)Paged optimizer + checkpointing≈ 15 GB: one GPU

Crisp summary

  • QLoRA = quantized frozen base + LoRA adapters; four ingredients: quantization, NF4, double quantization, paged optimizer.
  • Absmax INT8: X_int8 = round(127/max|X| · X); 127/max|X| is the per-block quantization constant.
  • NF4: 16 levels with equal-count buckets, dense near 0 because weights are roughly normal.
  • Worked example: W ÷ 0.82 → nearest codebook values → indices [0, 3, 5, 8, 11, 14]; dequantize with w = 0.82 × NF4[index].
  • Double quantization quantizes the per-block constants themselves.
  • Paged optimizer moves inactive pages to CPU; gradient checkpointing stores fewer activations and recomputes them.
  • Result: 7B base 14 GB → 3.5 GB; QLoRA fine-tuning ≈ 15 GB on a single GPU.

Section 4.1

HHH and preference alignment

≈ 5 min · Slides: ALIGN s3–7 · REV s49

Alignment aims for responses that are Helpful, Honest and Harmless (HHH).

PropertyDefinitionGood exampleFailure
HonestTruthful and appropriately calibrated: no fabrication, no overstated confidence, no sycophancy“Did Einstein fail math?” → “No, that's a popular myth; he excelled at math. The myth likely came from misread grading scales.”Confirms the myth because the user seems to expect it, or invents an anecdote
HelpfulA genuine effort to accomplish what the user actually needs: relevant, complete, useful, not evasive or genericA KeyError 'user_id' question → identifies the line, explains why the key is missing, suggests .get('user_id') with a default“KeyErrors happen when a key doesn't exist. Check your code carefully.” (true but useless)
HarmlessAvoids outputs that enable real-world harm, even when explicitly requestedDeclines step-by-step bomb-making instructions regardless of stated intentComplies because the request was framed as “for a chemistry class”

HHH is a trade-off

ScenarioTension
Detailed medical dosage adviceHelpful (a direct answer) vs Harmless (risk of misuse or harm if wrong)
An essay draft with a flawed argumentHelpful / pleasant (praise it) vs Honest (point out the flaw)
“How does SQL injection work?”Harmless (could enable attacks) vs Helpful (legitimate for developers and students learning defense)

Optimizing one property alone fails: helpfulness-only complies with harmful requests; harmlessness-only refuses anything mildly sensitive (over-refusal); honesty-only may bluntly volunteer harmful true information.

From HHH to preference alignment

  • HHH is a specification problem; preference alignment is the solution. RLHF and DPO convert the abstract target into something trainable.
  • Rankings, not rubrics: rather than formalizing HHH into scoring functions, labelers compare pairs of responses and pick the better one.
  • The preference model becomes a learned proxy for HHH: a differentiable, queryable estimate of how well a response satisfies it.
  • Tensions become operational: trade-offs are decided implicitly, response by response.
  • Preference-data quality is the new bottleneck: the challenge moves from philosophy (“define the principle”) to data curation (“collect comparisons”).
  • Methods differ in how they consume the signal: RLHF routes it through an explicit reward model plus RL; DPO uses it directly.
Pre-trainingFine-tuningPreference tuning

Fine-tuning + preference tuning together form post-training (Tie et al., 2025).

Crisp summary

  • HHH: honest (truthful, calibrated, not sycophantic), helpful (actually solves the need), harmless (refuses real-world harm even under a benign framing).
  • The three conflict (dosage advice, flawed essay, SQL injection); single-objective models over-comply, over-refuse or blurt harmful truths.
  • Preference alignment operationalizes HHH through pairwise human comparisons; the preference/reward model is a learned proxy for HHH.
  • The bottleneck shifts to preference-data quality. RLHF uses a reward model + RL; DPO uses preferences directly.
  • Pipeline: pre-training → fine-tuning → preference tuning.
Section 4.2

RL foundations for language models

≈ 5 min · Slides: ALIGN s8–22

A language model, recapped

: West 0.6, Kerala 0.1, Taj 0.002, Australia 0.0001. Generation is token by token: “Where is Kharagpur?” → Kharagpur → is → in → West → Bengal, each new token appended to the prompt.

Why reinforcement learning?

  • LLMs lack an intrinsic grasp of nuanced human preferences and societal norms.
  • Humans are excellent at evaluating and selecting outputs, intuitively weighing context, cultural nuance and ethics, which is hard to automate.
  • A traditional loss function for “align with human preferences” is impractical: human feedback (✓ / ✗) is non-differentiable, so there are no gradients to backpropagate. RL can learn from a reward signal anyway.

The RL setup (grid-world example)

Ingredients
  • Agent: a mouse; state: its (x, y) cell
  • Actions: up, down, left, right (an invalid move = stay put)
  • Rewards: empty cell 0; towards the cat −1; into the trap −1 and the episode ends; cheese +100
Dynamics
  • Policy:
  • Transition:
  • Loop: agent acts → environment returns a reward and the next state
  • Goal: a policy that maximizes expected return

A trajectory is the whole episode: .

Mapping RL onto an LLM

RL conceptLLM equivalent
Agent / policy The LLM itself; it learns “which token to generate given a prompt”
Initial state The prompt
Action The next output token
State Prompt + output so far (the new prompt)
RewardA verifier or a reward model that scores good responses

A trajectory in a language model

= “Where is Kolkata?” → = “Kolkata”, = “is”, = “in”, = “India”. We fine-tune the LM so it picks next tokens that maximize the reward.

Probability of a trajectory

Initial-state probability × probability of each action under the policy × probability of each next state.

Return and objective

J is the expected cumulative reward of the policy; RL maximizes it.

Crisp summary

  • RL is needed because human feedback is non-differentiable; RL learns from rewards without gradients through the judge.
  • RL vocabulary: agent, state, action, reward, policy π(a|s), transition P(s'|s,a), trajectory τ.
  • For LLMs: policy = the LLM, state = prompt + tokens so far, action = next token, reward = reward model or verifier.
  • P(τ|π) = P(s₀) Π π(a_t|s_t) P(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t).
  • Return: Σ r_t (finite) or Σ γᵗ r_t (discounted, 0 < γ < 1); objective J = E_τ[R(τ)].
Section 4.3

Policy gradient, REINFORCE and the advantage

≈ 4 min · Slides: ALIGN s23–31

Policy gradient

Find by gradient ascent:

The exact expectation needs every possible trajectory, which is intractable, so it is estimated from a sample D of trajectories:

REINFORCE

  1. Create a neural network that defines the policy (input: current state; output: probabilities over the action space).
  2. Use it to sample trajectories and their rewards.
  3. Use the sample to compute the gradient estimate.
  4. Run stochastic gradient ascent on the policy parameters.
  5. Go back to step 2.

The sample-based gradient is unbiased (on average it converges to the true gradient) but has high variance.

Reducing variance

1 · Reward-to-go

The future cannot influence the past, so action should only be credited with rewards from t onward: replace with . Dropping terms reduces variance.

2 · Baseline

Subtract a state-dependent baseline . A natural choice is the value function : the expected return from s under π.

3 · Advantage

is the value of taking a in s. The advantage says how much better a is than the average action in s.

Advantage for a language model

Given “Where is Shanghai?”, the next token “Shanghai” leads, in expectation, to better-than-average reward (positive advantage, so its probability is pushed up); “Chocolate” leads to worse-than-average reward (negative advantage, pushed down).

Crisp summary

  • Maximize J by gradient ascent; ∇J = E[Σ ∇log π(a_t|s_t) · R(τ)].
  • The exact gradient is intractable, so average over sampled trajectories (REINFORCE: sample → estimate → ascend → repeat).
  • The estimate is unbiased but high-variance.
  • Variance fixes: reward-to-go (only future rewards count), a baseline b(s_t) such as V(s), and the advantage A = Q − V.
  • Advantage in LMs: tokens that lead to better-than-average reward get reinforced.
Section 4.4

PPO: sample reuse, reward hacking and the KL penalty

≈ 7 min · Slides: ALIGN s32–40 · REV s55–57

PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) is the RL algorithm used in RLHF to update the language model so it generates higher-reward responses. It fixes two problems of plain policy gradient: wasted samples and drift.

Problem: fresh samples after every update

Vanilla policy gradient must sample new trajectories every time the parameters change, which is very inefficient for an LLM.

Solution: learn from an old policy's samples

Sample trajectories from an old (offline) policy and reuse them for multiple epochs, correcting with the probability ratio (an importance weight; it is not the reward):

Reward hacking

A preference-tuned LLM gone wrong

“Why is the sky blue?” → “Bang on! This is a great question. Thank you so much for asking. This is a demonstration of your sheer intellect…”

The policy exploits flaws in the reward model to earn high reward with unhelpful content. Fix: penalize the aligned model when it drifts from the original model, measured by the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between their token (logit) distributions.

The PPO objective used in the lecture

is the frozen SFT model; β sets how strongly drift is penalized. The revision lecture states the principle plainly: improve the model based on reward, but don't change it too much in a single update. (Standard PPO implementations also clip the ratio to for the same reason.)

Pieces in PPO (revision lecture)

Policy = the LLM; state s = the input prompt; action a = the next token; = probability the model generates a from s. For “What is 2 + 2?”: “4” → 0.80, “5” → 0.05, “3” → 0.05, … PPO's core quantity is the ratio : the model after the update over the model before it.

The PPO training loop

Old policy samples trajectories (states + actions), saved in memoryCompute rewards and advantages for every (state, action)Take a minibatchGradient ascent on the current policyRepeat for K epochsθ_old ← θ, sample again

There are not two live copies of the policy: the trajectories are sampled once, stored, and reused.

The four models in the PPO loop

ModelRoleOutputTrained?
Policy The LLM being alignedProbability distribution over next tokensYes, by RL
Reference The SFT model; anchor for the KL penaltyProbability distributionNo (frozen)
Reward model RScores a complete responseOne score for the whole sequenceTrained beforehand on preferences
Value model VEstimates expected future reward at each stepOne score per token / stateYes, alongside the policy

Policy and reference share the same architecture: a causally masked decoder (each hidden state sees only earlier tokens) → a linear layer giving logits at every position (prompt tokens p1…p5, action tokens a1…a3) → softmax giving the probability of the next action.

Crisp summary

  • Resampling after every update is wasteful; PPO samples with π_old, stores the trajectories and reuses them for K epochs via the ratio π_θ/π_θold.
  • Reward hacking: the policy games the reward model (flattery for “Why is the sky blue?”).
  • Fix: KL penalty −β·KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref) keeps the policy close to the frozen SFT reference; KL is non-negative and asymmetric.
  • Principle: improve with reward, but keep each update small.
  • Four models: policy (trained), reference (frozen SFT), reward model (sequence score), value model (per-token score); Â = r + γV(s') − V(s).
Section 4.5

Reward model and value model

≈ 4 min · Slides: ALIGN s41–48 · REV s53–54

Why compare instead of score?

Building a reward model from absolute scores would need prompts, responses and a universally accepted reward (say 0–1) for each, which is hard to label. People are good at comparison, so collect preference data instead: (prompt, answer 1, answer 2, which one is chosen).

The reward model turns preferences into something approximately measurable: answer → score, e.g. R(good answer) = 0.9, R(bad answer) = 0.1.

Reward-model architecture

Prompt + answer tokensTransformer (pretrained / SFT LLM backbone)Final hidden stateLinear layer with one outputScalar reward

Bradley–Terry loss

If the winner scores higher (), σ > 0.5 and the loss is small; if not, the loss is large. The only way to minimize it is to give high rewards to winning responses and low rewards to losing ones. The same shared-weight model scores and ; backprop updates only .

batch  = tokenizer([x + y_w, x + y_l], padding=True, return_tensors="pt")
scores = reward_model(**batch)          # shape (2,): a scalar per sequence
r_w, r_l = scores[0], scores[1]
loss = -F.logsigmoid(r_w - r_l)         # Bradley–Terry
loss.backward()                         # gradients flow through BOTH passes into shared θ
optimizer.step(); optimizer.zero_grad()

The revision lecture's version: , ; if A is preferred we want , with loss .

Value model

A linear layer with one output at every position (per token), trained on generated trajectories with rewards at each point:

Overall architecture: one language-model backbone with three heads: the LM head (policy logits), a reward head and a value head.

Crisp summary

  • Absolute reward labels are hard; pairwise preferences (prompt, answer 1, answer 2, chosen) are easy for people.
  • Reward model: LLM backbone + a linear head with one output on the final hidden state → scalar reward.
  • Bradley–Terry loss −log σ(r_w − r_l); code: −F.logsigmoid(r_w − r_l); one shared model scores both responses.
  • Value model: a per-token linear head trained with (V(s_t) − R̂_t)², where R̂_t is the reward-to-go.
  • In PPO the backbone carries LM, reward and value heads.
Section 4.6

InstructGPT, ChatGPT and the RLHF pipeline

≈ 4 min · Slides: ALIGN s49–50 · REV s50–52

Why RLHF?

Train the model so its answers are not just correct-looking but more helpful, safe and aligned with what humans prefer.

Motivation: “How can I learn Python?”

  1. “Python is a programming language. You can learn it by studying syntax.”
  2. “Start with the basics: variables, data types, loops, functions, and then build small projects. Practice regularly…”
  3. “Python is easy. Just watch some YouTube videos.”

All three look correct, but answer 2 is the most useful. The goal is to teach the model this kind of preference.

InstructGPT: three steps

StepDataWhat is trained
1 · Supervised fine-tuningA prompt is sampled; a labeler demonstrates the desired outputGPT-3 fine-tuned on the demonstrations (SFT)
2 · Reward modelSeveral model outputs are sampled for a prompt; a labeler ranks them (e.g. D > C > A = B)Reward model trained on the rankings
3 · PPOA new prompt is sampled; the policy generates an output; the RM scores it ()Policy updated with PPO using the reward

ChatGPT

Trained with the same methods as InstructGPT (instruction fine-tuning + RLHF for dialogue), with differences in data collection: SFT data came from human AI trainers playing both the user and the assistant (with access to model-written suggestions), mixed with the InstructGPT dataset converted to dialogue format. Further details are kept secret.

The full RLHF pipeline (revision lecture)

1 · Pre-trained LLM (unlabeled data)2 · SFT on high-quality instruction–response pairs → initial policy π₀3 · Reward-model training: multiple responses ranked by humans (A > B > D > C)4 · RL with PPO: maximize expected reward while staying close to π₀5 · Final aligned policy π*6 · Deploy: helpful, harmless, honest responses

Crisp summary

  • RLHF teaches preferences that correctness alone misses (the most useful of three “correct” Python answers).
  • InstructGPT: (1) SFT on labeler demonstrations; (2) labelers rank several outputs → reward model; (3) PPO against the reward model.
  • ChatGPT used the same recipe with dialogue data written by trainers playing both roles, mixed with InstructGPT data.
  • Pipeline: pre-trained LLM → SFT (π₀) → human rankings → reward model → PPO near π₀ → aligned π* → deploy.
Section 4.7

DPO: direct preference optimization

≈ 6 min · Slides: ALIGN s51–56 · REV s58–63

Issues with PPO-based RLHF

  • Several stages: fit a reward model to human preferences; run RL to optimize the policy for high reward; manage reward hacking by limiting drift from the original model.
  • An indirect method that trains or juggles many models: policy, reward model, value function, reference model.
  • RL is generally difficult to train and unstable.

Can we align directly? DPO needs no reward model and no RL: it trains the language model directly on preference pairs.

RL workflow

Preference data → reward model → policy model

DPO (RL-free)

Preference data → policy model

The DPO loss

= chosen (winner), = rejected (loser), = frozen reference (the SFT model), β = how strongly the policy is tied to the reference.

The intuition (revision lecture)

Training data

Prompt: “Explain photosynthesis simply.” Chosen: “Plants use sunlight to turn water and carbon dioxide into food, releasing oxygen.” Rejected: “Photosynthesis is a biological process involving complex biochemical reactions in chloroplasts…”

The initial model is not ideal: chosen 30%, rejected 70%. DPO changes it so the chosen answer gets higher probability and the rejected one lower.

Why relative probabilities? Say the pre-trained model gives P(A|Q) = 0.60 for the chosen answer and P(B|Q) = 0.40 for the rejected one. A bad update could flip this to 0.30 / 0.70. DPO asks the new model to raise and lower , i.e. to beat the pre-trained model on both counts:

Useful check (illustrative arithmetic): at the start , both log-ratios are 0, so the loss is . With β = 1, moving to 0.75 / 0.25 from 0.60 / 0.40 gives a margin of log(1.25) − log(0.625) ≈ 0.69, σ ≈ 0.67, loss ≈ 0.41: the loss falls as the chosen answer gains relative probability.

DPO workflow

Prompts {x}Sample completions y₁, y₂ ~ π_ref(·|x)Humans label preferences offline → D = {x, y_chosen, y_rejected}Optimize π_θ to minimize L_DPO

The entire workflow

Download a static preference datasetSFT on the chosen completions: minimize −log π(y_c|x)DPO training from that SFT reference

Crisp summary

  • PPO-RLHF is indirect and unstable: reward model + RL + KL control across four models.
  • DPO is RL-free: preference data → policy directly; no reward model, no value model, no sampling loop.
  • Loss: −log σ(β[log π_θ(y_w|x)/π_ref(y_w|x) − log π_θ(y_l|x)/π_ref(y_l|x)]).
  • It increases the chosen answer's probability relative to the reference and decreases the rejected one's (photosynthesis: 30% chosen / 70% rejected must flip).
  • At initialization the loss is log 2 ≈ 0.693; β controls how far the policy may move from π_ref.
  • Workflow: static preference data → SFT on chosen answers (reference) → DPO.

Further reading from the lecture: Christiano et al., Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences (NeurIPS 2017); Nathan Lambert, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (arXiv 2504.12501); Cameron Wolfe, PPO for LLMs: A Guide for Normal People and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).

Section 4.8

Revision, RLAIF and safety in practice

≈ 4 min · Slides: FT-I s32 · REV s2, s11

Three routes to alignment fine-tuning

RouteSignalMechanism
Human feedback (RLHF)Humans rank candidate answersA reward model learns the ranking; PPO steers the policy toward it
DPO(chosen, rejected) pairsTrains directly on the pairs
RevisionWritten principlesThe model critiques and revises its own outputs against the principles

The revision lecture's alignment slide also writes the optimization step as “RLHF / RLAIF”: in RL from AI feedback, an AI model rather than a human provides the preference judgements (it also appears as “RL with AI feedback” in the PoLM scope of Module 3).

Hands-on topics from the 15 Aug session

The session's agenda paired the revision with a small-language-model (SLM) lab: PEFT and DPO on an SLM, plus three safety practices. The deck has no theory slides for the safety items; the definitions below are standard background.

Output guardrails with content filtering

A check on what the model returns (rules, classifiers or a second model) that blocks or rewrites unsafe content before it reaches the user.

PII detection

Finding personally identifiable information (names, phone numbers, emails, ID numbers) in inputs or outputs so it can be masked or blocked.

Red-team testing

Deliberately attacking the model with adversarial prompts (jailbreaks, harmful requests, prompt injection) to expose failures before deployment.

Crisp summary

  • Alignment fine-tuning routes: RLHF (rank → reward model → PPO), DPO (train on pairs), revision (self-critique against written principles).
  • RLAIF replaces human preference labels with AI feedback.
  • The SLM lab practiced PEFT and DPO, then three deployment safeguards: output guardrails/content filtering, PII detection and red-team testing.

Four landmark vision-language models, one template. The module ends by comparing and composing them.

Lecture outcomes: explain contrastive vs generative vs promptable VLMs; derive CLIP's loss and zero-shot mechanism; trace how a pixel becomes an LLM token in LLaVA and Qwen-VL; describe SAM's promptable task and data engine; compare all four on architecture, data and objective.
