Section 5.1

VLM foundations

≈ 8 min · Slides: M4L1 s3–10, s94–95

What is a vision-language model?

  • Input: image(s) + text (a caption, question, instruction or prompt). Output: text, a label, a similarity score or a mask.
  • It jointly represents and reasons over image and text in a shared computational space.
  • Core promise: older computer vision had fixed tasks and fixed label sets (a 1,000-class classifier only ever knows 1,000 classes). VLMs build visual understanding on top of language models, so they generalize open-vocabulary to anything expressible in text.
Family 1 · trained from scratch (CLIP, BLIP)

A text encoder and a vision encoder trained jointly with contrastive / decoder pre-training objectives, then aligned with supervised fine-tuning.

Family 2 · pretrained LLM as backbone (LLaVA, Qwen-VL)

Vision encoder → image embedding → projector → LLM, which also takes the text embeddings.

Why multimodal, and why now?

  • Human perception is multimodal: we combine vision, language and world knowledge effortlessly.
  • Downstream demand: search and retrieval, accessibility, robotics, autonomous agents, content moderation, medical imaging.
  • Data availability: billions of noisy (image, alt-text) pairs on the web, a nearly free supervisory signal.
  • Transformer unification: the same attention machinery now processes pixels (ViT) and tokens (LLM).

A short history

YearMilestoneContribution
2012AlexNetDeep CNNs win ImageNet
2017Transformer“Attention is all you need”
2020ViTImages as sequences of patches
2021CLIP / ALIGNContrastive image–text pre-training
2022FlamingoFew-shot VLM via cross-attention
2023LLaVA / SAMInstruction-tuned visual chat; promptable segmentation
2023Qwen-VLGrounding, OCR and multi-image in one model
2024SAM 2 / Qwen2-VLVideo segmentation; dynamic resolution

Recap: the Vision Transformer (ViT)

Patchify: split the image into 16×16-pixel patches, flatten eachLinear projection of each patch into the hidden size (like a word embedding)Add positional embeddings (attention is order-agnostic)Prepend a learnable [CLS] token; its final output often represents the whole imageStandard transformer encoder: multi-head self-attention + MLP blocks

CLIP, LLaVA's vision tower, Qwen-VL's encoder and SAM's encoder are all ViT variants: understand ViT once and you understand the visual front-end of every model here.

Three paradigms

ParadigmInputOutputExampleNote
ContrastiveImage + candidate text labelsSimilarity scoresCLIPTwo independent encoders pull matching pairs together; great for retrieval and zero-shot classification, but no free-form text
Generative / instruction-followingImage + free-text instructionFree-form generated textLLaVA, Qwen-VLVision encoder feeds visual tokens to an autoregressive LLM: chat, reasoning, grounding
Promptable dense predictionImage + spatial prompt (point, box, mask)Pixel-level maskSAMA foundation model for segmentation, not language

The generic anatomy of a VLM

Image → vision encoder (CNN / ViT)Text → text encoder / tokenizerFusion / connector: projection, cross-attention or shared spaceOutput: logits, text or mask

Every model in this module is a variation on this template; they differ in the connector and in what the output is used for.

Where fusion happens

Dual encoder, no fusion

CLIP: the towers interact only through a final dot product. Fast, but no joint reasoning.

Early fusion into a decoder

LLaVA, Qwen-VL: visual tokens are treated as a “foreign language”, placed before the text tokens, and fused by the LLM's self-attention.

Cross-attention fusion

SAM's mask decoder, Qwen-VL's adapter: a dedicated cross-attention module explicitly mixes two token sets.

The four models at a glance

ModelOrganization · yearParadigmKey idea
CLIPOpenAI · 2021Contrastive dual encoderLearn a shared embedding space from 400M web (image, text) pairs
LLaVAWisconsin / MSR · 2023Generative, instruction-tunedConnect a frozen CLIP encoder to an LLM through a simple projector
Qwen-VLAlibaba · 2023Generative + groundedA compressive vision-language adapter for grounding, OCR and multi-image
SAMMeta AI · 2023Promptable segmentationA foundation model for masks driven by a 1.1B-mask data engine

Crisp summary

  • A VLM takes image(s) + text and outputs text, a label, a similarity score or a mask; its promise is open-vocabulary generalization via language.
  • Two families: trained from scratch (CLIP, BLIP) vs pretrained-LLM backbone with a projector (LLaVA, Qwen-VL).
  • Drivers: multimodal perception, demand, free web alt-text data, transformer unification (ViT + LLM).
  • ViT: 16×16 patches → linear projection → position embeddings + [CLS] → transformer encoder; every model here uses one.
  • Paradigms: contrastive (CLIP → scores), generative (LLaVA/Qwen-VL → text), promptable dense (SAM → masks).
  • Fusion lens: none / dot product (CLIP), early fusion in the LLM (LLaVA, Qwen-VL), cross-attention (SAM decoder, Qwen-VL adapter).
Section 5.2

CLIP: dual encoders and contrastive pretraining

≈ 8 min · Slides: M4L1 s11–20

Motivation: learn from language, not labels

Classical classifiers (ResNet on ImageNet) are trained on a fixed, closed vocabulary of ~1,000 classes; adding a category means collecting labeled data and retraining the head. CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) instead learns to predict which caption goes with which image, straight from raw web text. Captions carry far richer supervision than a class index, and treating labels as text means classification becomes nearest-neighbor search in a shared space: anything expressible in words can be classified zero-shot.

CLIP at a glance

ArchitectureTwo independent encoders, one for images and one for text, with no cross-attention between them
ObjectiveContrastive: pull matching (image, text) pairs together, push every other pair in the batch apart
Training dataWIT (WebImageText): 400 million (image, text) pairs scraped from the public internet
InferenceZero-shot: compare an image embedding with text embeddings of candidate class names
Image (“Pepper the Aussie pup”) → image encoder (ResNet or ViT) → embedding IText “a photo of a dog” → text encoder (Transformer) → embedding TShared space: cosine similarity I · T / τ over an N × N matrix

Image encoder choices

VariantImage encoderEmbedding dimNotes
RN50 / RN101Modified ResNet-50 / 1011024Attention pooling replaces global average pooling
RN50x4 / x16 / x64EfficientNet-style scaled ResNet640–1024Compute-matched scaling of RN50
ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16Vision Transformer, base512The patch size in the name sets the token-grid resolution
ViT-L/14Vision Transformer, large768Strongest released variant (L = large, 14 = 14×14-pixel patches)
ViT-L/14@336pxViT-L/14 fine-tuned at higher resolution768Best published zero-shot accuracy, at higher compute

Each encoder outputs one global feature vector per image, linearly projected into the shared embedding space. Rule of thumb: bigger vision encoder → better zero-shot accuracy → more compute.

Text encoder

  • A standard Transformer: 63M parameters, 12 layers, 512 wide, 8 heads (small next to the image encoders).
  • Lower-cased byte-pair encoding (BPE) with a 49K-token vocabulary; causal (masked) self-attention; captions capped at 76 tokens.
  • The sentence embedding is the activation at the [EOS] token position (not an average of tokens), passed through a learned linear projection to the image-embedding size.

The contrastive objective

For a batch of N (image, text) pairs, compute all N × N similarities. The N diagonal entries are the true pairs (positives); the N² − N off-diagonal entries are negatives, so each image has N − 1 negatives in its row, with no manual negative mining. The loss is a symmetric InfoNCE: cross-entropy over rows (image → text) and over columns (text → image), averaged.

  • τ is a learnable temperature: it rescales the similarities before the softmax and controls how peaked the distribution is.
  • Large batches (32,768 in CLIP) provide more in-batch negatives, a key ingredient of contrastive quality.

Training data and recipe

  • WIT: 400M pairs built from ~500,000 search queries, filtered for query–caption relevance.
  • Batch 32,768; 32 epochs; Adam with decoupled weight decay; cosine LR schedule.
  • Efficiency tricks: mixed precision, gradient checkpointing, half-precision Adam statistics, sharding across GPUs.
  • Compute: the largest ResNet needed enormous compute (the slide quotes ~592 V100 “GPU-years”; the CLIP paper reports 18 days on 592 V100 GPUs), which motivated the more efficient ViT variants.

The training loop in pseudocode

I_f = image_encoder(I)                    # [n, d_i]
T_f = text_encoder(T)                     # [n, d_t]
I_e = l2_normalize(W_i @ I_f)             # project + normalize -> [n, d_e]
T_e = l2_normalize(W_t @ T_f)
logits = (I_e @ T_e.T) * exp(temperature) # [n, n] similarity matrix
labels = arange(n)                        # diagonal = matching pairs
loss_i = cross_entropy(logits,   labels)  # image -> text
loss_t = cross_entropy(logits.T, labels)  # text  -> image
loss   = (loss_i + loss_t) / 2

Crisp summary

  • CLIP replaces a fixed 1,000-class head with language supervision: learn which caption matches which image.
  • Two independent encoders, no cross-attention; trained on WIT, 400M web pairs.
  • Image encoders: ResNets (attention pooling) or ViTs (B/32, B/16, L/14, L/14@336px best); one global vector per image, 512–1024-d.
  • Text encoder: 63M-param, 12-layer, 512-wide, 8-head Transformer; 49K BPE; 76-token cap; embedding taken at [EOS].
  • Loss: symmetric InfoNCE over the N × N matrix (N positives, N² − N negatives; N − 1 negatives per image); learnable τ sets softmax sharpness.
  • Recipe: batch 32,768, 32 epochs, Adam + decoupled weight decay, cosine LR, mixed precision.
Section 5.3

CLIP: zero-shot transfer, results and limits

≈ 6 min · Slides: M4L1 s21–28, s96

Zero-shot classification, step by step

  1. Embed the target image once with the image encoder.
  2. Turn every candidate class name into a sentence, e.g. “a photo of a {label}”, and embed each with the text encoder.
  3. Compute the cosine similarity between the image embedding and every class-sentence embedding.
  4. A softmax over the similarities gives a probability distribution over classes; pick the highest.

Prompt engineering matters: ensembling about 80 hand-written templates (“a photo of a big {label}”, “a sketch of a {label}”, …) measurably improves accuracy. No classification head is trained; any text can act as a label.

Two ways to evaluate a pretrained encoder

Linear probing

Freeze the encoder and train a new linear classifier on labeled data from the target dataset. Measures representation quality; needs labels.

Zero-shot transfer

No target-dataset training at all: class names are embedded by the text encoder and compared with image embeddings.

CLIP's finding: zero-shot CLIP is competitive with, and sometimes beats, linear-probed ResNet features, despite using no target labels. This reframed evaluation: judge a pretrained VLM by how well it generalizes without task-specific fine-tuning.

Headline results

76.2%zero-shot ImageNet top-1, matching a fully supervised ResNet-50
27+datasets evaluated zero-shot, from OCR to satellite imagery to action recognition
400Mimage–text pairs, no manual labels; performance scales smoothly with compute and model size
Dataset (natural distribution shift)ImageNet ResNet-101Zero-shot CLIP ViT-L
ImageNet76.276.2
ImageNet V264.370.1
ImageNet Rendition37.788.9
ObjectNet32.672.3
ImageNet Sketch25.260.2
ImageNet Adversarial2.777.1

Same ImageNet accuracy, far more robust under shift: CLIP generalized to sketches it was never trained on.

Other details

  • Image and text embeddings are L2-normalized, so their dot product equals cosine similarity.
  • The temperature τ in I·T/τ controls softmax sharpness; CLIP learns τ rather than fixing it.

Where CLIP is used today

Image–text retrieval

Rank a large image (or text) corpus by embedding similarity for search.

Guiding generative models

CLIP similarity is the core signal behind DALL·E 2's prior and early text-to-image guidance.

Backbone reuse

CLIP's frozen visual encoder is the vision tower inside LLaVA, and initializes Qwen-VL's ViT.

Moderation & tagging

Open-vocabulary tagging without retraining a classifier for every new category.

Limitations

  • Sacrifices fine-grained detail for coarse-grained semantics: weak at counting objects, reading fine text and spatial relations (“left of”, “behind”).
  • Sensitive to prompt phrasing: accuracy swings with template wording.
  • Inherits biases of web-scraped pairs, which were not curated for fairness or balance.
  • Produces only a similarity score, never free-form language: exactly the gap LLaVA and Qwen-VL close.

Crisp summary

  • Zero-shot: embed the image; embed “a photo of a {label}” for each class; cosine similarity; softmax; argmax. Ensembling ~80 templates helps.
  • Linear probe needs labels; zero-shot needs none, and zero-shot CLIP rivals linear-probed ResNets.
  • 76.2% zero-shot ImageNet top-1 (= supervised ResNet-50), 27+ datasets, and much better robustness (ImageNet-A 2.7 → 77.1, Sketch 25.2 → 60.2).
  • Embeddings are L2-normalized; τ is learned.
  • Uses: retrieval, generative guidance (DALL·E 2), backbone for LLaVA/Qwen-VL, open-vocabulary moderation.
  • Limits: coarse semantics (counting, OCR, spatial relations), prompt sensitivity, web bias, no text generation.
Section 5.4

LLaVA: architecture and GPT-4 instruction data

≈ 8 min · Slides: M4L1 s29–37

Motivation: from similarity scores to visual chat

  • CLIP learns vision–language representations but cannot describe, reason about or answer questions about an image.
  • GPT-4V showed multimodal chat was possible, but it was closed and not reproducible.
  • LLaVA (Liu et al., 2023) asks: can we reuse a pretrained vision encoder and a pretrained LLM and just teach them to follow instructions? Yes, with a lightweight connector and a clever recipe for instruction data.

Architecture: vision encoder → projector → LLM

Image Frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 → features Projection W (linear, or a 2-layer MLP in v1.5) → visual tokens LLM (Vicuna / LLaMA) reads , where are the instruction tokensAutoregressive response

Idea: treat the image as a “foreign language” and let the LLM do the rest. Vicuna is an open-source chat assistant made by supervised instruction fine-tuning of LLaMA / Llama 2; it was chosen for its strong instruction-following ability at the time.

Why a projection is necessary

A CLIP image vector and an LLM word embedding may have the same size on paper, but they live in unrelated geometries: “close together” means different things in each space. Without W, the image of a dog lands at an arbitrary point in the LLM's space, not near “dog” or “animal”. Training W teaches it where that point should land. Such mappings are simple (rotation- and translation-like), so a small projector suffices.

The vision encoder and projection layer

  • Vision tower: a frozen, pretrained CLIP ViT-L/14, reused as-is.
  • Patch-level (grid) features are taken from before (and after) the last transformer layer, preserving more localized detail than a pooled vector.
  • LLaVA v1 projector: a single trainable linear layer. LLaVA-1.5: a 2-layer MLP with GELU, more accurate thanks to non-linear capacity.
  • Simplicity works because the LLM is powerful enough to interpret aligned visual tokens: the connector's job is translation, not reasoning.

How image tokens enter the language model

Each image becomes a fixed number of visual tokens (e.g. 256) with the same dimensionality as a word embedding, inserted alongside text: [system prompt] [visual tokens] [human instruction] [assistant response]. The LLM attends over the whole sequence with ordinary self-attention; no separate cross-attention module is needed. Complexity is pushed into the already-trained LLM, not the fusion mechanism.

Worked example: one training sequence

[SYSTEM] “A chat between a curious user and an AI assistant…”
[IMAGE TOKENS] 256 vectors from CLIP ViT-L/14 → projector: the model's only view of the pixels
[USER] “What is unusual about this image?”
[ASSISTANT] “The man is ironing clothes on an ironing board attached to the back of a moving taxi.” ← loss computed only here

Visual instruction-tuning data generated by GPT-4

No large dataset of (image, instruction, response) triples existed, so the authors built one automatically. COCO images already have captions and bounding boxes; these were converted into text-only symbolic prompts for GPT-4, which never sees the image.

Context type 1 · captions

“A group of people standing outside of a black vehicle with various luggage…”

Context type 2 · boxes

person: [0.681, 0.242, 0.774, 0.694], backpack: [0.384, 0.696, 0.485, 0.914], suitcase: …

From these, GPT-4 writes about 158K samples of three types (example image: people packing luggage into an SUV in a parking garage):

TypeWhat it teachesExample
ConversationMulti-turn visual Q&A grounded in the image“What type of vehicle is featured?” → “A black SUV.”
Detailed descriptionLong, free-form visual descriptions“Describe this image in detail.”
Complex reasoningMulti-step inference beyond surface content“What challenges do these people face?” → fitting all the luggage into the SUV

Crisp summary

  • LLaVA = frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 → projector W → LLM (Vicuna/LLaMA); the image is a “foreign language” for the LLM.
  • The projector is required because CLIP and LLM spaces have unrelated geometries; v1 linear, v1.5 2-layer MLP with GELU.
  • Grid (patch) features from around the last ViT layer; visual tokens (e.g. 256) sit in the sequence with text; plain self-attention, no cross-attention.
  • Training sequence: [system][image tokens][user][assistant]; loss only on the assistant's answer.
  • Data: GPT-4 (text-only, never sees images) turns COCO captions + boxes into ~158K samples: conversation, detailed description, complex reasoning.
Section 5.5

LLaVA: training, versions, evaluation and limits

≈ 6 min · Slides: M4L1 s38–47

Two-stage training recipe

StageFrozenTrainedDataGoal
1 · Feature-alignment pre-trainingVision encoder and LLMProjection layer only~595K filtered CC3M image–caption pairsAlign visual features with the LLM's word-embedding space
2 · End-to-end instruction tuningVision encoderProjector + LLM158K GPT-4-generated instruction samplesInstruction following, conversation, reasoning

Loss: standard autoregressive next-token cross-entropy, computed only over the assistant's response tokens.

LLaVA-1.5 and LLaVA-NeXT

  • LLaVA-1.5: MLP projector (instead of linear); academic VQA datasets mixed into instruction tuning; response-formatting prompts to control answer length; higher input resolution (336px: CLIP ViT-L/336px with Vicuna v1.5 13B). Large gains at low added cost.
  • LLaVA-NeXT (1.6) “AnyRes”: a high-resolution image is split into tiles (a grid configuration such as 2 × 2), each tile is encoded separately by CLIP, and all tile features plus a downsampled global view are concatenated. Captures fine detail without retraining the vision encoder: much better OCR, chart/document understanding and fine-grained recognition, at the cost of more visual tokens per image.
Training samplesPre-trainingInstruction tuning
LLaVA-1.50.67M0.56M
Qwen-VL-Chat1,400M50M
InstructBLIP129M1.2M

LLaVA-1.5 is far more data-efficient than its peers.

Evaluating LLaVA

LLaVA-BenchSmall curated set of images and questions, judged by GPT-4: open-ended chat ability
ScienceQAMultiple-choice science questions with diagrams: grounded reasoning
VQAv2 / GQAStandard visual question answering benchmarks
POPEProbes object hallucination: does the model claim to see things that aren't there?

Open vs closed: LLaVA vs GPT-4V

AspectGPT-4VLLaVA
AccessClosed, API-onlyFully open weights and training recipe
Vision encoderUndisclosedFrozen CLIP ViT-L/14 (published)
Training dataUndisclosed158K published instruction samples + CC3M subset
ReproducibilityNot reproducible by researchersTrainable on a handful of A100s in ~1 day
Role in the fieldProof the task is possibleProof it can be done openly and cheaply

Why LLaVA was a big deal

  • Stage 1 trains only a small projector: a few hours on 8 A100 GPUs. Stage 2 starts from strong pretrained weights (Vicuna): roughly one day end-to-end for the 7B/13B models.
  • Training a multimodal model from scratch would need CLIP-scale image–text pre-training plus LLM pre-training: orders of magnitude more compute.
  • That low barrier made LLaVA the foundation of dozens of open-source VLMs.
LLaVA-Med

The same recipe on biomedical figure–caption pairs with GPT-4-generated medical instructions.

LLaVA-Interactive / LLaVA-Plus

Tool use: call external vision models (segmentation, editing) mid-conversation.

Video-LLaVA

Swap or extend the frozen encoder to handle sampled video frames.

Common thread: the two-stage alignment-then-instruction recipe and the lightweight connector generalize far beyond chat.

Limitations

  • Hallucination: describing objects, attributes or relations not present.
  • Resolution bottleneck (base version): a fixed low-res CLIP input struggles with small text and fine detail.
  • Weak localization and counting: the projector compresses spatial information.
  • Inherits CLIP's blind spots because the encoder is frozen.

Crisp summary

  • Stage 1: freeze vision encoder + LLM, train only the projector on ~595K CC3M pairs (alignment). Stage 2: freeze the vision encoder, train projector + LLM on 158K GPT-4 samples.
  • Loss = next-token cross-entropy on assistant tokens only.
  • LLaVA-1.5: MLP projector, academic VQA data, answer-format prompts, 336px; extremely data-efficient (0.67M + 0.56M samples).
  • LLaVA-NeXT AnyRes: tiles + downsampled global view → better OCR/charts, more tokens.
  • Benchmarks: LLaVA-Bench (GPT-4 judge), ScienceQA, VQAv2/GQA, POPE (hallucination).
  • Cheap (hours for stage 1, ~1 day total), open, reproducible; family: LLaVA-Med, LLaVA-Plus/Interactive (tools), Video-LLaVA.
  • Limits: hallucination, low resolution, weak localization/counting, CLIP's blind spots.
Section 5.6

Qwen-VL: a grounded, multi-image VLM

≈ 11 min · Slides: M4L1 s48–65

Motivation: beyond chat

LLaVA-style models are strong conversationalists but weak at precise spatial grounding and dense text reading (OCR, optical character recognition). Qwen-VL (Bai et al., Alibaba, 2023) targets captioning, VQA, grounding, OCR and multi-image / multi-round dialogue in one model. Its architectural bet: compress variable-resolution visual features into a fixed, efficient token budget without losing spatial information.

ImageViT initialized from OpenCLIP ViT-bigGPosition-aware VL adapter: one cross-attention layer, 256 learnable queries, 2D absolute position encoding → fixed 256 tokensQwen LLM: text + 256 visual tokens + <box>/<ref> grounding tokensGrounded response: text + bounding boxes

The vision encoder

  • A ViT initialized from OpenCLIP's ViT-bigG (~1.9B parameters).
  • Resolution 224×224 during initial pre-training, raised to 448×448 for fine-grained tasks such as OCR and grounding.
  • Patch size 14×14; output is a variable-length grid of patch features, passed to the adapter rather than pooled.

The position-aware vision-language adapter

Problem: a 448×448 image yields hundreds of patch tokens, too many to feed an LLM efficiently at scale. Solution: a single, randomly initialized cross-attention layer with a fixed set of 256 trainable query embeddings. Each query attends over all patch features and produces one output token: 256 in, 256 out, whatever the resolution.

  • Q: learnable embeddings, randomly initialized and trained end-to-end; not derived from the pixels, and the same 256 queries are reused for every image.
  • K, V: ViT patch features plus 2D positional encoding (row, column), so which region each patch came from survives the compression.
  • P, the number of patches, grows with resolution; the output is always exactly 256 tokens, each blending image content (from K, V) with the identity of its query.
  • Contrast with LLaVA, which feeds every patch through (or tiles them). Fixed-length visual tokens keep sequence length and compute constant, which matters for multi-image, multi-round dialogue.

Grounding through special text tokens

<box>…</box>Wraps a bounding box; coordinates are written as text, normalized to the 0–1000 range
<ref>…</ref>Wraps the referring phrase a box belongs to, linking language spans to regions
<img>…</img>Marks where an image's visual tokens are inserted in the sequence

Worked example: referring-expression grounding

User: “Find the red umbrella in the image.”
Model: <ref>the red umbrella</ref><box>(342,128),(410,256)</box>

The LLM generated ordinary text tokens: the coordinates come from next-token prediction like any other word. The same mechanism supports multi-object grounding, region captioning (box → description) and region-based Q&A with no task-specific output head.

A grounded-caption training sample: <img>coyo700m/1.jpg</img>Generate the caption in English with grounding: Beautiful shot of <ref>bees</ref><box>(661,612),(833,812)</box><box>(120,555),(265,770)</box> gathering nectars from <ref>an apricot flower</ref><box>(224,13),(399,313)</box><eos>

Multi-image and multi-round

Several <img> blocks can appear in one sequence, labeled “Picture 1: <img>…</img>”, and dialogue history stays in context like a chat LLM. With grounding this supports requests like “compare the object in image 1 with the region I'm pointing to in image 2”. This breadth (multi-image, grounding, OCR, chat) distinguishes Qwen-VL from LLaVA's chat-first focus.

Three-stage training pipeline

StageResolutionDataTrained / frozen
1 · Pre-training224px~1.4B weakly labeled web image–text pairs (captions, web-crawled, in-house)ViT + adapter trained; LLM frozen
2 · Multi-task pre-training448pxHigh-quality curated, interleaved data; seven tasks trained jointly (captioning, VQA, grounding, OCR, text-only generation, …)Whole model trainable
3 · Supervised instruction fine-tuning448pxConversational, multi-image, multi-round instruction data (LLM self-instruct plus manually annotated / model-generated dialogue for localization and multi-image) → Qwen-VL-ChatLLM + adapter trained; vision encoder frozen again to preserve its representations

Qwen-VL vs LLaVA

AspectLLaVAQwen-VL
ConnectorLinear / 2-layer MLP (all patches kept)Cross-attention adapter (compressed to 256 tokens)
Visual token countScales with image resolution / tilesFixed regardless of resolution
GroundingNot built-inNative, via <box> / <ref> tokens
Multi-image dialogueLimited in the base versionDesigned in from stage 3
Training stages2 (alignment, instruction tuning)3 (pre-train, multi-task, instruction tuning)

OCR and fine-grained recognition

  • 448px training in stages 2–3 lets Qwen-VL read dense, small text: receipts, signage, documents, charts.
  • Native grounding means it can answer “where” as well as “what”, e.g. locate a specific line item on a receipt.
  • OCR is one of the seven jointly trained tasks, not an afterthought; the fixed token budget means adding tasks doesn't blow up sequence length.

Family, limits and what came next

ModelLLMVision encoderRole
Qwen-VLQwen-7BViT-bigG (~1.9B)Base pretrained model
Qwen-VL-ChatQwen-7BViT-bigG (~1.9B)Instruction/chat fine-tuned (stage 3)
Qwen2-VLQwen2 (several sizes)Dynamic-resolution ViTNaive dynamic resolution + M-RoPE
  • The fixed 256-token compression can still lose fine spatial detail compared with keeping every patch.
  • Three-stage training is more complex and costlier to reproduce than LLaVA's two stages.
  • Qwen2-VL replaces the fixed compressor with naive dynamic resolution (a variable token count per image) and M-RoPE, a multimodal rotary position embedding unifying spatial and temporal position.

Crisp summary

  • Qwen-VL: ViT (from OpenCLIP ViT-bigG, 14×14 patches, 224 → 448px) → position-aware adapter → Qwen-7B LLM.
  • Adapter: one cross-attention layer with 256 learnable queries over P patch keys/values + 2D position encoding → always 256 visual tokens.
  • Grounding as text: <box>(x1,y1),(x2,y2)</box> normalized 0–1000, <ref> phrase, <img> insertion point; coordinates come from next-token prediction, no special head.
  • Multi-image via several <img> blocks (“Picture 1: …”) and multi-round history.
  • Training: (1) 224px, 1.4B pairs, LLM frozen; (2) 448px multi-task (7 tasks incl. OCR), all trainable; (3) SFT → Qwen-VL-Chat, ViT frozen.
  • vs LLaVA: compressed fixed tokens, native grounding, multi-image, 3 stages. Limits: compression loses detail; costlier recipe. Qwen2-VL adds dynamic resolution + M-RoPE.
Section 5.7

SAM: Segment Anything

≈ 13 min · Slides: M4L1 s66–83 · M4L2 s4–17

Motivation: a foundation model for segmentation

NLP has foundation models that generalize via prompting; segmentation had no equivalent. SAM (Kirillov et al., Meta AI, 2023) defines promptable segmentation: given an image and a prompt, return a valid mask for whatever the prompt indicates. A prompt can be a point, a bounding box, a rough mask or (experimentally) text. Trained to be promptable at massive scale, SAM transfers zero-shot to segmentation tasks it never saw labels for.

Three components

Image encoder: MAE-pretrained ViT-H/16, heavy (~0.15 s), run once per image → image embedding (256 × 64 × 64)Prompt encoder: lightweight, per prompt (points, box, mask, text)Mask decoder: 2-layer transformer with two-way cross-attention, fast (~50 ms)3 candidate masks + IoU / confidence scores
  • Image encoder: a ViT-H/16 pretrained with masked autoencoding (MAE), then fine-tuned for detection/segmentation. It runs exactly once per image and is the most expensive step; its embedding is cached and reused for every prompt on that image. This heavy-encoder / cheap-decoder split is what makes real-time interactive tools possible.
  • Prompt encoder: sparse prompts (points, boxes) = positional encodings summed with learned embeddings per prompt type; dense prompts (masks) = convolutional embedding (strided-conv downsampling) summed element-wise with the image embedding; text prompts = CLIP text-encoder embedding (experimental).
  • Mask decoder: a lightweight 2-layer transformer decoder with modified two-way attention, then upsampling to a full-resolution mask.

Prompt types and formats

PromptFormatEncodingTypical use
Point (foreground/background click)(N, x, y, label): one (x, y) with a binary labelPositional encoding + learned fg/bg embeddingFast interactive selection
Box(N, x1, y1, x2, y2): two cornersPositional encoding of the two cornersPrecise single-object segmentation
Mask(1, 1024, 1024): a rough draft or “hint”Convolutional embedding summed with the image embeddingRefining an existing rough mask
Text (experimental)A natural-language descriptionCLIP text-encoder embeddingLanguage-driven segmentation

Two-way attention inside the mask decoder

  1. Prompt (output) tokens attend to image tokens: each token gathers the relevant image evidence.
  2. Image tokens attend to prompt tokens: the image representation itself is updated and sharpened by the prompt.

Each block runs self-attention on the tokens → token-to-image attention → MLP → image-to-token attention. Two blocks are stacked; then the image embedding is upsampled (transposed convolutions), a final token-to-image attention runs, and a dot product between each updated output token and the upsampled features produces each mask, plus an IoU score per mask. Positional encodings are re-added to the image embedding at every attention layer. Mnemonic from the slide: Query = what we are looking for, Key = what we have, Value = what we want to propagate.

Resolving ambiguity with multi-mask output

A single point is ambiguous: a click on a shirt could mean the shirt, the person or a button. SAM's decoder predicts three masks at once (whole / part / sub-part), and an auxiliary IoU-prediction head estimates each mask's quality so the best one can be chosen automatically.

Training the mask decoder: focal + dice loss

A mask is mostly background, so a plain pixel-wise loss is dominated by easy background pixels. SAM combines two complementary losses:

Focal loss: pixel-level imbalance

The factor shrinks the loss for pixels already classified correctly, focusing training on hard, misclassified pixels (usually boundaries) → sharper edges.

Dice loss: object-size imbalance

Measures region overlap between the predicted mask X and the ground truth Y, rewarding shape and completeness whether the object is large or tiny.

MSE = mean squared error between the predicted IoU and the actual IoU of each candidate mask.

The data engine behind SA-1B

StageHow masks are produced
1 · Assisted-manualProfessional annotators label masks with SAM's real-time assistance; the model is periodically retrained on the new data, improving both speed and SAM (the figure labels this stage “fully manual annotation”: humans draw high-quality masks → small dataset → an initial, weak model)
2 · Semi-automaticSAM proposes confident masks automatically; annotators focus on adding missed objects, boosting diversity
3 · Fully automaticSAM is prompted with a regular 32 × 32 grid of points per image; confident and stable masks are kept and near-duplicates removed with non-max suppression. This stage produced the vast majority of SA-1B
11Mlicensed, privacy-respecting images
1.1Bhigh-quality masks, ~100 per image
3data-engine stages, each more automated

SA-1B was, at release, by far the largest segmentation dataset ever created. The loop is model → annotate → data → train → model.

Zero-shot transfer and efficiency

  • Edge detection: competitive zero-shot despite never being trained for it.
  • Object proposals / instance segmentation: strong when paired with a separate detector for boxes.
  • Text-to-mask (experimental) via the CLIP-based text prompt path.
  • Interactivity: the ~50 ms decoder allows real-time, in-browser point-and-click segmentation once the image embedding is computed.

Conclusion: pre-SAM interactive models were trained on one dataset and one narrow object domain and needed retraining to move domains (e.g. medical → satellite). SAM's scale and promptable design let it transfer zero-shot across domains.

Applications and the bigger picture

Applications
  • Medical imaging: assisted annotation (with domain fine-tuning); prompts fit a clinician's click-to-select workflow
  • Robotics: object masks for grasp planning and scene understanding
  • Creative & video tools: background removal, rotoscoping, object editing
  • AR / mapping: instance-level scene decomposition, geospatial imagery
Bigger picture
  • SAM has no (Lecture 1) / very limited (Lecture 2) notion of semantic class or language: it segments, it doesn't recognize or describe
  • Grounded-SAM: a grounding/detection VLM locates and names the object; SAM produces the pixel-precise mask
  • SAM 2: extends prompting to video with a streaming memory-attention module and a memory bank that propagates masks across frames
  • Limits: very thin structures, tiny objects, and masks carry no class label

Crisp summary

  • Promptable segmentation: image + prompt (point, box, mask, text) → valid mask; zero-shot transfer from training at scale.
  • Heavy MAE-pretrained ViT-H/16 encoder (~0.15 s) runs once and is cached; lightweight prompt encoder; fast two-way-attention mask decoder (~50 ms).
  • Prompt formats: points (N,x,y,label), boxes (N,x1,y1,x2,y2), masks (1,1024,1024), text via CLIP.
  • Ambiguity: three masks (whole/part/sub-part) + IoU head picks the best.
  • Loss: 20·focal (hard boundary pixels) + 1·dice (region overlap, size-independent) + MSE for the IoU head.
  • Data engine: assisted-manual → semi-automatic → fully automatic (32×32 point grid + NMS) → SA-1B: 11M images, 1.1B masks.
  • Composes with grounding models (Grounded-SAM); SAM 2 adds video memory; no class labels on masks.
Section 5.8

Synthesis: comparing and composing the four

≈ 10 min · Slides: M4L1 s84–93 · M4L2 s18–19

Cross-model comparison

CLIPLLaVAQwen-VLSAM
ParadigmContrastiveGenerative (chat)Generative + groundedPromptable segmentation
Vision backboneResNet / ViT (from scratch)Frozen CLIP ViT-L/14ViT initialized from OpenCLIP bigGMAE-pretrained ViT-H
FusionShared embedding spaceLinear / MLP projectorCross-attention adapter (256 tokens)Two-way cross-attention decoder
OutputSimilarity score / labelFree-form textText + bounding boxesSegmentation mask + IoU
Core training signal400M web (image, text) pairs158K GPT-4-generated instructions1.4B pairs + multi-task + instruction data1.1B masks from the SA-1B data engine

The shared thread: ViT as a universal visual backbone

All four turn pixels into a token sequence with a ViT, trained differently: CLIP trains its ViT from scratch with contrastive supervision; LLaVA reuses CLIP's ViT frozen; Qwen-VL initializes from OpenCLIP; SAM uses an MAE-pretrained ViT. This “pretrain once, adapt everywhere” pattern mirrors BERT/GPT backbone reuse in NLP. What differs is not how they see but what they do with what they saw (match, describe, ground or segment), where fusion happens and how they are trained.

How they compose in real systems

Grounded-SAM

A grounding/detection model (often CLIP-adjacent) proposes boxes and labels; SAM turns each box into a pixel-precise mask.

VLM agents as tool users

An LLaVA/Qwen-VL-style agent calls SAM as an external tool when a task needs a precise mask rather than a description.

Retrieval-augmented generation

CLIP embeddings retrieve relevant images or documents that a generative VLM then reasons over (Module 7).

Diffusion guidance

CLIP similarity still underlies much of text-to-image generation and image editing.

Design trade-offs

Frozen vs fine-tuned backboneLLaVA keeps CLIP frozen (cheap, fast); Qwen-VL fine-tunes its ViT (more capable, costlier)
Token efficiency vs spatial fidelityQwen-VL's fixed 256 tokens trade detail for constant compute; LLaVA-NeXT's tiling trades compute for detail
Data strategyCLIP and Qwen-VL lean on scale (hundreds of millions to billions of noisy pairs); LLaVA and SAM lean on smaller volumes of carefully engineered or human-in-the-loop data
Specialization vs generalitySAM does one task extremely well; Qwen-VL trades some peak performance for breadth

Key takeaways

  • A VLM is structurally a vision encoder + a connector + a consumer of the fused representation; the four differ mainly in the last two.
  • Contrastive pre-training (CLIP) gives excellent reusable representations but no language generation.
  • Instruction tuning (LLaVA) turns a frozen encoder + LLM into a visual chat assistant with a strikingly simple connector.
  • Adapter compression with grounding tokens (Qwen-VL) extends this to grounding, OCR and multi-image reasoning.
  • Promptable, ambiguity-aware decoding (SAM) generalizes segmentation the way prompting generalized NLP.

Discussion questions from the lecture

QuestionA good line of answer
How would you add grounding to a LLaVA-style model with minimal architecture change?Copy Qwen-VL: express boxes as text tokens (<box>…</box> with normalized coordinates) and train on grounding data; no new head needed
Why might fixed 256-token compression hurt reading a dense table of numbers?Many small, precise glyphs compete for a fixed budget, so fine spatial detail is lost
SAM knows “where” but not “what”. What does that make hard?Anything needing class names or language: counting a category, semantic search, captioning; pair it with a grounding model
CLIP needs huge batches for negatives. What does that imply?Contrastive pre-training is compute- and data-hungry, whereas LLaVA-style instruction tuning reuses pretrained parts with little data and compute

Emerging trends

  • Any-resolution, any-aspect-ratio vision encoders (Qwen2-VL dynamic resolution) replacing fixed-size tiling.
  • Unified position embeddings across modalities (M-RoPE) and across time for native video understanding.
  • Any-to-any models that both interpret and produce images, not just text.
  • Tool-using multimodal agents that call specialists such as SAM on demand.

Glossary

Contrastive lossPulls matching pairs together and pushes non-matching pairs apart in embedding space
Zero-shot transferApplying a model to a task or category it was never explicitly trained on
Vision-language connectorThe module translating visual features into a form the LLM (or joint space) can consume
GroundingLinking a piece of language to a specific region of an image
Promptable modelAdapts its output to an arbitrary prompt at inference time, without retraining
Data engineAn iterative pipeline where a model assists, and is improved by, its own data annotation

Crisp summary

  • Compare on paradigm, backbone, fusion, output and training signal (400M pairs · 158K GPT-4 samples · 1.4B pairs + multi-task · 1.1B masks).
  • All use a ViT (CLIP from scratch, LLaVA frozen CLIP, Qwen-VL from OpenCLIP, SAM MAE-pretrained); they differ in what they do with the features.
  • They compose: Grounded-SAM, VLM agents calling SAM, CLIP-powered retrieval for generative VLMs, CLIP-guided diffusion.
  • Trade-offs: frozen vs fine-tuned backbone, tokens vs spatial fidelity, scale vs curated data, specialization vs generality.
  • Trends: dynamic resolution, M-RoPE across modalities and time, any-to-any models, tool-using multimodal agents.

Recap line from the lecture: contrastive → generative → grounded → promptable; next lecture composes VLMs into tool-using pipelines. Further reading: Radford et al. 2021 (CLIP, “Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision”); Liu et al. 2023 (LLaVA, “Visual Instruction Tuning”, and LLaVA-1.5, “Improved Baselines with Visual Instruction Tuning”); Bai et al. 2023 (Qwen-VL); Kirillov et al. 2023 (Segment Anything) and Ravi et al. 2024 (SAM 2); Dosovitskiy et al. 2020 (ViT, “An Image is Worth 16x16 Words”).

Section 6.1

Image captioning: task, models and prompting

≈ 7 min · Slides: M4L2 s20–27

“Imagine a computer that could look at an arbitrary scene … and produce a verbal description. … I suspect that scene analysis will be one of the last cognitive tasks to be performed well by computers.” (Azriel Rosenfeld, a founder of computer vision, 1998)

What is image captioning?

  • Describing an image's content: objects, attributes, scene and overall context. It is not answering a specific question.
  • Distinct from classification: the output is free-form language, not a fixed label.
  • Used for accessibility alt-text, product cataloging, content moderation, social-media captioning and image-search indexing.

Which model fits, and why

Before ViTs: in 2015 Andrej Karpathy fed a pretrained CNN's representation in as the hidden state of an RNN that generated the words, one of the pivotal vision-and-language papers. The line continued with “Show and Tell” → “Show, Attend and Tell” → pre-training the RNN too → today's VLMs.

LLaVA / Qwen-style generative captioning

The default choice: a vision encoder plus an LLM produces natural, fluent descriptions.

CLIP for lightweight tagging

When you only need labels or tags, zero-shot classification is cheaper and faster.

Rule of thumb: need a sentence → generative model; need a tag or category → contrastive model.

From CLIP to “Cap”

Contrastive pre-training uses a vision encoder and a text encoder and a contrastive loss on D-dimensional embeddings. The autoregressive captioning alternative (“Cap”) pairs a ViT encoder with a transformer decoder: the decoder cross-attends to the M image tokens ([M, D]) under a causal self-attention mask and is trained with cross-entropy over the vocabulary ([N, V]) to generate the caption, e.g. “A small cow”. (D = model width, M = number of image tokens, N = number of text tokens, V = vocabulary size.)

Prompting for consistent captions

  • Zero-shot templated prompts work well for general description.
  • Constrain scope and length explicitly: “one sentence, under 125 characters, describing only what is visually present”.
  • For cataloging at scale, fix the template across every call: consistency matters more than any single caption's creativity.

Worked example

Prompt: “Write a one-sentence caption describing only what is visually present in this image.”
Output: “A snow-capped mountain range under a clear sky, with the sun low on the horizon.”

Common pitfalls

  • Hallucination: describing objects or details not actually present.
  • Over-generic captions: “a photo of a scene” tells the reader nothing.
  • Missing the salient detail: describing the background instead of the subject.
  • Inherited bias from the training data.

A real example: an Indian street scene (two riders on a motorcycle carrying a satellite dish)

ModelWhat it saidVerdict
Qwen-VL 2B“A couple is riding a motorcycle… The woman is wearing a blue shirt and red pants… carrying a large satellite dish… The street is quiet and empty”Gets the dish, but invents details (who the riders are, clothing colors)
LLaVA-1.5 7B“…The motorcycle is parked on the side of a street… A handbag can be seen placed on the ground… a casual and fun outing for the couple”Hallucinates a parked bike, a handbag and the mood
LLaVA-1.6 13B“…The person in the back is holding a large, flat object that appears to be a satellite dish. Both individuals are wearing helmets… license plate reads ‘KASI EA 5030’”Best: accurate, and reads the plate thanks to AnyRes high-resolution OCR

Crisp summary

  • Captioning describes objects, attributes, scene and context in free-form language; it differs from classification (fixed label) and VQA (a specific question).
  • History: CNN → RNN captioning (Karpathy 2015; Show & Tell; Show, Attend & Tell) → today's VLMs.
  • Rule of thumb: sentence → generative VLM (LLaVA/Qwen); tag → CLIP zero-shot.
  • “Cap” = ViT encoder + autoregressive decoder trained with cross-entropy, an alternative to contrastive pre-training.
  • Prompting: constrain scope and length (“one sentence, < 125 characters, only what is visible”); fix one template for cataloging.
  • Pitfalls: hallucination, generic captions, missed salient detail, bias. LLaVA-1.6 13B beat Qwen-VL 2B and LLaVA-1.5 7B on the street example, even reading the license plate.
Section 6.2

Captioning: hardness, datasets, training and metrics

≈ 5 min · Slides: M4L2 s28–34

Why captioning is hard

  • Fine-grained distinctions: similar breeds, models or species need detail most captioners gloss over.
  • Compositionality: describing relationships between objects, not just listing them; this needs spatial (sometimes causal) understanding and commonsense for occlusions.
  • Salience is subjective: what's worth mentioning vs background clutter has no single right answer.
  • Evaluation is hardly an exact science: BLEU / ROUGE / METEOR are n-gram based; SPICE is scene-graph based (the lecturer's example evaluates it on the COMPOSITE dataset, Aditya et al. 2015); CLIPScore uses CLIP.
  • Long-tail concepts: rare objects and unusual scenes are under-represented (the slide's example: Lays vs Lijjat).
  • Subjectivity: there is no one correct caption; the right detail depends on the use case.

Popular datasets

DatasetScaleNotes
COCO Captions (2014)330K images, 5 captions eachGold-standard benchmark, human-written
Flickr30K (2014)31K images, 5 captions eachSmaller, similar style to COCO
Conceptual Captions CC3M / CC12M (2018)3M–12M pairsNoisy web alt-text, used for pre-training
Visual Genome (2016)108K images, dense regionsObjects, attributes and relationships annotated
LAION-5B (2022)5B+ pairsWeb-scale and noisy; powers foundation-model pre-training

The field moved from a human-annotated era (SBU 2011, Flickr8k 2013, Flickr30k 2014, MS COCO 2014, Visual Genome) to a web-scale alt-text era (Conceptual Captions 2018, nocaps 2019, LAION-5B 2022). CapArena (2025) is a platform where humans judge which of two models' captions is better: precise, informative and not hallucinating.

How state-of-the-art captioners are trained

Stage 1 · broad pre-training: contrastive or generative on noisy web pairs (LAION, CC12M)Stage 2 · curated fine-tuning on human captions (COCO) for fluent, accurate styleStage 3 · instruction tuning (the LLaVA recipe) for conversational captioning

Data quality: BLIP-style bootstrapping trains a captioner and a filter together to clean noisy web captions before reuse.

Performance (CIDEr, directional)

Model generationCOCO CIDErNoCaps CIDEr
Pre-transformer baselines (~2015–18)~110–120—
Early VLM captioners (BLIP-2 class)~140+~120
Recent open models (InternVL3 class)~143 (zero-shot)~126

NoCaps = novel object captioning at scale (ICCV 2019): train on COCO, validate/test on images with in-domain, near-domain and out-of-domain objects. Scores shift quickly and vary by protocol.

Remaining challenges

  • Hallucination is still unsolved; even state-of-the-art models describe plausible but absent objects.
  • Automatic metrics (CIDEr, BLEU) correlate poorly with human judgment of usefulness.
  • Bias: captions can reflect and amplify demographic or cultural skew.
  • Style control (a tone or brand voice) still needs heavy prompt engineering or fine-tuning.
  • Cross-lingual and cross-cultural generalization lags English.

Crisp summary

  • Hard because of fine-grained detail, compositional relations, subjective salience, imperfect metrics, long-tail concepts and subjectivity.
  • Metrics: BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR (n-gram), SPICE (scene graph), CLIPScore (CLIP), CIDEr (benchmark tables).
  • Datasets: COCO (330K × 5 captions, gold standard), Flickr30K (31K), CC3M/12M (noisy alt-text), Visual Genome (108K dense regions), LAION-5B (5B+); CapArena for human pairwise judging.
  • Training: noisy web pre-training → curated COCO fine-tuning → instruction tuning; BLIP-style bootstrapping cleans captions.
  • COCO CIDEr ~110–120 → ~140+ → ~143; NoCaps tests novel objects.
  • Open problems: hallucination, metric–human mismatch, bias, style control, non-English cultures.
Section 6.3

Visual question answering (VQA)

≈ 9 min · Slides: M4L2 s35–49

What is VQA?

Answering a specific, open-ended question grounded in an image. Unlike captioning, the question drives what matters; everything else can be ignored. Question types: (a) yes/no (“Are there shadows on the sidewalk?”), (b) multiple choice (“What kind of bears are these?”), (c) counting (“How many windows?”), (d) open-ended (“What is the man doing?” → walking). Used in customer-support screenshot triage, visual search assistants, education and accessibility Q&A.

Which model fits

Before ViTs: CNN image features and RNN question features were fused (element-wise product) and fed to a softmax over candidate answers (e.g. “elephant” 0.970) or to an RNN answer generator.

  • LLaVA-style models: strong for general, conversational visual Q&A.
  • Qwen-VL: preferred when the question needs grounding, pointing or reading text in the image.
  • Rule of thumb: a general question about the whole image → either model; a question about a specific region or needing OCR → Qwen-VL.

Prompting for reliable VQA

  • A zero-shot direct question works for most everyday queries.
  • Chain-of-thought for counting or comparison: “first list every object and its color, then count how many are red”. The intermediate list is auditable.
  • Few-shot examples help when the question uses domain vocabulary the model doesn't default to.

Worked example

Q: “How many distinct peaks are visible in this image?” A: “Two: a smaller peak on the left and a taller, sunlit peak on the right.”

Are VLMs looking at the image? (2026 studies)

Looking correctly?

LLaVA-1.5's focus regions on counting questions: correct focus + correct answer; correct focus but wrong answer (misinterpretation); wrong focus → wrong answer; and occasionally a correct answer despite attending to irrelevant regions.

Looking at all?

Given the Mona Lisa and a fully blurred version, LLaVA-1.5 still answers about “a painting” (even naming Van Gogh). The probability of most answer tokens barely changes with or without the image: many tokens come from the language prior, not the visual input.

Common pitfalls

  • Presupposition hallucination: “What color is the cat?” answered confidently when there is no cat. Fix: ground the prompt and explicitly allow “not present” as an answer.
  • Overconfidence: wrong answers stated with the same certainty as right ones.
  • Ambiguous questions: “Is this good?” needs a defined criterion.

Why VQA is hard

  • Three skills at once: visual perception, language understanding, and world/commonsense knowledge with reasoning.
  • Question ambiguity before the image is even considered.
  • Answers beyond the pixels: counting, spatial reasoning or external knowledge often can't be read directly off the image.
  • Open-ended answer space: no fixed label set, so evaluation itself is hard.

Popular datasets

DatasetScaleTests
VQAv2~1.1M questions on COCO imagesThe standard general-purpose benchmark
GQA~22M questions generated from scene graphsCompositional reasoning
OK-VQA~14K questionsExternal / world knowledge beyond the image
TextVQA~45K questionsReading text within the image
VizWiz~31K questionsReal questions from blind / low-vision users; naturally noisy photos

How state-of-the-art VQA models are trained

  • Start from a base generative VLM (LLaVA / Qwen-VL recipe), then fine-tune on VQA-style instruction data.
  • Mix VQAv2, GQA, OK-VQA and TextVQA to broaden question-type coverage.
  • Answer-format supervision: train short, direct answers where benchmarks expect them, not verbose chat.
  • Preference tuning (RLHF-style) to reduce hallucinated or overconfident answers. Preference data can be made synthetically: x = [image + question], y = correct answer, y' = an incorrect answer created by
    • a random answer: image + question + <random answer>;
    • a random question: image + <random question> + answer;
    • an image perturbation that “makes the V matter”: <image with blackened objects> + question + answer.

Performance: the evaluation caveat

  • In human-judged side-by-side tests, GPT-4V and Qwen-VL-Chat were rated comparably well on VQAv2 / OK-VQA-style questions, zero-shot.
  • Strict automatic VQA-accuracy metrics penalize verbose, correct-but-differently-phrased answers; GPT-4V's free-form style scored poorly on them despite strong human ratings.
  • Takeaway: benchmark numbers can undersell real capability, so how you evaluate matters as much as which model you use. The field is moving toward verifying the reasoning: produce an explanation, evaluate the explanation, verify the chain of thought.
  • GQA-style compositional reasoning remains a weak point for open and closed models.

Remaining challenges

  • Commonsense / world-knowledge questions (OK-VQA style) lag pure perception questions.
  • Counting is unreliable past roughly 5–10 objects, especially with occlusion.
  • Models answer confidently even when a question presupposes something false or is unanswerable.
  • Compositional, multi-step questions (GQA style) underperform simple look-ups.

Crisp summary

  • VQA answers a specific question about an image (yes/no, multiple choice, counting, open-ended); captioning describes generally.
  • LLaVA for general conversational VQA; Qwen-VL when grounding, pointing or OCR is needed.
  • Prompting: direct zero-shot; chain-of-thought for counting/comparison (auditable list first); few-shot for domain vocabulary.
  • VLMs often lean on language priors (blurred Mona Lisa still gets an answer); presupposition hallucination needs an explicit “not present” option.
  • Datasets: VQAv2 (~1.1M, COCO), GQA (~22M, compositional), OK-VQA (~14K, knowledge), TextVQA (~45K, OCR), VizWiz (~31K, blind users).
  • Training: base VLM + mixed VQA data + short-answer supervision + preference tuning with synthetic negatives (random answer, random question, blackened objects).
  • Strict metrics penalize verbose correct answers (GPT-4V); counting fails beyond ~5–10 objects.
Section 6.4

Document intelligence

≈ 11 min · Slides: M4L2 s50–66

What is document intelligence?

Extracting structured information from documents (invoices, forms, receipts, contracts) by combining OCR with layout understanding. The output isn't prose; it is specific fields a downstream system can consume. Used for invoice processing, expense automation, contract review and form digitization.

Which model fits, and why it needs more innovation

  • Qwen-VL is the natural fit: native OCR plus grounding lets it read dense text and locate where a field sits on the page.
  • Dedicated OCR pipelines are faster and cheaper for pure text extraction but weaker at reasoning about layout and relations between fields.
  • Rule of thumb: structured, layout-aware extraction → VLM; simple bulk text extraction → dedicated OCR.
  • Most image tasks do well at low resolution (224×224, 448×448) because they need high-level semantics; documents don't. Running OCR outside and pasting the text into a VLM loses the spatial layout. DocVLM and DAVE address this.

Prompting for structured extraction

  • State the exact output schema; don't just describe the fields, show the JSON shape.
  • Name every field explicitly; don't rely on the model to guess which fields matter.
  • For multi-field documents, ask for one JSON object per document, not free text.

Worked example: an invoice

Document: Vendor: Acme Supplies Ltd. · Invoice #: INV-20394 · Date: 14 Mar 2026 · Total: $481.50
Prompt: “Extract vendor, invoice number, date, and total. Respond only as JSON: {vendor, invoice_number, date, total}”

{"vendor": "Acme Supplies Ltd.", "invoice_number": "INV-20394",
 "date": "2026-03-14", "total": "481.50"}

Common pitfalls and why it is hard

Pitfalls
  • Layout variability: a prompt tuned on one invoice template fails on another (tax documents)
  • Low-quality scans: skew, blur, low resolution degrade OCR
  • Hallucinated fields: a plausible value is invented when a field is missing
  • High-stakes documents need human verification; never auto-approve financial or legal fields
Why it is hard
  • Three skills at once: OCR precision, layout understanding and reasoning about field relationships
  • Extreme layout diversity across document types, vendors, regions, languages
  • Real-world scan quality: skew, noise, handwriting, low resolution, multi-column layouts
  • High stakes leave little room for silent error

Case study: DAVE (Huang et al., ICLR 2026), a vision encoder for documents and web agents

  • Problem: CLIP/SigLIP-style encoders lack the low-level structural and spatial features documents and UIs need; DINO-style self-supervised encoders have them but transfer poorly beyond natural images.
  • Idea: a purpose-built encoder that learns structure from unlabeled document and web images, fused with a frozen generalist encoder (SigLIP2) for semantics.
  • Stage 1, self-supervised MAE pre-training: masked image → encoder → decoder → pixel reconstruction. The modified MAE reconstructs raw pixel values rather than per-patch-normalized targets, because normalization is unstable on the low inter-patch variance of documents.
  • Stage 2, supervised multi-decoder pre-training (grounding, layout prediction, OCR) with several LLM decoders, plus:
    • Weight-space model merging: train one encoder instance per LLM decoder (Qwen, Llama, Phi), then learn merge coefficients (not simple averaging) to combine them into one decoder-agnostic encoder.
    • Ensemble training: concatenate the frozen SigLIP2 encoder with the specialized one, keeping general semantics while specializing in structure and layout.
  • Results: state of the art on DocBank and DocLayNet; +10.5% average over SigLIP2 on document/web VL benchmarks; +5% on Mind2Web web-agent tasks without losing general VQA ability. Ablations show merging is the single biggest driver (55.6% → 63.4%).

Optional case study: DocVLM

  • OCR encoder: a DocFormerV2-based T5 encoder (344M parameters, encoder-only) that encodes OCR text tokens plus their 2D layout / bounding-box positions; its visual branch is dropped to avoid redundancy.
  • Query compression: 64 learnable queries are processed jointly with the OCR and instruction embeddings, distilling the OCR/layout signal into a compact, instruction-aware representation.
  • Fusion: the compressed query outputs are projected to the VLM's hidden size and concatenated with the visual tokens before the frozen LLM; no LLM architecture changes.
  • Model-agnostic: plugs into any VLM; the base VLM stays frozen throughout.

Datasets

DatasetScaleNotes
DocVQA~50K questions, 12K+ documentsStandard document-VQA benchmark, scored with ANLS
InfographicVQAInfographic-style documentsDense visual + text layout; harder than plain scans
RVL-CDIP400K documents, 16 classesDocument-type classification
FUNSD~200 noisy scanned formsForm understanding; key–value / entity extraction

How state-of-the-art systems are trained

  • Resolution is the biggest lever: Qwen-VL's progression 224px → 448px → dynamic resolution is the single largest driver of document gains.
  • Joint multi-task pre-training: OCR, layout-QA and grounding data mixed together (Qwen-VL's Stage 2).
  • Synthetic document generation: rendered text, tables and forms at scale.
  • Domain fine-tuning: invoice- or receipt-specific tuning on a general document-VLM backbone.
ModelDocVQA (ANLS)ChartQA (accuracy)Year
Qwen-VL (original)65.165.72023
Qwen2-VL-7B94.583.02024
Current leading models~96%+~89%+2025

Some of the fastest year-over-year gains of any VLM task, driven largely by resolution and OCR-focused data.

Remaining challenges

  • Handwriting is still clearly weaker than printed text.
  • Multi-page documents and cross-page reasoning.
  • Table structure: merged cells, nested headers.
  • Numerical precision matters enormously, and models don't yet reliably flag low-confidence reads.
  • Low-resource languages and non-Latin scripts lag English and Chinese.

Crisp summary

  • Document intelligence = OCR + layout → structured fields (invoices, forms, receipts, contracts).
  • Qwen-VL fits (OCR + grounding); dedicated OCR is cheaper for bulk text but weak on layout. Documents need high resolution; external OCR loses layout.
  • Prompt with an explicit JSON schema, every field named, one object per document (invoice → {vendor, invoice_number, date, total}).
  • Pitfalls: template variability, poor scans, hallucinated missing fields; route high-stakes fields to humans.
  • DAVE: MAE on raw pixels (unlabeled doc/web images) → multi-decoder supervised stage, learned weight merging (biggest gain, 55.6 → 63.4) + SigLIP2 ensemble; +10.5% vs SigLIP2, +5% Mind2Web.
  • DocVLM: 344M OCR+layout T5 encoder, 64 learnable queries, concatenated to visual tokens; base VLM frozen.
  • DocVQA (ANLS), InfographicVQA, RVL-CDIP (400K, 16 classes), FUNSD (~200 forms); DocVQA 65.1 → 94.5 → ~96+.
Section 6.5

Visual reasoning and chart QA

≈ 9 min · Slides: M4L2 s67–83

What is visual reasoning?

Multi-step inference beyond surface recognition: spatial relationships, counting, comparison, cause and effect. Unlike VQA, the answer requires combining multiple observations, not reading one off the image. Used in quality inspection, safety audits, complex diagram interpretation and comparative analysis.

Which model fits

  • Reasoning strength tracks the LLM backbone: a stronger language model reasons better, whichever vision encoder feeds it.
  • LLaVA-style and Qwen-VL are both viable; Qwen-VL has an edge when reasoning must reference a specific region.
  • Rule of thumb: the vision encoder gets you the pixels; the LLM does the actual reasoning.

Prompting with chain-of-thought

Decompose explicitly: ask the model to list relevant observations before answering (“first identify every relevant object, then reason step by step to the answer”). Intermediate reasoning becomes auditable, so errors are easier to catch than in one confident jump.

Direct prompt

“Is it safe to park here?” → higher risk of a confident but wrong yes/no.

Chain-of-thought prompt

“First list every visible sign and marking, then decide if parking is allowed.” → surfaces the visible “No Parking” sign before answering.

Pitfalls and why it is hard

Pitfalls
  • Compounding errors: one wrong intermediate observation propagates to the answer
  • False confidence: steps look rigorous but are wrong
  • No self-check: without asking the model to verify its steps, errors go uncaught (mitigation: ask it to verify its intermediate steps)
Why it is hard
  • Multi-step inference chains several observations
  • Compounding errors derail the final answer
  • External knowledge (physics, math, domain expertise) beyond what is visible
  • Hard to verify: “reasoned correctly” vs “pattern-matched a similar training example”

Datasets

DatasetScale / focusTests
MMMU~11.5K college-level questionsExpert-level multimodal reasoning across disciplines
MathVistaMath-focused visual reasoningVisual perception + mathematical problem solving
ScienceQA~21K science questions with diagramsGrade-school to high-school science reasoning
NLVR2Image-pair reasoningCompositional / relational reasoning across two images
WinogroundCompositional reasoningFamously hard: near-random performance for many models

How state-of-the-art systems are trained

  • A strong reasoning LLM trained with chain-of-thought data transfers that strength once vision-grounded (the Lecture 1 synthesis point).
  • Explicit rationale data: instruction tuning increasingly includes step-by-step traces, not just final answers.
  • Reasoning-specific preference / RL tuning, mirroring text-only reasoning LLMs.
  • Curriculum mixing: general VQA, math, science and diagram data combined during fine-tuning rather than trained in isolation.

Performance

  • MMMU: open models in the low-50s% in early 2024; leading open and closed models in the low-to-mid 60s% by mid-2024.
  • MathVista: leading models in the high-50s to 60s%, versus a much higher human baseline.
  • Visual reasoning shows among the largest gaps between open and closed models, and between any model and human experts.

Remaining challenges

  • Multi-step arithmetic or geometric reasoning grounded in an image is still unreliable.
  • Models don't know when they don't know: confident wrong answers on hard questions.
  • Weak at counterfactual or hypothetical reasoning (“what would happen if…”).
  • Benchmark contamination: some gains may reflect memorization, not reasoning.

Chart & data QA

Reading and reasoning over charts and graphs. Primary models: Qwen-VL or high-resolution LLaVA. Prompting strategy: extract the values first, then reason, and be honest about uncertainty. ChartQA accuracy rose from 65.7 (Qwen-VL, 2023) to 83.0 (Qwen2-VL-7B, 2024) to ~89%+ (2025).

Recap: application → model → prompting strategy

ApplicationPrimary modelPrompting strategy
Image understandingLLaVA-style / CLIPZero-shot, scoped and length-constrained
Visual Q&ALLaVA-style / Qwen-VLZero-shot, or chain-of-thought for counting / comparison
Document intelligenceQwen-VLStructured output with an explicit JSON schema
Visual reasoningLLaVA-style / Qwen-VLChain-of-thought, decomposed into explicit steps
Chart & data QAQwen-VL / high-res LLaVAExtract values first, then reason, plus honesty about uncertainty

Key takeaways of the lecture

  • Every application maps back to the four architectures; the skill is matching task shape to model paradigm.
  • SAM segments; it doesn't recognize, read or reason. It is a component to compose, not a standalone answer.
  • Prompting is task-specific: scope constraints for captioning, chain-of-thought for reasoning and counting, schemas for extraction.
  • Every task has a known failure mode: plan for it before you deploy, not after.

Crisp summary

  • Visual reasoning combines several observations (spatial relations, counting, comparison, cause–effect); VQA often reads one fact.
  • Reasoning quality tracks the LLM backbone: “the encoder gets pixels, the LLM reasons”; Qwen-VL helps for region references.
  • Chain-of-thought (list observations, then decide) makes reasoning auditable: the “No Parking” sign example.
  • Risks: compounding errors, false confidence, no self-check → ask the model to verify its steps.
  • Datasets: MMMU (~11.5K college level), MathVista, ScienceQA (~21K), NLVR2 (image pairs), Winoground (near-random for many models).
  • MMMU low-50s → low/mid-60s% (2024); largest open-vs-closed and model-vs-human gaps.
  • Chart QA: Qwen-VL / high-res LLaVA; extract values first, then reason; ChartQA 65.7 → 83.0 → ~89+.
