Section 7.1

Text search and dense retrieval

≈ 5 min · Slides: M4L3 s8–10, s13–15, s23–24

What is text search?

Given a query, find the most relevant passages in a large text corpus: the first half of every RAG pipeline. Retrieval returns a ranked list of existing passages; it doesn't generate new text.

ApproachHow it matchesStrengthsWeakness
Keyword search (TF-IDF, BM25)Exact wordsFast, interpretableMisses synonyms and paraphrases
Semantic search (dense embeddings)Meaning, not wording: “canceling a subscription” retrieves “end my plan”Handles paraphraseCan miss exact terms, negation, numbers
Hybrid searchBlends keyword and semantic signalsBest of bothTwo systems to run

How dense retrieval works

Query → text encoderPassages → text encoder (same space)Shared vector spaceNearest neighbors → ranked results

A bi-encoder embeds query and documents separately into the same vector space, so retrieval becomes nearest-neighbor search. At scale, approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes such as FAISS or HNSW keep this fast over millions of passages, because exact search doesn't scale; ANN trades a little accuracy for large speed gains. Reranking, or hybrid BM25 + dense scoring, further improves precision.

Worked example

Query: “How do I reset my password?”

  1. “To reset your password, go to Settings…” 0.91
  2. “Account recovery options include…” 0.84
  3. “If you forgot your login credentials…” 0.79

None repeat the query's exact wording: the match is on meaning, not keywords.

Benchmarks, training and performance

  • Benchmarks: MS MARCO (passage ranking), BEIR (zero-shot generalization), MTEB (56+ tasks including retrieval).
  • Training: contrastive learning pulls a query and its correct passage together (the CLIP idea applied to text), sharpened by hard-negative mining against near-miss wrong answers. Confusable negatives teach far more than random ones.
  • State of play: leading models average around 74 on the full MTEB suite and around 72 on the harder retrieval subset, and climb almost every quarter. Retrieval itself is scored with precision, recall and F1.

Remaining challenges

  • Long documents don't fit neatly into one embedding: chunking strategy strongly affects retrieval quality.
  • Domain shift: a web-search model may underperform on legal or medical text without fine-tuning.
  • Embeddings can miss negation and numbers: “revenue grew” and “revenue did not grow” can embed as deceptively similar.
  • Evaluation is imperfect: a passage can be on-topic without actually answering the question.

Crisp summary

  • Text search retrieves ranked existing passages: the first half of RAG.
  • BM25/TF-IDF match exact words (fast, interpretable, miss paraphrases); dense embeddings match meaning; hybrid blends both.
  • Bi-encoder: query and documents encoded separately into one space → nearest-neighbor search; FAISS/HNSW ANN indexes make it scale; reranking boosts precision.
  • Benchmarks: MS MARCO, BEIR (zero-shot), MTEB (56+ tasks; leaders ≈74 overall, ≈72 retrieval).
  • Trained contrastively with hard negatives.
  • Challenges: chunking long docs, domain shift, negation/numbers, topical ≠ answering.
Section 7.2

RAG for NLP and ColBERT late interaction

≈ 4 min · Slides: M4L3 s11–12

RAG for NLP in one slide (Lewis et al.)

Query encoder q(x)Document index d(z): the non-parametric retriever p_ηMaximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) → top-K documents z_iGenerator p_θ: a parametric seq2seq modelMarginalize over the retrieved documents → answer
  • The retrieved document z is treated as a latent variable; training back-propagates end-to-end through the query encoder q and the generator p_θ.
  • One architecture serves many tasks: question answering (“Define ‘middle ear’”), fact verification (“Barack Obama was born in Hawaii” → supports) and Jeopardy question generation (“The Divine Comedy” → “a 14th-century work in three sections: Inferno, Purgatorio, Paradiso”).

ColBERT: late interaction for text (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020)

Instead of one vector per passage, ColBERT keeps one embedding per token and matches at the token level.

  • Training triplet: query q (“what causes global warming?”), a relevant passage d⁺, and a negative d⁻ (“the capital of France is Paris”). A shared BERT encoder produces token embeddings for the query (|Q| × d) and each document (|D| × d).
  • MaxSim scoring: each query token finds its most similar document token; the sum of those maxima is the relevance score:
  • Loss: a pairwise / in-batch contrastive loss that pushes above :
  • Offline: index every document's token embeddings in a vector index (FAISS). Online: encode the query, run ANN search with MaxSim, return the top-k passages.

This “many small vectors, matched finely” idea is exactly what ColPali later applies to page images (Section 7.5).

Crisp summary

  • RAG (Lewis et al.): query encoder + document index (non-parametric retriever) → MIPS top-K → seq2seq generator (parametric) → marginalize over documents; z is latent; trained end-to-end.
  • Same model handles QA, fact verification and Jeopardy-style question generation.
  • ColBERT: per-token embeddings from a shared BERT; score = Σ over query tokens of the max similarity to any document token (MaxSim).
  • Trained with a contrastive loss on (q, d⁺, d⁻) triplets; offline token-level indexing, online ANN + MaxSim.
Section 7.3

Image search: cross-modal retrieval

≈ 4 min · Slides: M4L3 s16–22, s25–26

What is image search?

  • Text-to-image: type a description, retrieve matching images (the most common direction).
  • Image-to-image: give an example image, retrieve visually similar ones.
  • Which model fits (CLIP recap): CLIP's shared embedding space is exactly what's needed; a text query and a candidate image are compared directly, with no translation step.
  • Used for e-commerce product search, stock-photo libraries, reverse image search and content moderation at scale.

How cross-modal retrieval works

Text (or image) query → CLIP encoderImage corpus → CLIP image encoderShared vector spaceNearest neighbors → ranked images

The query and document encoders are different networks (one for text, one for images), but CLIP's contrastive training places their outputs in the same space, so nearest-neighbor search works across modalities. The same ANN indexes (FAISS, HNSW) serve here too: only what's embedded changes.

Worked example

Query: “snow-capped mountains at sunset” → Rank 1 (score 0.88), Rank 2 (0.81). No caption or tag was attached to either image; the match comes purely from CLIP's shared space, computed at query time.

The lecture's demo ran image-to-image and text-to-image search with DINO / SigLIP embeddings + FAISS on Flickr8k / COCO. The best visual encoders named: DINOv2, DINOv3, SigLIP-2.

Benchmarks, training and performance

  • Benchmarks: Flickr30K and MS COCO (retrieval splits), scored with Recall@1/5/10. Recall@5 asks whether the correct result appears in the top 5.
  • Training: the same contrastive recipe as CLIP; no separate retrieval-specific training is needed, and scale drives most of the gain.
  • Zero-shot Flickr30K, directionally: base CLIP-scale models reach roughly 51% image→text Recall@1; modern VLM-scale encoders roughly 85%.

Remaining challenges

  • Fine-grained queries: “a red car” works; “the specific red sedan facing left in the third row” does not.
  • Compositional queries combining several constraints are a known weak point of CLIP-style embeddings.
  • Bias in the corpus and training data skews what surfaces as “most relevant”.
  • Long, detailed text queries exceed what the text encoder was trained to represent.

Crisp summary

  • Two directions: text-to-image (most common) and image-to-image.
  • CLIP's shared space lets text and images be compared directly; different encoders, same space; same FAISS/HNSW indexes as text search.
  • No captions or tags needed: “snow-capped mountains at sunset” matched purely in embedding space.
  • Strong encoders: DINOv2/v3, SigLIP-2. Benchmarks: Flickr30K, COCO with Recall@K (Flickr30K R@1 ≈ 51% base CLIP → ≈ 85% modern).
  • Weak spots: fine-grained and compositional queries, bias, long queries.
Section 7.4

Multimodal RAG: what, why and how

≈ 7 min · Slides: M4L3 s3–6, s28–35

Definition

Multimodal RAG extends retrieval-augmented generation with diverse data types (text, images, audio, video) from external knowledge sources. By integrating retrieved information dynamically, it addresses hallucination and outdated knowledge, improving factual grounding, accuracy and reasoning.

RAG recapped: retrieve relevant content for a query, then generate an answer grounded in it rather than in memorized knowledge. The multimodal extension: the retrieved content can be images, tables, charts or entire document pages.

Example taskInputRetrieved knowledgeAnswer
Visual QA“Where is this place in China?” + photoGreat Wall texts and imagesJiangjunlou watchtower, Gubeikou Great Wall
Document VQA“What economic strategies can healthcare systems adopt for chronic diseases?”Document pages and chartsA grounded summary
Medical VQA“Is there any focal airspace consolidation on the X-ray?”Similar X-rays and knowledgeNo
ClassificationA rabbit photoAngora rabbit knowledgeA brown-haired Angora rabbit

Why real documents need it

Text-only RAG fails

Q: “What is the ‘actual’ value per 1000 during 1975?” (Figure C.2, age-adjusted motor-vehicle-accident mortality, Canada). Retrieval returns only the caption and surrounding text; the figure itself isn't retrieved, so the LLM “cannot determine” the value.

Multimodal RAG passes

The figure image is retrieved (rank 1, image + caption). The model locates 1975 on the x-axis, reads the solid “actual” curve and answers ≈ 0.24.

  • A financial report's key number often lives in a chart, not a sentence; a manual's critical detail is often a diagram.
  • Traditional RAG extracts only text, discarding exactly the visual information that carries the answer.
  • This is the document-intelligence problem of Lecture 2, reapplied at the scale of a whole retrieval system.

The full pipeline in one picture

User query (e.g. “Explain the historical significance of this painting [Starry Night] and create a modern reinterpretation”)Query pre-processing: rewriting, expansion, dropout → query encoderMultimodal corpus → multimodal encoder → shared embedding spaceRetrieval: modality-centric search (text, vision/video, audio, document), similarity search (MIPS variants), re-ranking (example selection, relevance scoring, filtering)Fusion: score fusion and alignment, cross-attention, unified projectionsAugmentation: context enrichment; adaptive / iterative retrievalGeneration by a multimodal LLM: in-context learning, CoT, instruction tuning, source attribution, agentic interaction

Training losses in the picture: alignment loss, generation loss and noise management.

Architecture: retriever + generator

User queryRetriever searches indexed document pagesTop-k retrieved pagesGenerator (a VLM): query + pages → answerGrounded answer

Pieces of the puzzle: given query q and documents D, retrieve , then answer . Retrieval has an offline indexing phase and an online querying phase. A good retriever supports multiple modalities, performs strongly, and is fast at both querying and indexing. A good reader/generator has strong reasoning, good instruction fine-tuning and works with simple prompting.

Two retrieval strategies

Parse-then-embed (traditional)

Run OCR and layout analysis first, extract text and tables, then embed the extracted text.

Retrieval in vision space

Skip parsing: embed a screenshot of the whole page directly with a vision-language model.

Vision space is gaining ground because OCR and layout analysis are brittle and lossy, especially on charts, tables and unusual layouts; embedding the page image sidesteps that failure point.

Storage strategies shape the search

StrategyHowSearch
Ground everything into one modalitye.g. a multimodal LLM turns images into text summaries → text encoder → single-modal DBUnified-representation search
Embed all modalities into a shared spaceA multimodal encoder → one multimodal DBKeep original modalities; cross-modality search
Separate databases per modalityImage encoder → image DB; text encoder → text DBSearch each separately

Crisp summary

  • Multimodal RAG retrieves images, tables, charts or pages (not just text) and generates a grounded answer, reducing hallucination and stale knowledge.
  • Text-only RAG can't see the chart: the 1975 mortality question fails on caption text and succeeds (≈0.24) when the figure is retrieved.
  • Architecture: retriever (offline indexing, online querying) → top-k pages → VLM generator; d ~ p(d|q), a ~ q(a|q,d).
  • Strategies: parse-then-embed (OCR + layout, brittle) vs vision-space retrieval (embed page screenshots).
  • Storage: unify into one modality, one shared multimodal space, or separate per-modality databases.
Section 7.5

ColPali: document retrieval in vision space

≈ 8 min · Slides: M4L3 s32, s36–40, s47–49

Late-interaction retrieval

Instead of compressing a page into one vector, represent it as many small vectors, one per image patch or text token. At query time each part of the query is matched against the best-fitting part of the document, and those fine-grained scores are combined, which is richer than a single dot product. The technique comes from ColBERT (text); ColPali uses the same mechanism for page images.

ColPali vs a standard pipeline (Faysse et al., ICLR 2025)

Standard retrievalColPali
Offline indexingPDF → OCR → layout detection → captioning of figures + chunking → text embedding modelPage image → vision encoder → LLM (PaliGemma) → projection → per-patch embeddings
Indexing time7.22 s / page0.39 s / page
Online queryText embedding, ~22 ms / queryQuery through the LLM → per-token embeddings → MaxSim sum, ~30 ms / query
Quality (NDCG@5)0.660.81

Architecture

Backbone: PaliGemma-3B (a VLM) with a linear projection to D = 128, the same embedding size as ColBERT, producing one vector per image patch for documents and one per token for queries, instead of one pooled vector.

Each query token finds its best-matching patch via the max; all the best matches are summed.

Training: an in-batch contrastive loss that pushes each pair's positive score above the hardest in-batch negative , end-to-end, with no OCR:

Latency

Offline indexing (per page)Latency
PDF parser (layout detection + OCR + captioning)7.22 s
SigLIP0.12 s
ColPali (page encoding)0.39 s

Offline indexing with ColPali is much simpler and faster than standard pipelines; at runtime, query latency is very good for all systems (≤ 22 ms on an NVIDIA L4) thanks to fast query encoding and similarity matching.

Indexing multimodal documents

  • Chunking matters as much as in text RAG: too small loses context, too large dilutes relevance.
  • Page-level indexing (one page → one set of embeddings) is the simplest unit, and it's what ColPali-style systems use.
  • Whatever you choose, the index must answer “which page has this?”, not just “which document?”.

Benchmark: ViDoRe

ViDoRe (Visual Document Retrieval) measures page-level retrieval across domains, languages and visual styles over ~127K PDF pages. Its primary metric is nDCG@5, which rewards ranking the correct page near the very top.

ViDoRe example

“Where is the S-3's single point receptacle located?” → the relevant pages (refuelling procedure text + diagrams, with the answer region boxed) → “On the right side of the fuselage, immediately aft of the main landing-gear well.”

How state-of-the-art systems are built

  • ColPali initializes from a pretrained VLM backbone (PaliGemma) and is fine-tuned specifically for page-level embeddings.
  • Training data: (query, document-page-image) pairs, so the model learns what a page looks like when it actually answers a question.
  • Result: one simple pipeline replaces OCR + layout analysis + text embedding: three brittle steps collapsed into one.
Approach (ViDoRe, nDCG@5)Relative performance
BM25 on OCR-extracted textBaseline: weakest of those compared
Text embeddings on OCR text (e.g. BGE-M3)Moderate improvement over BM25
ColPali (vision-space retrieval)Strongest: beats even pipelines that use a strong proprietary VLM to caption the visual elements

Crisp summary

  • Late interaction (from ColBERT): many vectors per page/query; score = Σ over query tokens of max similarity to any patch.
  • ColPali: PaliGemma-3B + linear projection to D = 128; one vector per patch (pages) / per token (queries); no OCR.
  • Loss: (1/b) Σ softplus(s⁻ − s⁺) against the hardest in-batch negative.
  • Indexing 0.39 s/page vs 7.22 s for the PDF-parsing pipeline; NDCG@5 0.81 vs 0.66. Querying stays fast for every system (~22–30 ms per query in the overview figure; ≤ 22 ms on an NVIDIA L4 in the latency study).
  • Page-level indexing; the index must answer “which page?”.
  • ViDoRe: ~127K PDF pages, nDCG@5. Ranking: BM25 on OCR < BGE-M3 on OCR < ColPali.
Section 7.6

Grounded generation: prompting, pitfalls, challenges

≈ 5 min · Slides: M4L3 s41–46, s50–51, s60–62

The generation step

The retrieved pages (as images, extracted text, or both) are passed to a VLM with the original query. Its job is to read them and answer from them rather than from memorized knowledge: the VQA and document-intelligence skills of earlier lectures, now applied to content the system chose itself.

Prompting for grounded, citation-aware answers

  • Instruct the model to answer only from the retrieved content; this reduces, but does not eliminate, hallucination.
  • Ask for a citation or page reference with the answer so it can be verified against the source.
  • Explicitly permit “not found in the retrieved documents” when nothing retrieved answers the question. Abstention is easier said than done.

Worked example

Query: “What was Q3 revenue growth?” Retrieved: a “Q3 Regional Sales Report” bar chart (Q1–Q4). Answer: “Q3 revenue grew about 46% over Q2, based on the bar chart on the retrieved page: Q3 is both the tallest bar and the largest jump from the prior quarter.”

Common pitfalls

  • Retrieval failure: if the right page isn't retrieved, no amount of good prompting fixes the answer.
  • Hallucination despite retrieval: the model can ignore the retrieved content and answer from memory.
  • Irrelevant context: a topically related but unhelpful page can distract the generator.
  • Over-trusting citations: a cited page number doesn't guarantee the answer came from it.

Why it is hard

  • Chunking trades context against precision; there is no universally correct chunk size.
  • Aligning text and visual relevance in one ranking is harder than ranking either alone.
  • Multi-page reasoning, where the answer spans two retrieved pages, is still open.
  • Evaluating a full RAG pipeline means evaluating retrieval and generation together, which compounds the difficulty of each.

Remaining challenges

  • Late-interaction indexes are larger and costlier to store than single-vector ones, since every patch gets its own vector.
  • Harder benchmark versions show today's strong scores don't fully generalize to messier real documents.
  • Multi-page and multi-document reasoning remain largely unsolved.
  • No standardized way yet to evaluate faithfulness: whether an answer is genuinely supported by what was retrieved.

When to use which retrieval strategy

CorpusUse
Pure text, no visual structureText search alone; no need for multimodal complexity
Photos or products, simple queriesImage search with CLIP-style embeddings
Real documents mixing text, tables and chartsMultimodal RAG, ideally with vision-space retrieval; worth the added cost

Crisp summary

  • Generation = a VLM answering from the retrieved pages (VQA + document intelligence on system-chosen content).
  • Prompt: answer only from retrieved content, cite the page, allow “not found” (abstention is hard).
  • Pitfalls: retrieval failure (unfixable by prompting), hallucination despite retrieval, distracting context, over-trusted citations.
  • Hard: chunk size, joint text/visual ranking, multi-page answers, evaluating retrieval + generation together.
  • Open: costly late-interaction indexes, weak generalization to messy docs, multi-document reasoning, no standard faithfulness metric.
  • Choose text search for plain text, CLIP image search for photos/products, vision-space multimodal RAG for mixed real documents.
Section 7.7

The multimodal RAG landscape

≈ 8 min · Slides: M4L3 s52–59, s64–65

A survey of the field (Abootorabi et al., 2025, Ask in Any Modality: A Comprehensive Survey on Multimodal RAG): where it is used, what gets retrieved, how retrieved knowledge is fused and reasoned over, and how systems are trained.

1 · Where multimodal RAG is used

CategoryApplications
Content generationImage captioning, text-to-image synthesis, visual storytelling, multimodal summarization
Knowledge-intensive QAOpen-domain and knowledge-seeking QA, video-based QA, fact verification
HealthcareMedical VQA (MMed-RAG), report generation (RULE), patient support (AsthmaBot)
Software engineeringCode completion (DocPrompting), commit messages (RACE), code summarization (REDCODER)
Fashion, e-commerce & emergingStyle-aware product search, autonomous driving (RAG-Driver), geolocation (Img2Loc)

Imagen → Re-Imagen

Plain Imagen hallucinates rare entities (a Barbado da Terceira dog, Picarones, Umngqusho, the Monument to the Fallen Shipyard Workers of 1970). Re-Imagen retrieves reference images of the entity first and generates far more faithful pictures: retrieval augmentation for generation, not just QA.

2 · What gets retrieved: four modalities

Retrieval typeHow it works
Text-centricBM25 and dense retrievers (BGE-M3) dominate; ColBERT-style token-level matching improves precision
Vision-centricRetrieve with image representations directly: reference-image queries, composed image retrieval
Video-centricAdds temporal dynamics: incremental retrieval, long-context video understanding
Document & layoutRetrieve whole page images (ColPali), integrating text, tables and layout together

3 · Fusing what's retrieved

  • Score fusion & alignment: embed modalities into a shared (often CLIP-based) space and combine similarity scores directly.
  • Attention-based fusion: cross-attention dynamically weights retrieved evidence against the query.
  • Unified frameworks: project text, tables and images into one representation before generation, sometimes converting images to captions or vice versa.

3 · Reasoning over retrieved knowledge

  • In-context learning: retrieved examples serve as few-shot demonstrations, no retraining.
  • Structured reasoning (CoT): decompose a complex query into steps; some systems branch into a “Tree of RAG” to explore multiple reasoning paths.
  • Instruction tuning: teach the generator to invoke retrieval, judge relevance and answer, rather than always retrieving blindly.
  • Source attribution: the strongest systems cite exactly which evidence (a page, a region) supports each part of the answer.

4 · How multimodal RAG systems are trained

  • Multi-stage: pre-train on large paired data to learn cross-modal relationships, then fine-tune for the task with cross-modal attention.
  • Alignment loss: contrastive (InfoNCE) training pulls a query and its correct content together and pushes mismatches apart; hard negatives sharpen it.
  • Generation loss: cross-entropy for text; diffusion- or GAN-style losses when the output is an image.
  • Robustness training: deliberately inject irrelevant or noisy retrieved content so the generator learns to ignore it.

4 · Training retriever and generator together

  • Core difficulty: which documents should have been retrieved is not observed; it is a hidden (latent) variable.
  • EM-style (Expectation–Maximization) view: alternate an E-step-like pass (score and retrieve with the current model) and an M-step-like pass (update the model to make the correct answer more likely given what was retrieved). This framing goes back to the original RAG and REALM papers, which marginalize over the top-k retrieved documents.
  • Retriever and generator improve each other: better retrieval makes generation easier to train, and generation feedback reshapes what the retriever prioritizes.
  • In practice: most production systems use a simpler two-stage recipe: pre-train retriever and generator separately, then fine-tune jointly on task data.

Recap and takeaways

TaskModel / techniqueKey idea
Text searchBi-encoder embeddings + ANN indexSemantic match beats exact keyword match
Image searchCLIP-style shared embedding spaceText and image queries compared directly
Multimodal RAG for QAVision-space retrieval + VLM generationGround answers in retrieved, real document content
  • Retrieval and generation are separate skills: a great generator with poor retrieval still gives poor answers.
  • The same embed-and-nearest-neighbor pattern powers text, image and document retrieval; only what's embedded changes.
  • Vision-space retrieval is displacing brittle OCR pipelines wherever documents are visually rich.
  • Grounding reduces hallucination but does not eliminate it: verify, don't just trust, a cited source.

Crisp summary

  • Applications: content generation, knowledge QA, healthcare (MMed-RAG, RULE, AsthmaBot), software engineering (DocPrompting, RACE, REDCODER), e-commerce/driving/geolocation (RAG-Driver, Img2Loc); Re-Imagen shows retrieval fixing rare-entity hallucination.
  • Retrieval modalities: text-centric (BM25, BGE-M3, ColBERT), vision-centric, video-centric, document/layout (ColPali).
  • Fusion: score fusion in a shared space, cross-attention, unified representations.
  • Reasoning: in-context examples, CoT / Tree of RAG, instruction tuning to decide when to retrieve, source attribution.
  • Training: multi-stage; InfoNCE alignment with hard negatives; cross-entropy (or diffusion/GAN) generation loss; noise-injection robustness.
  • Joint training treats the retrieved document as latent (EM-style, RAG/REALM marginalize over top-k); practice: separate pre-training, then joint fine-tuning.

Module 8 of 8

From RAG to Assistants and Agents

Average time to complete≈ 50 min
Reading ≈ 33 min · 5 sections · Module check ≈ 15 min

Source lecturesRAG to Assistants and Agents (Debaditya Roy, IIT Kharagpur)

One running example carries the whole lecture: “Plan my Paris trip for next week for 4 days, staying within the company travel policy and a ₹80,000 budget.” Each step up the ladder (RAG, assistant, tool-using assistant, agent, multi-agent) adds exactly one capability, and the lecture shows what each one buys and costs.

  1. 8.1Why RAG isn't enough: questions vs tasks≈ 7 min
  2. 8.2Assistants: context, tool calling and MCP≈ 5 min
  3. 8.3Workflows vs agents and the agent loop≈ 6 min
  4. 8.4What the loop costs and three loop shapes≈ 6 min
  5. 8.5Retrieval as a tool, memory and multi-agent design≈ 9 min
  6. ✓Module check: 10 random questions (bank of 50)≈ 15 min
Section 8.1

Why RAG isn't enough: questions vs tasks

≈ 7 min · Slides: AGENTS s2–8

The Paris request is hard in four ways

1 · Private knowledge

The governing policy is an internal document, absent from the model's parameters.

2 · Time-varying data

Fares and availability change hourly and cannot be stored in the weights.

3 · Hard constraints

Two conditions must hold jointly: policy compliance and a ₹80,000 ceiling.

4 · Unknown control flow

The right next step is determined by the outcome of the previous one.

From LLM to multi-agent: the ladder

StageAddsCapabilityOn the Paris request
01 LLMBase modelGenerates a language responseA plausible-sounding itinerary with no factual basis
02 RAG+ RetrievalAccesses external knowledgeFetches the official company travel policy
03 Assistant+ ContextRemembers the conversation threadRetains the trip dates and the budget constraint
04 Tool-using assistant+ ToolsExecutes actions in the worldCalls the live flight and hotel search APIs
05 Agent+ DecisionsChooses its own next stepRe-plans when the compliance check fails
06 Multi-agent+ DelegationCoordinates specialized sub-tasksSplits flights, hotels, meetings and expenses

The same model, two very different questions

Answered from weights

“What is the capital of France?” → “Paris.” Public, stable, in the training data.

Confidently invented

“What does our travel policy allow for flights to Paris?” → “Employees may book business class on international routes…” Private, versioned, never in the training data.

Four failure modes of a bare LLM: knowledge cutoff (nothing after the training day), no private data (internal wikis, policies, tickets), hallucination (fluent is not the same as correct) and no traceability (it cannot point to a source).

RAG applied to the travel policy

1 · Ingestion: travel_policy_2026.pdf, 40 pages → 118 chunks → vectors2 · Retrieval: query → top-3 nearest clauses (§4.2 cabin, §4.7 hotel cap)3 · Augmentation: clauses pasted into the prompt above the user's question4 · Generation: answer written only from those clauses, with a citation

What the user sees

“What does the policy allow for flights to Paris?” → “Economy class only for flights under 8 hours, and bookings must be made at least 7 days in advance.”
Source: travel_policy_2026.pdf · page 12, §4.2: “International travel: economy class only for sectors under 8 hours. Hotel tariff must not exceed ₹8,000 per night. Bookings shall be made at least 7 days in advance.”

Core principle: retrieve before you generate. The answer is grounded in evidence, not memory.

Change the request, break the design

The question “What does the policy allow?” needs one retrieval. The task “Plan my Paris trip within policy and ₹80,000” needs: retrieve travel policy → search flights → search hotels → check prices against budget → compare options → check constraints (may fail → replan) → produce a recommendation. There is no fixed sequence: if the compliance check fails, earlier decisions may need to be revisited. RAG answers the question; task completion requires decisions, actions and feedback.

Question answering (what RAG does)Task completion (what the Paris request needs)
InputA questionA goal plus constraints
WorkOne retrieval, one generationMany steps, order decided at runtime
OutputTextA decision, a change in the world
FailureA wrong sentenceA booking that breaks policy
Ends whenThe model stops generatingThe goal is satisfied, or judged impossible
Actions

The system must invoke external tools.

Decisions

The system must select among possible actions.

Interaction

The system may need clarification or approval.

Crisp summary

  • The Paris request combines private knowledge, time-varying data, joint hard constraints and unknown control flow.
  • Ladder: LLM → RAG (+retrieval) → assistant (+context) → tool-using assistant (+tools) → agent (+decisions) → multi-agent (+delegation).
  • Bare LLM failure modes: knowledge cutoff, no private data, hallucination, no traceability.
  • RAG pipeline: ingestion (40 pages → 118 chunks → vectors) → top-3 retrieval → augmentation → cited generation. Principle: retrieve before you generate.
  • Question answering ends when generation stops; task completion needs many runtime-ordered steps, actions, decisions and interaction, and ends when the goal is met or judged impossible.
Section 8.2

Assistants: context, tool calling and MCP

≈ 5 min · Slides: AGENTS s9–13

Add context: the system remembers the thread

A three-turn conversation

User: I'm travelling to Paris next week for 4 days. What does the policy allow? → Assistant: Economy class, and the booking must be 7 days ahead. [§4.2] (knowledge: retrieval over the policy store)

User: And the hotel? (“the hotel” = the Paris hotel: context carried across turns) → Assistant: Up to ₹8,000 per night for Paris. [§4.7]

User: Find me one under that. → Assistant: I can read the policy, but I have no way to search hotels. (capabilities: tools that touch the outside world are missing)

Turn 3 is unanswerable without turn 1. Context is state, not a longer prompt.

Add capabilities: the assistant calls a tool

User: “Find me a flight to Paris”The model decides: emits a structured requestYour code acts: runs search_flights(…) and hands the result back
{"name": "search_flights",
 "arguments": {"origin": "BOM", "dest": "CDG",
               "date": "2026-08-22", "cabin": "economy"}}
  • Crucial: the model never touches the API. It emits a request; your code executes it and returns the result.
  • Note the cabin argument: “economy” came from the retrieved policy, not from the user's sentence. Knowledge is already shaping the action.

MCP: tools behind one standard interface

Hand-written tool schemas don't scale past a handful of tools. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) makes a tool something you connect to, not something you re-declare.

Agent = MCP client① discovers tools: list_tools()② calls them: call_tool()MCP servers: Policy docs (resources) · Flights API (tools) · Calendar (tools)

At runtime the agent finds search_flights on the Flights server, then calls it for BOM → CDG.

Without MCP

You hand-write a JSON schema for every tool: type, name, description (“Live fares…”), parameters (origin, dest, date as strings; cabin as an enum of economy/business), required fields; about 20 lines for one tool, and then you wire the call yourself. Add a tool or change a field and you edit the prompt and redeploy the agent.

With MCP
session = connect("travel.corp/mcp")
tools = session.list_tools()        # ① ask what it can do
session.call_tool("search_flights",
    {"origin": "BOM", "dest": "CDG"})  # ② call by name

Tools are discovered at runtime; the server owns the schema. A tool added on the server just appears: no prompt edit, no redeploy.

Crisp summary

  • Assistant = RAG + context: conversation history is state (“the hotel” only makes sense after turn 1).
  • Without tools the assistant can read the policy but cannot act (“no way to search hotels”).
  • Tool calling: the model emits a structured request (name + arguments); your code executes it and returns the result. The model never touches the API.
  • Knowledge shapes actions: the cabin = economy argument came from the retrieved policy.
  • MCP: the agent is an MCP client that discovers tools (list_tools) and calls them (call_tool) on servers exposing tools or resources.
  • Without MCP: ~20 lines of schema per tool, edit and redeploy for changes. With MCP: runtime discovery, server-owned schemas, no redeploy.
Section 8.3

Workflows vs agents and the agent loop

≈ 6 min · Slides: AGENTS s14–18

The only difference that matters

Tool-using assistant: you choose the order

retrieve_policy() → search_flights() → search_hotels() → rank_and_return(). Written once at development time; the model only fills in arguments.

Agent: the model chooses the order

goal + tools → decide → act, observe → decide again… in a loop. Decided every iteration, at run time, from what just came back.

The test: if you can draw the flowchart before the request arrives, you do not need an agent.

Workflow vs agent

Use a workflow when…Use an agent when…
The steps are the same for every inputThe number of steps depends on the data
Auditors need the same path every timeA later step can invalidate an earlier one
Latency and cost must be bounded exactlyTools fail often and recovery must be dynamic
A wrong extra tool call is expensive or irreversibleThe input space is open-ended, not enumerable
Example: monthly expense-report generationExample: the Paris request, or triaging a live incident

In practice you ship both: a deterministic workflow for the parts you can name, with an agent embedded at the one step where the path is genuinely unknown.

A closed loop, not a pipeline

GoalThink: what is missing?Act: call one toolObserve: read the resultRemember: write it to stateGoal reached? No → loop again; yes → itinerary
Bounded

A step budget and a cost ceiling, or it never stops.

Observable

Every Think / Act / Observe triple is logged and replayable.

Recoverable

A failed tool is an observation, not a crash.

Why the loop is the whole idea: the plan is never written in advance; it is regenerated after every observation.

The agent loop in action

#ThinkActObserve
1Constraints first: I cannot price anything yetretrieve_policy("flights, hotels")Economy only; hotel ≤ ₹8,000/night; book ≥ 7 days ahead
2Search inside the cabin the policy allowssearch_flights(BOM, CDG, 15 Aug, economy)4 fares, ₹38,400 – ₹61,200
3The cheapest fare leaves ₹41,600 for the restsearch_hotels(Paris, 4 nights, ≤ 8000)6 hotels, ₹5,900 – ₹7,800 per night
4Total ₹65,600: under budget, so verify compliancecheck_policy(itinerary)FAIL: departure is 5 days away; the policy needs 7
5The budget was never the problem. Shift the datessearch_flights(BOM, CDG, 22 Aug, economy)₹34,900, departs in 8 days
6Compliant and ₹17,900 under budgetdraft_itinerary()Present to the user for approval

Step 4 is the reason agents exist: a fixed pipeline would have returned the non-compliant itinerary.

Crisp summary

  • Tool-using assistant: the developer fixes the order of calls. Agent: the model chooses the next step each iteration from the last result.
  • The test: if you can draw the flowchart in advance, build a workflow, not an agent.
  • Workflow: same steps every time, auditable path, exact cost bounds, irreversible calls (expense reports). Agent: data-dependent steps, later steps invalidate earlier ones, flaky tools, open-ended inputs (Paris trip, incident triage). Ship both.
  • Loop: think → act (one tool) → observe → remember → goal reached? It must be bounded, observable and recoverable.
  • Trace: policy → 15 Aug flight (₹38,400) → hotels → total ₹65,600 → compliance FAIL (5 days < 7) → re-search 22 Aug (₹34,900) → compliant, ₹17,900 under budget.
Section 8.4

What the loop costs and three loop shapes

≈ 6 min · Slides: AGENTS s20–22

What the loop costs

Full history, every step

The model is stateless, so each step re-sends the goal, the tool schemas and every prior step. Step 1: ~1 KB of context; step 5 re-sends the first four steps; by step 8, steps 1–7 are being paid for yet again.

Cost grows super-linearly

Each new step pays for all the steps before it, so doubling the step budget more than doubles the bill.

The window is a hard wall

Verbose tool outputs hit the context limit before the step budget does. Managing that is the real work.

Why super-linear: if every step adds about c tokens and step k must re-read all k steps, n steps cost roughly , which grows like .

Truncate each observationSummarize superseded stepsKeep only the last N steps in full

Context engineering: frameworks give you these memory strategies; without one, you write them yourself.

Three shapes of the same loop

The loop is fixed; how much the model plans ahead is a design choice with real cost and latency consequences.

ReActPlan-and-ExecuteReflection
IdeaInterleave one thought, one action: decide each step from the last resultDraft the whole plan first, then run it; commit up frontProduce, critique, revise: loop on the draft, not the task
CycleThink → Act → Observe → Think…Plan 1–7 → Execute → Replan on failureDraft → Critique → Revise
+Cheapest to run and easiest to debugSteps can run in parallel; cost is predictableVisible quality lift on written output
−Can wander on long horizonsThe plan is written before any evidence arrivesDoubles or triples token spend
UseThe Paris trace aboveDeep research, batch jobsItinerary write-up, code review

The Paris request in each shape

ReAct

THINK need the rules first → ACT retrieve_policy() → OBS economy; book ≥ 7 days → ACT search_flights 15 Aug → FAIL departs in 5 days → THINK shift the dates → DONE compliant plan.

Plan-and-Execute

PLAN 1 policy · 2 flights · 3 hotels · 4 price-check · 5 comply → EXEC run steps 1–5 → FAIL step 5: 2 days short → PLAN replan the tail only → DONE re-run 2–5, ship.

Reflection

DRAFT full 4-day itinerary → CRITIQUE departs in 5 days, needs 7 → REVISE move to 22 Aug → CRITIQUE fare now ₹34,900 ✓ → DONE ship the itinerary.

Crisp summary

  • The model is stateless, so every step re-sends goal, tool schemas and all prior steps: cost grows super-linearly (≈ quadratic), and doubling steps more than doubles cost.
  • The context window is the hard wall; manage it by truncating observations, summarizing superseded steps and keeping only the last N in full (context engineering).
  • ReAct: one thought, one action; cheapest and easiest to debug, but can wander.
  • Plan-and-Execute: plan up front, parallel and predictable, but the plan predates the evidence; replan on failure.
  • Reflection: draft → critique → revise; better written output at 2–3× tokens.
Section 8.5

Retrieval as a tool, memory and multi-agent design

≈ 9 min · Slides: AGENTS s24–29

Retrieval becomes one tool among several

In classic RAG, query → retrieve → augment → generate, and retrieval always runs exactly once. Inside the agent loop, retrieve_policy() sits beside search_flights(), search_hotels() and check_policy(): the agent decides whether to retrieve, with what query, and how often.

1 · Query rewriting

“Plan my Paris trip” is a terrible search query; the agent issues “international cabin class policy” instead.

2 · Retrieve more than once

Policy in step 1, then the per-diem clause again in step 4 when the numbers stop adding up.

3 · Skip retrieval entirely

Nothing in the policy store answers “what is today's fare?”, so it calls the API, not the index.

4 · Verify against the source

After drafting, re-retrieve and check the itinerary clause by clause.

Three things the agent must remember

MemoryLives forHoldsParis examples
Conversation stateOne threadWhat the user said and what we replied“next week” = 22–26 Aug · prefers direct flights · approved the ₹80,000 cap
Task stateOne runThe scratchpad: what is done, what is leftpolicy: retrieved ✓ · flights: ₹34,900 held · budget left: ₹45,100 · compliance: re-check needed
Long-term memoryAcross sessionsFacts worth keeping after the task endsemployee grade: L4 · home airport: BOM · last trip rejected for late booking

Without task state there is no loop: “what is still missing” can only be answered against a record of what already happened.

Split the goal, not the model

The request grows: “Plan the entire trip: flights, hotel, the three client meetings, and the expense estimate.” One agent now struggles:

One agent, 14 toolsTool selection degrades as the list grows
One context windowMeeting notes crowd out the policy clauses
One prompt“Be a flight expert and a scheduler and an accountant”
One failure domainA calendar timeout stalls the fare search too
Orchestrator: decomposes · routes · assemblesFlight agent (fares, cabin rules) · Hotel agent (tariff cap, location) · Meeting agent (calendars, time zones) · Expense agent (per-diem, totals)Shared state: policy facts · running total · checkpointsHuman approval

Cost: every handoff is a chance to lose context. Start with one agent.

Agent landscape (as of the lecture)

FrameworkWhat changedEcosystem
Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0Semantic Kernel and AutoGen merged into one runtime (April 2026)Azure / .NET
OpenAI Agents SDKHandoffs, guardrails and tracing as first-class primitivesOpenAI
Claude Agent SDKHierarchical subagent spawning, MCP-native, safety-first defaultsAnthropic
Google ADKHierarchical agent trees, built-in dev UI, A2A supportGoogle Cloud
Pydantic AI v2Typed inputs and outputs, model-agnostic; v2 stable in June 2026Python-first
Strands · Mastra · AgnoAWS-native, TypeScript-native and lightweight-runtime optionsAWS / TS / OSS

Three rules: pick by stack, not by benchmark; the loop is portable, the state store is not; the protocol layer (MCP etc.) outlives any SDK.

The same request, six times

StageThe request it can handleSystem capabilityWhat changed
LLM“What is the capital of France?”Language generationNothing external
RAG“What is our international travel policy?”Retrieve, then generateExternal knowledge
Assistant“I'm in Paris next week for 4 days: what does it allow?”Knowledge + contextState across turns
Tool-using assistant“Find flights to Paris.”Calls an external serviceIt can act
Agent“Plan my Paris trip within policy, under ₹80,000.”Retrieval + tools + state + decisionsIt chooses the order
Multi-agent“Plan the whole trip, meetings and expenses.”Specialized agents, coordinatedThe task is decomposed

Each row adds one capability, and nothing below is thrown away: the agent still chunks, still embeds, still retrieves.

Five things to carry forward

  1. RAG answers. Agents finish. The dividing line is task completion, not intelligence.
  2. Control flow is the definition. If you can draw the flowchart in advance, build a workflow.
  3. The loop is small. Think, act, observe, remember, repeat: about twenty lines without a framework.
  4. RAG lives inside the agent. Retrieval becomes a tool the agent chooses to call, and chunk quality now drives actions.
  5. State is the hard part. Durable checkpoints, and a human before anything irreversible.

Crisp summary

  • In an agent, retrieval is an optional tool: rewrite the query, retrieve repeatedly, skip it for live data (call the API), and re-retrieve to verify the draft.
  • Memory: conversation state (one thread), task state/scratchpad (one run; without it there is no loop), long-term memory (across sessions).
  • Multi-agent: when one agent has too many tools (14), a crowded context, a do-everything prompt and one failure domain, an orchestrator routes to specialist agents over shared state, with human approval. Handoffs lose context, so start with one agent.
  • Frameworks: Microsoft Agent Framework, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK (MCP-native), Google ADK (A2A), Pydantic AI, Strands/Mastra/Agno. Pick by stack; the loop is portable, the state store is not; protocols outlive SDKs.
  • Carry forward: RAG answers, agents finish; control flow defines an agent; the loop is small; RAG lives inside the agent; state is the hard part (checkpoints + human before irreversible steps).

Last-minute revision

All crisp summaries

Every section's crisp summary on one page, grouped by module. Section titles link back to the full notes.

Reading time ≈ 60 min.

Module 1LLM Fine-Tuning Foundations

1.1 Language models, LLMs and scale

  • An LM estimates : a probability for every possible next token.
  • An LLM is the same idea scaled up: billions of parameters (GPT-3 = 175B), trillions of tokens, deep transformer stacks.
  • Scale brings emergent abilities: fluent generation, in-context learning (few-shot, no retraining), reasoning and knowledge.
  • Families to know: GPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic, safety-focused), Gemini (Google, multimodal), Llama (Meta, open weights).

1.2 The three transformer families

  • Encoder-only (BERT family): bidirectional attention, masked-LM pre-training (~15% masked), best for understanding and embeddings, not free generation.
  • Decoder-only (GPT, Claude, LLaMA, Mistral, Gemini): causal mask, next-token objective, autoregressive generation with KV-caching; the dominant LLM design.
  • Encoder–decoder (Transformer, T5, BART, mT5, Marian): bidirectional encoder + causal decoder joined by cross-attention; span-corruption or paired-data training; translation and summarization.
  • All three repeat the same block: attention → Add & Norm → FFN → Add & Norm, N times.

1.3 Training stages and why fine-tune

  • Three stages: pre-training (self-supervised next-token on unlabeled web text) → fine-tuning (train some weights for a use case) → safety/alignment (feedback-driven tuning toward human preference).
  • Fine-tune for four reasons: domain expertise, consistent behavior/format, higher accuracy on narrow tasks, lower cost and latency.
  • Proof points: BloombergGPT (finance) and Med-PaLM 2 (≈86% on USMLE-style questions).
  • A fine-tuned model answers in the expected form and specialty; the base model rambles or stays generic.

1.4 What fine-tuning actually updates

  • Per head: ; attention = .
  • Shapes: : ; : ; concat of 2 heads is ; maps back to .
  • Trainable pieces: attention projections, FFN, layer norms, embeddings, LM head. Fine-tuning = changing some or all of these.

1.5 Decision framework: prompt, RAG or fine-tune

  • Prompting changes instructions; RAG changes the information the model sees; fine-tuning changes the weights.
  • Knowledge that is fresh, private or huge → RAG (external knowledge “extremely high”).
  • Strict style, format or new syntax (e.g. ICD-10 coding) → fine-tuning (format control “extremely high”, latency “very low”, setup cost high).
  • Standard task the model already knows → prompt engineering (minimal setup, low latency).
  • RAG adds medium latency because of the retrieval step.

1.6 Fine-tuning approaches: the two axes

  • Two axes: what is trained (full vs PEFT) and which objective (unsupervised, supervised, alignment).
  • Unsupervised FT = pre-training objective on unlabeled domain text; labels come free from the next token (medical example: AdamW, LR 2e-5, 1–3 epochs).
  • SFT = imitate demonstrations; teaches behavior and format (it powered InstructGPT's first stage).
  • Alignment FT = RLHF (rank → reward model → PPO), DPO (chosen/rejected pairs) or revision against written principles.
  • Full FT moves every weight: best adaptation, ~16 bytes/param with Adam, one checkpoint per task, risk of forgetting.
  • PEFT families: additive, selective, re-parameterization (LoRA, QLoRA).

1.7 Supervised and instruction fine-tuning

  • SFT = training on human-made input → output pairs so the model imitates correct answers (loop: predict → compare → loss → AdamW update → repeat).
  • Typical SFT settings on the slide: teacher forcing, cross-entropy, AdamW, LR 1e-5–5e-5, 1–3 epochs, batch 8–32; evaluate with ROUGE/BLEU/AI evals.
  • IFT is SFT where the input is an explicit instruction; data = {instruction, input, output}; template ### Instruction / ### Input / ### Response.
  • Before IFT a base model continues text (“French is a Romance language…”); after IFT it executes the instruction (“Bonjour”).
  • SFT targets task performance (can be one task); IFT targets instruction-following across many tasks.

1.8 Multi-task fine-tuning

  • One model, many tasks at once (sentiment, QA, summarization, NER), learning a shared representation.
  • Architecture: shared transformer body + separate heads (generative QA, classification with pooling + softmax over C classes, summarization, MCQ with softmax over options).
  • Replaces several single-task models with one; sequential multi-task training risks forgetting.

1.9 Curriculum fine-tuning

  • Curriculum = ordered training (easy → hard) instead of random order; needs a difficulty measure and a pacing schedule.
  • Benefits: faster convergence, stability (fewer spikes), better generalization (flatter minima), data/compute efficiency.
  • Pipeline: pool → score difficulty → bucket → scheduled training → evaluate and re-pace (feedback loop).
  • Difficulty can be static (length, rarity), model-based (loss, perplexity, margin) or external (human labels, grade level).
  • Strategies: Baby Steps (cumulative), One-Pass (discard, forgetting risk), Self-Paced (loss threshold), Competence-Based (pacing c(t)), Anti-curriculum (hard first).

1.10 Making full fine-tuning efficient

  • Full FT of a 10B model in FP16 with Adam: 20 GB weights + 20 GB grads + 120 GB optimizer states = 160 GB (~16 bytes/param) → seven 24 GB GPUs.
  • Scale of the problem: InstructGPT 175B parameters; GPT-4 training ≈ 25,000 A100s for months, ≈ $100M.
  • Full FT is expensive in time and memory but adapts best.
  • Cheaper variants: one layer at a time, block-wise (contiguous blocks), progressive layer-wise unfreezing.

Module 2Training Mechanics, Stability & Data

2.1 How LLMs learn: the training loop

  • Loop: tokenize → mini-batch [B×T] → forward → cross-entropy → backward → θ ← θ − η·∂L/∂θ → repeat millions of times.
  • Vocabularies are ~50k–250k tokens; sequences are packed into context windows of T tokens; logits have shape [B×T×V]; targets are inputs shifted by one.
  • Mini-batches beat full-batch (too slow) and B = 1 (too noisy).
  • Softmax turns logits into probabilities; per-token loss is −log p(true token); worked batch loss = 0.86.
  • LR ~1e-4 with warmup + decay; Adam (adaptive per-parameter steps) instead of plain SGD.
  • Step = one update; epoch = one pass; stop when validation loss flattens. Noisy per-batch loss is normal.

2.2 Training instability and how to tame it

  • Instability is a feedback loop: oversized update → worse loss → bigger gradient → worse update.
  • Causes: sharp valleys, fp16 overflow (> ~65,504 → Inf), outlier batches (10–100× gradient norm), depth amplifying perturbations.
  • Symptoms: loss spike (recovers, wastes steps, clusters after warmup) → gradient explosion (norm grows exponentially, precedes divergence) → divergence (no recovery, gibberish output).
  • Gradient clipping at max_grad_norm = 1.0 keeps direction, bounds magnitude; >20% of steps clipping means the LR is too high.
  • Use warmup + cosine instead of a constant LR (legal SFT example: late spikes gone, val loss −4%).
  • Checklist: clip 1.0 · cosine · warmup 3% · bf16 not fp16 · peak LR 1e-5–2e-5 (full) / 1e-4–2e-4 (LoRA) · alert at 5–10× median grad-norm · keep last 3 checkpoints.

2.3 Catastrophic forgetting

  • Catastrophic forgetting: narrow fine-tuning overwrites general knowledge; it is silent unless you track general benchmarks (legal FT example: target 41→88 while GSM8K 62→39, IFEval 71→47).
  • Causes: shared distributed weights, narrow gradient signal, drift from θ₀, no replay/anchor in AdamW.
  • Rehearsal: 1–10% general data in every batch (95/5 interleave).
  • L2-SP: uniform ‖θ−θ₀‖² pull; EWC: Fisher-weighted pull; λ trades underfitting vs forgetting.
  • Conservative settings first: LR 1e-5–2e-5, 1–2 epochs, cosine + warmup, early-stop on canary evals.
  • WiSE-FT: θ = (1−α)θ_base + αθ_ft, sweep α 0.3–0.9, works because both sit in one connected low-loss region.
  • Freeze embeddings + lower blocks; tuning the top 25–50% captures most gains.

2.4 Learning-rate scheduling

  • You need big steps early and small steps late: constant-high is noisy, constant-low never converges, warmup + decay wins.
  • Phases: fragile start (0–3%, warm up), rapid learning (3–60%, peak LR), convergence (60–100%, decay).
  • Four knobs: warmup (default 3%, 5–10% if unstable), peak LR (most important: 1e-5–2e-5 full, 1e-4–2e-4 LoRA), decay shape, floor (0 or ~10% of peak).
  • Formulas: warmup η_max·t/T_w; linear to zero; cosine η_min + ½(η_max−η_min)(1+cos(πt/T)).
  • Shapes: constant (short runs), linear (no-surprises), cosine (modern default), step decay (val-driven, ReduceLROnPlateau), cosine restarts (several candidates), WSD (unknown length, decay in last 10–20%).
  • For instability: lengthen warmup first, then lower the peak.

2.5 Choosing the batch size

  • Effective batch = micro-batch × gradient-accumulation steps × GPUs (2 × 16 × 4 = 128).
  • Recipe: fix max sequence length → fill GPU memory with micro-batch → reach the target with gradient accumulation.
  • Small batch: generalizes better, noisy, slower. Large batch: stable and fast, fewer updates, may need higher LR and generalize worse.
  • Linear scaling rule: double the batch → roughly double the LR (32 → 2e-5, 64 → 4e-5).
  • Guide: 24 GB → eff. 16–64; 40 GB → 32–128; 80 GB → 64–256.
  • Jitter that never shrinks → batch too small; both losses plateau high with few steps → batch too large (aim ≥ 500–1,000 optimizer steps).

2.6 Data quality problems

  • Five challenges: quality, insufficient data, imbalance, splitting/leakage, distribution shift.
  • Noise: boilerplate, SEO spam, OCR errors, gibberish, AI-generated slop (feedback-loop risk).
  • Wrong labels: misinformation, buggy code, language-ID errors, noisy quality classifiers.
  • Duplicates: waste compute, cause verbatim memorization (privacy/copyright), and benchmark contamination inflates scores.
  • Formatting chaos (HTML/LaTeX/PDF, Unicode, digit grouping) and outdated facts (cutoff, deprecated APIs, conflicting snapshots) also degrade learning.

2.7 Too little data, edge cases, diversity and imbalance

  • Small data → high variance/overfitting; transfer learning is the dominant fix, plus augmentation, validated synthetic data, regularized right-sized models, cross-validation, few/zero-shot.
  • Edge cases (snow for self-driving, novel fraud, 1-in-100k defects) → targeted collection, simulation, active learning on uncertain production samples.
  • Low diversity (accents, demographics, geography) → stratified sourcing, per-subgroup metrics, bias audits, diverse annotators.
  • Imbalance (fraud 0.2%) → accuracy paradox; use precision/recall/F1/PR-AUC, SMOTE or undersampling, class weights or focal loss.

2.8 Data splitting and distribution shift

  • Split 70/15/15: train fits parameters, validation tunes hyper-parameters, test is touched once.
  • Leakage traps: preprocessing before the split, duplicates across splits, random splits of time series, the same patient/user in train and test.
  • Fixes: split first, stratify, time-based and group-aware splits, k-fold CV for small data.
  • Shifts: usage (documents → dialogue; base models continue text), temporal (cutoff, code drift), domain (general → specialist, enterprise gap).
  • Mitigate with alignment (IT + RLHF), mid-training/annealing, continual domain-adaptive pre-training with replay, retrieval/tools, production monitoring.

2.9 Reading the loss curves

  • Underfitting: both curves high and flat early (high bias).
  • Overfitting: train → 0 while validation turns back up (high variance); stop at the val minimum.
  • No learning: both flat at the starting value; nothing is updating.
  • Healthy: curves fall together, small stable gap, smooth diminishing returns, checkpoint at the lowest validation loss.

Module 3Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)

3.1 Why PEFT: post-training and the cost of scale

  • PEFT is a post-training technique (PoLM taxonomy: fine-tuning → alignment → reasoning → efficiency).
  • Abilities emerge abruptly with scale (7B → 70B → 400B+), but adaptation cost grows with it.
  • Full FT of 7B ≈ 14 + 14 + 28 + 28 + 8 = 92 GB (Adam states = 56 GB = 4× weights) → 5× RTX 4090 or 2× A100-80GB.
  • Sequential multi-task fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting.
  • PEFT trains < 1% of parameters (≈4M of 7B) in ~15 GB on a single GPU with no accuracy loss.

3.2 The PEFT family tree

  • Four PEFT families: additive (adapters, AdapterFusion), soft prompting (prefix tuning, SMoP), selective (BitFit, diff pruning), re-parameterization (LoRA, QLoRA).
  • Additive adds modules; selective trains a subset of existing weights; re-parameterization trains a low-rank update and merges it away at inference.
  • LoRA numbers: a 4096 × 4096 weight = 16M params; rank 8 trains ≈ 65K.
  • Quantization: 7B FP16 14 GB → 4-bit 3.5 GB; QLoRA ≈ 15 GB total with ~24 MB adapters.
  • Multi-task: 3 full copies = 42 GB vs one 14 GB backbone + 24 MB per task.

3.3 Adapters: setups, requirements, sequential adapters

  • Setups: explicit task ID, AdapterFusion (combine all task adapters), adapter routing (gated), one multi-task adapter.
  • Adapter = down-project (d → m) → non-linearity → up-project (m → d) + skip.
  • Requirements: few parameters, and near-identity init (h' = h + f(h), f ≈ 0) so training starts from pretrained behavior.
  • Houlsby: two sequential adapters per layer (after attention, after FFN); 2dm + m + d params each vs 16d² + 19d per layer (≈1% at d = 768, m = 64).
  • GLUE: adapters 80.0 with 3.6% trained vs full FT 80.4 with 100%.
  • Weaknesses: added latency, cost grows with depth, sequential (not parallelisable), costly multi-task serving.

3.4 Residual adapters and what adapters buy you

  • Residual adapter: Adapter(H) = ReLU(LN(H)·W^E)·W^D + H, with W^E (d×m) and W^D (m×d).
  • It runs in parallel with the frozen FFN (outputs summed with the residual), unlike Houlsby's sequential adapters.
  • Lin et al. use one GPT-2 with per-task adapters (CQA, NLG, SUM, NMT, DLG) plus task/segment embeddings and task tokens such as <bos_qa>, <document>, <question>, <answer>.
  • Adapters ≈ full fine-tuning quality at ~2% of parameters; task-specific adapters avoid catastrophic forgetting.
  • They beat top-layer tuning because they add capacity at every layer with far fewer parameters.

3.5 Soft prompts: prompt tuning and prefix tuning

  • Adapters adapt in architectural space; soft prompts adapt in token space by learning virtual tokens while the LM stays frozen.
  • Manual prompts are brittle (19.8–51.1 for near-identical wordings); learned continuous prompts reach ~58.
  • Prompt tuning: m trainable vectors prepended to the input embeddings; gradients flow only into them.
  • Prefix tuning: z = [PREFIX; x; y] (GPT-2) or [PREFIX; x; PREFIX'; y] (BART); prefix activations are free parameters fed as extra K/V at every layer.
  • Prefix training is stabilized by re-parameterizing through an MLP from a smaller matrix P'.
  • One frozen model + one tiny prefix per task replaces a full model copy per task.

3.6 Smarter soft prompts: SMoP, APT, IDPG, SPT

  • Prompt tuning often needs ~100 soft tokens; remedies are short prompts, multiple prompts and gating.
  • SMoP: k short prompts + a softmax router over the averaged input embedding; one prompt is active per input (sparse).
  • APT: per-layer prefix length via token-level gates α = sigmoid(hW) and layer-level weights λ; bottom layers get longer prefixes (CoNLL04 uses bottom layers, COPA uses top layers).
  • IDPG: a small generator G(M(x), T) produces instance-dependent prompts from a frozen encoder; params m(d+1) + td(m+1).
  • LPT inserts prompts mid-network; SPT learns where to insert them under a K-layer budget.

3.7 LoRA: low-rank adaptation

  • LoRA freezes W and learns the update as a low-rank product: W + (α/r)·BA, with B (d×r), A (r×d), r ≪ d.
  • Forward pass: h = Wx + (α/r)BAx; B starts at 0 so the model starts as the pretrained one.
  • Only A and B receive gradients; at inference they merge into W, so there is zero added latency.
  • Savings: 4096 × 4096 (16.8M) vs rank 8 (≈65K) trainable parameters.
  • Memory for 10B: full FT 160 GB vs LoRA 40 GB; the FP16 base is the remaining bottleneck.

3.8 QLoRA: quantized LoRA

  • QLoRA = quantized frozen base + LoRA adapters; four ingredients: quantization, NF4, double quantization, paged optimizer.
  • Absmax INT8: X_int8 = round(127/max|X| · X); 127/max|X| is the per-block quantization constant.
  • NF4: 16 levels with equal-count buckets, dense near 0 because weights are roughly normal.
  • Worked example: W ÷ 0.82 → nearest codebook values → indices [0, 3, 5, 8, 11, 14]; dequantize with w = 0.82 × NF4[index].
  • Double quantization quantizes the per-block constants themselves.
  • Paged optimizer moves inactive pages to CPU; gradient checkpointing stores fewer activations and recomputes them.
  • Result: 7B base 14 GB → 3.5 GB; QLoRA fine-tuning ≈ 15 GB on a single GPU.

Module 4LLM Alignment: RLHF & DPO

4.1 HHH and preference alignment

  • HHH: honest (truthful, calibrated, not sycophantic), helpful (actually solves the need), harmless (refuses real-world harm even under a benign framing).
  • The three conflict (dosage advice, flawed essay, SQL injection); single-objective models over-comply, over-refuse or blurt harmful truths.
  • Preference alignment operationalizes HHH through pairwise human comparisons; the preference/reward model is a learned proxy for HHH.
  • The bottleneck shifts to preference-data quality. RLHF uses a reward model + RL; DPO uses preferences directly.
  • Pipeline: pre-training → fine-tuning → preference tuning.

4.2 RL foundations for language models

  • RL is needed because human feedback is non-differentiable; RL learns from rewards without gradients through the judge.
  • RL vocabulary: agent, state, action, reward, policy π(a|s), transition P(s'|s,a), trajectory τ.
  • For LLMs: policy = the LLM, state = prompt + tokens so far, action = next token, reward = reward model or verifier.
  • P(τ|π) = P(s₀) Π π(a_t|s_t) P(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t).
  • Return: Σ r_t (finite) or Σ γᵗ r_t (discounted, 0 < γ < 1); objective J = E_τ[R(τ)].

4.3 Policy gradient, REINFORCE and the advantage

  • Maximize J by gradient ascent; ∇J = E[Σ ∇log π(a_t|s_t) · R(τ)].
  • The exact gradient is intractable, so average over sampled trajectories (REINFORCE: sample → estimate → ascend → repeat).
  • The estimate is unbiased but high-variance.
  • Variance fixes: reward-to-go (only future rewards count), a baseline b(s_t) such as V(s), and the advantage A = Q − V.
  • Advantage in LMs: tokens that lead to better-than-average reward get reinforced.

4.4 PPO: sample reuse, reward hacking and the KL penalty

  • Resampling after every update is wasteful; PPO samples with π_old, stores the trajectories and reuses them for K epochs via the ratio π_θ/π_θold.
  • Reward hacking: the policy games the reward model (flattery for “Why is the sky blue?”).
  • Fix: KL penalty −β·KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref) keeps the policy close to the frozen SFT reference; KL is non-negative and asymmetric.
  • Principle: improve with reward, but keep each update small.
  • Four models: policy (trained), reference (frozen SFT), reward model (sequence score), value model (per-token score); Â = r + γV(s') − V(s).

4.5 Reward model and value model

  • Absolute reward labels are hard; pairwise preferences (prompt, answer 1, answer 2, chosen) are easy for people.
  • Reward model: LLM backbone + a linear head with one output on the final hidden state → scalar reward.
  • Bradley–Terry loss −log σ(r_w − r_l); code: −F.logsigmoid(r_w − r_l); one shared model scores both responses.
  • Value model: a per-token linear head trained with (V(s_t) − R̂_t)², where R̂_t is the reward-to-go.
  • In PPO the backbone carries LM, reward and value heads.

4.6 InstructGPT, ChatGPT and the RLHF pipeline

  • RLHF teaches preferences that correctness alone misses (the most useful of three “correct” Python answers).
  • InstructGPT: (1) SFT on labeler demonstrations; (2) labelers rank several outputs → reward model; (3) PPO against the reward model.
  • ChatGPT used the same recipe with dialogue data written by trainers playing both roles, mixed with InstructGPT data.
  • Pipeline: pre-trained LLM → SFT (π₀) → human rankings → reward model → PPO near π₀ → aligned π* → deploy.

4.7 DPO: direct preference optimization

  • PPO-RLHF is indirect and unstable: reward model + RL + KL control across four models.
  • DPO is RL-free: preference data → policy directly; no reward model, no value model, no sampling loop.
  • Loss: −log σ(β[log π_θ(y_w|x)/π_ref(y_w|x) − log π_θ(y_l|x)/π_ref(y_l|x)]).
  • It increases the chosen answer's probability relative to the reference and decreases the rejected one's (photosynthesis: 30% chosen / 70% rejected must flip).
  • At initialization the loss is log 2 ≈ 0.693; β controls how far the policy may move from π_ref.
  • Workflow: static preference data → SFT on chosen answers (reference) → DPO.

4.8 Revision, RLAIF and safety in practice

  • Alignment fine-tuning routes: RLHF (rank → reward model → PPO), DPO (train on pairs), revision (self-critique against written principles).
  • RLAIF replaces human preference labels with AI feedback.
  • The SLM lab practiced PEFT and DPO, then three deployment safeguards: output guardrails/content filtering, PII detection and red-team testing.

Module 5Vision-Language Model Architectures

5.1 VLM foundations

  • A VLM takes image(s) + text and outputs text, a label, a similarity score or a mask; its promise is open-vocabulary generalization via language.
  • Two families: trained from scratch (CLIP, BLIP) vs pretrained-LLM backbone with a projector (LLaVA, Qwen-VL).
  • Drivers: multimodal perception, demand, free web alt-text data, transformer unification (ViT + LLM).
  • ViT: 16×16 patches → linear projection → position embeddings + [CLS] → transformer encoder; every model here uses one.
  • Paradigms: contrastive (CLIP → scores), generative (LLaVA/Qwen-VL → text), promptable dense (SAM → masks).
  • Fusion lens: none / dot product (CLIP), early fusion in the LLM (LLaVA, Qwen-VL), cross-attention (SAM decoder, Qwen-VL adapter).

5.2 CLIP: dual encoders and contrastive pretraining

  • CLIP replaces a fixed 1,000-class head with language supervision: learn which caption matches which image.
  • Two independent encoders, no cross-attention; trained on WIT, 400M web pairs.
  • Image encoders: ResNets (attention pooling) or ViTs (B/32, B/16, L/14, L/14@336px best); one global vector per image, 512–1024-d.
  • Text encoder: 63M-param, 12-layer, 512-wide, 8-head Transformer; 49K BPE; 76-token cap; embedding taken at [EOS].
  • Loss: symmetric InfoNCE over the N × N matrix (N positives, N² − N negatives; N − 1 negatives per image); learnable τ sets softmax sharpness.
  • Recipe: batch 32,768, 32 epochs, Adam + decoupled weight decay, cosine LR, mixed precision.

5.3 CLIP: zero-shot transfer, results and limits

  • Zero-shot: embed the image; embed “a photo of a {label}” for each class; cosine similarity; softmax; argmax. Ensembling ~80 templates helps.
  • Linear probe needs labels; zero-shot needs none, and zero-shot CLIP rivals linear-probed ResNets.
  • 76.2% zero-shot ImageNet top-1 (= supervised ResNet-50), 27+ datasets, and much better robustness (ImageNet-A 2.7 → 77.1, Sketch 25.2 → 60.2).
  • Embeddings are L2-normalized; τ is learned.
  • Uses: retrieval, generative guidance (DALL·E 2), backbone for LLaVA/Qwen-VL, open-vocabulary moderation.
  • Limits: coarse semantics (counting, OCR, spatial relations), prompt sensitivity, web bias, no text generation.

5.4 LLaVA: architecture and GPT-4 instruction data

  • LLaVA = frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 → projector W → LLM (Vicuna/LLaMA); the image is a “foreign language” for the LLM.
  • The projector is required because CLIP and LLM spaces have unrelated geometries; v1 linear, v1.5 2-layer MLP with GELU.
  • Grid (patch) features from around the last ViT layer; visual tokens (e.g. 256) sit in the sequence with text; plain self-attention, no cross-attention.
  • Training sequence: [system][image tokens][user][assistant]; loss only on the assistant's answer.
  • Data: GPT-4 (text-only, never sees images) turns COCO captions + boxes into ~158K samples: conversation, detailed description, complex reasoning.

5.5 LLaVA: training, versions, evaluation and limits

  • Stage 1: freeze vision encoder + LLM, train only the projector on ~595K CC3M pairs (alignment). Stage 2: freeze the vision encoder, train projector + LLM on 158K GPT-4 samples.
  • Loss = next-token cross-entropy on assistant tokens only.
  • LLaVA-1.5: MLP projector, academic VQA data, answer-format prompts, 336px; extremely data-efficient (0.67M + 0.56M samples).
  • LLaVA-NeXT AnyRes: tiles + downsampled global view → better OCR/charts, more tokens.
  • Benchmarks: LLaVA-Bench (GPT-4 judge), ScienceQA, VQAv2/GQA, POPE (hallucination).
  • Cheap (hours for stage 1, ~1 day total), open, reproducible; family: LLaVA-Med, LLaVA-Plus/Interactive (tools), Video-LLaVA.
  • Limits: hallucination, low resolution, weak localization/counting, CLIP's blind spots.

5.6 Qwen-VL: a grounded, multi-image VLM

  • Qwen-VL: ViT (from OpenCLIP ViT-bigG, 14×14 patches, 224 → 448px) → position-aware adapter → Qwen-7B LLM.
  • Adapter: one cross-attention layer with 256 learnable queries over P patch keys/values + 2D position encoding → always 256 visual tokens.
  • Grounding as text: <box>(x1,y1),(x2,y2)</box> normalized 0–1000, <ref> phrase, <img> insertion point; coordinates come from next-token prediction, no special head.
  • Multi-image via several <img> blocks (“Picture 1: …”) and multi-round history.
  • Training: (1) 224px, 1.4B pairs, LLM frozen; (2) 448px multi-task (7 tasks incl. OCR), all trainable; (3) SFT → Qwen-VL-Chat, ViT frozen.
  • vs LLaVA: compressed fixed tokens, native grounding, multi-image, 3 stages. Limits: compression loses detail; costlier recipe. Qwen2-VL adds dynamic resolution + M-RoPE.

5.7 SAM: Segment Anything

  • Promptable segmentation: image + prompt (point, box, mask, text) → valid mask; zero-shot transfer from training at scale.
  • Heavy MAE-pretrained ViT-H/16 encoder (~0.15 s) runs once and is cached; lightweight prompt encoder; fast two-way-attention mask decoder (~50 ms).
  • Prompt formats: points (N,x,y,label), boxes (N,x1,y1,x2,y2), masks (1,1024,1024), text via CLIP.
  • Ambiguity: three masks (whole/part/sub-part) + IoU head picks the best.
  • Loss: 20·focal (hard boundary pixels) + 1·dice (region overlap, size-independent) + MSE for the IoU head.
  • Data engine: assisted-manual → semi-automatic → fully automatic (32×32 point grid + NMS) → SA-1B: 11M images, 1.1B masks.
  • Composes with grounding models (Grounded-SAM); SAM 2 adds video memory; no class labels on masks.

5.8 Synthesis: comparing and composing the four

  • Compare on paradigm, backbone, fusion, output and training signal (400M pairs · 158K GPT-4 samples · 1.4B pairs + multi-task · 1.1B masks).
  • All use a ViT (CLIP from scratch, LLaVA frozen CLIP, Qwen-VL from OpenCLIP, SAM MAE-pretrained); they differ in what they do with the features.
  • They compose: Grounded-SAM, VLM agents calling SAM, CLIP-powered retrieval for generative VLMs, CLIP-guided diffusion.
  • Trade-offs: frozen vs fine-tuned backbone, tokens vs spatial fidelity, scale vs curated data, specialization vs generality.
  • Trends: dynamic resolution, M-RoPE across modalities and time, any-to-any models, tool-using multimodal agents.

Module 6Applications of VLMs

6.1 Image captioning: task, models and prompting

  • Captioning describes objects, attributes, scene and context in free-form language; it differs from classification (fixed label) and VQA (a specific question).
  • History: CNN → RNN captioning (Karpathy 2015; Show & Tell; Show, Attend & Tell) → today's VLMs.
  • Rule of thumb: sentence → generative VLM (LLaVA/Qwen); tag → CLIP zero-shot.
  • “Cap” = ViT encoder + autoregressive decoder trained with cross-entropy, an alternative to contrastive pre-training.
  • Prompting: constrain scope and length (“one sentence, < 125 characters, only what is visible”); fix one template for cataloging.
  • Pitfalls: hallucination, generic captions, missed salient detail, bias. LLaVA-1.6 13B beat Qwen-VL 2B and LLaVA-1.5 7B on the street example, even reading the license plate.

6.2 Captioning: hardness, datasets, training and metrics

  • Hard because of fine-grained detail, compositional relations, subjective salience, imperfect metrics, long-tail concepts and subjectivity.
  • Metrics: BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR (n-gram), SPICE (scene graph), CLIPScore (CLIP), CIDEr (benchmark tables).
  • Datasets: COCO (330K × 5 captions, gold standard), Flickr30K (31K), CC3M/12M (noisy alt-text), Visual Genome (108K dense regions), LAION-5B (5B+); CapArena for human pairwise judging.
  • Training: noisy web pre-training → curated COCO fine-tuning → instruction tuning; BLIP-style bootstrapping cleans captions.
  • COCO CIDEr ~110–120 → ~140+ → ~143; NoCaps tests novel objects.
  • Open problems: hallucination, metric–human mismatch, bias, style control, non-English cultures.

6.3 Visual question answering (VQA)

  • VQA answers a specific question about an image (yes/no, multiple choice, counting, open-ended); captioning describes generally.
  • LLaVA for general conversational VQA; Qwen-VL when grounding, pointing or OCR is needed.
  • Prompting: direct zero-shot; chain-of-thought for counting/comparison (auditable list first); few-shot for domain vocabulary.
  • VLMs often lean on language priors (blurred Mona Lisa still gets an answer); presupposition hallucination needs an explicit “not present” option.
  • Datasets: VQAv2 (~1.1M, COCO), GQA (~22M, compositional), OK-VQA (~14K, knowledge), TextVQA (~45K, OCR), VizWiz (~31K, blind users).
  • Training: base VLM + mixed VQA data + short-answer supervision + preference tuning with synthetic negatives (random answer, random question, blackened objects).
  • Strict metrics penalize verbose correct answers (GPT-4V); counting fails beyond ~5–10 objects.

6.4 Document intelligence

  • Document intelligence = OCR + layout → structured fields (invoices, forms, receipts, contracts).
  • Qwen-VL fits (OCR + grounding); dedicated OCR is cheaper for bulk text but weak on layout. Documents need high resolution; external OCR loses layout.
  • Prompt with an explicit JSON schema, every field named, one object per document (invoice → {vendor, invoice_number, date, total}).
  • Pitfalls: template variability, poor scans, hallucinated missing fields; route high-stakes fields to humans.
  • DAVE: MAE on raw pixels (unlabeled doc/web images) → multi-decoder supervised stage, learned weight merging (biggest gain, 55.6 → 63.4) + SigLIP2 ensemble; +10.5% vs SigLIP2, +5% Mind2Web.
  • DocVLM: 344M OCR+layout T5 encoder, 64 learnable queries, concatenated to visual tokens; base VLM frozen.
  • DocVQA (ANLS), InfographicVQA, RVL-CDIP (400K, 16 classes), FUNSD (~200 forms); DocVQA 65.1 → 94.5 → ~96+.

6.5 Visual reasoning and chart QA

  • Visual reasoning combines several observations (spatial relations, counting, comparison, cause–effect); VQA often reads one fact.
  • Reasoning quality tracks the LLM backbone: “the encoder gets pixels, the LLM reasons”; Qwen-VL helps for region references.
  • Chain-of-thought (list observations, then decide) makes reasoning auditable: the “No Parking” sign example.
  • Risks: compounding errors, false confidence, no self-check → ask the model to verify its steps.
  • Datasets: MMMU (~11.5K college level), MathVista, ScienceQA (~21K), NLVR2 (image pairs), Winoground (near-random for many models).
  • MMMU low-50s → low/mid-60s% (2024); largest open-vs-closed and model-vs-human gaps.
  • Chart QA: Qwen-VL / high-res LLaVA; extract values first, then reason; ChartQA 65.7 → 83.0 → ~89+.
