Module 7Text Search, Image Search & Multimodal RAG

7.1 Text search and dense retrieval

  • Text search retrieves ranked existing passages: the first half of RAG.
  • BM25/TF-IDF match exact words (fast, interpretable, miss paraphrases); dense embeddings match meaning; hybrid blends both.
  • Bi-encoder: query and documents encoded separately into one space → nearest-neighbor search; FAISS/HNSW ANN indexes make it scale; reranking boosts precision.
  • Benchmarks: MS MARCO, BEIR (zero-shot), MTEB (56+ tasks; leaders ≈74 overall, ≈72 retrieval).
  • Trained contrastively with hard negatives.
  • Challenges: chunking long docs, domain shift, negation/numbers, topical ≠ answering.

7.2 RAG for NLP and ColBERT late interaction

  • RAG (Lewis et al.): query encoder + document index (non-parametric retriever) → MIPS top-K → seq2seq generator (parametric) → marginalize over documents; z is latent; trained end-to-end.
  • Same model handles QA, fact verification and Jeopardy-style question generation.
  • ColBERT: per-token embeddings from a shared BERT; score = Σ over query tokens of the max similarity to any document token (MaxSim).
  • Trained with a contrastive loss on (q, d⁺, d⁻) triplets; offline token-level indexing, online ANN + MaxSim.

7.3 Image search: cross-modal retrieval

  • Two directions: text-to-image (most common) and image-to-image.
  • CLIP's shared space lets text and images be compared directly; different encoders, same space; same FAISS/HNSW indexes as text search.
  • No captions or tags needed: “snow-capped mountains at sunset” matched purely in embedding space.
  • Strong encoders: DINOv2/v3, SigLIP-2. Benchmarks: Flickr30K, COCO with Recall@K (Flickr30K R@1 ≈ 51% base CLIP → ≈ 85% modern).
  • Weak spots: fine-grained and compositional queries, bias, long queries.

7.4 Multimodal RAG: what, why and how

  • Multimodal RAG retrieves images, tables, charts or pages (not just text) and generates a grounded answer, reducing hallucination and stale knowledge.
  • Text-only RAG can't see the chart: the 1975 mortality question fails on caption text and succeeds (≈0.24) when the figure is retrieved.
  • Architecture: retriever (offline indexing, online querying) → top-k pages → VLM generator; d ~ p(d|q), a ~ q(a|q,d).
  • Strategies: parse-then-embed (OCR + layout, brittle) vs vision-space retrieval (embed page screenshots).
  • Storage: unify into one modality, one shared multimodal space, or separate per-modality databases.

7.5 ColPali: document retrieval in vision space

  • Late interaction (from ColBERT): many vectors per page/query; score = Σ over query tokens of max similarity to any patch.
  • ColPali: PaliGemma-3B + linear projection to D = 128; one vector per patch (pages) / per token (queries); no OCR.
  • Loss: (1/b) Σ softplus(s⁻ − s⁺) against the hardest in-batch negative.
  • Indexing 0.39 s/page vs 7.22 s for the PDF-parsing pipeline; NDCG@5 0.81 vs 0.66. Querying stays fast for every system (~22–30 ms per query in the overview figure; ≤ 22 ms on an NVIDIA L4 in the latency study).
  • Page-level indexing; the index must answer “which page?”.
  • ViDoRe: ~127K PDF pages, nDCG@5. Ranking: BM25 on OCR < BGE-M3 on OCR < ColPali.

7.6 Grounded generation: prompting, pitfalls, challenges

  • Generation = a VLM answering from the retrieved pages (VQA + document intelligence on system-chosen content).
  • Prompt: answer only from retrieved content, cite the page, allow “not found” (abstention is hard).
  • Pitfalls: retrieval failure (unfixable by prompting), hallucination despite retrieval, distracting context, over-trusted citations.
  • Hard: chunk size, joint text/visual ranking, multi-page answers, evaluating retrieval + generation together.
  • Open: costly late-interaction indexes, weak generalization to messy docs, multi-document reasoning, no standard faithfulness metric.
  • Choose text search for plain text, CLIP image search for photos/products, vision-space multimodal RAG for mixed real documents.

7.7 The multimodal RAG landscape

  • Applications: content generation, knowledge QA, healthcare (MMed-RAG, RULE, AsthmaBot), software engineering (DocPrompting, RACE, REDCODER), e-commerce/driving/geolocation (RAG-Driver, Img2Loc); Re-Imagen shows retrieval fixing rare-entity hallucination.
  • Retrieval modalities: text-centric (BM25, BGE-M3, ColBERT), vision-centric, video-centric, document/layout (ColPali).
  • Fusion: score fusion in a shared space, cross-attention, unified representations.
  • Reasoning: in-context examples, CoT / Tree of RAG, instruction tuning to decide when to retrieve, source attribution.
  • Training: multi-stage; InfoNCE alignment with hard negatives; cross-entropy (or diffusion/GAN) generation loss; noise-injection robustness.
  • Joint training treats the retrieved document as latent (EM-style, RAG/REALM marginalize over top-k); practice: separate pre-training, then joint fine-tuning.

Module 8From RAG to Assistants and Agents

8.1 Why RAG isn't enough: questions vs tasks

  • The Paris request combines private knowledge, time-varying data, joint hard constraints and unknown control flow.
  • Ladder: LLM → RAG (+retrieval) → assistant (+context) → tool-using assistant (+tools) → agent (+decisions) → multi-agent (+delegation).
  • Bare LLM failure modes: knowledge cutoff, no private data, hallucination, no traceability.
  • RAG pipeline: ingestion (40 pages → 118 chunks → vectors) → top-3 retrieval → augmentation → cited generation. Principle: retrieve before you generate.
  • Question answering ends when generation stops; task completion needs many runtime-ordered steps, actions, decisions and interaction, and ends when the goal is met or judged impossible.

8.2 Assistants: context, tool calling and MCP

  • Assistant = RAG + context: conversation history is state (“the hotel” only makes sense after turn 1).
  • Without tools the assistant can read the policy but cannot act (“no way to search hotels”).
  • Tool calling: the model emits a structured request (name + arguments); your code executes it and returns the result. The model never touches the API.
  • Knowledge shapes actions: the cabin = economy argument came from the retrieved policy.
  • MCP: the agent is an MCP client that discovers tools (list_tools) and calls them (call_tool) on servers exposing tools or resources.
  • Without MCP: ~20 lines of schema per tool, edit and redeploy for changes. With MCP: runtime discovery, server-owned schemas, no redeploy.

8.3 Workflows vs agents and the agent loop

  • Tool-using assistant: the developer fixes the order of calls. Agent: the model chooses the next step each iteration from the last result.
  • The test: if you can draw the flowchart in advance, build a workflow, not an agent.
  • Workflow: same steps every time, auditable path, exact cost bounds, irreversible calls (expense reports). Agent: data-dependent steps, later steps invalidate earlier ones, flaky tools, open-ended inputs (Paris trip, incident triage). Ship both.
  • Loop: think → act (one tool) → observe → remember → goal reached? It must be bounded, observable and recoverable.
  • Trace: policy → 15 Aug flight (₹38,400) → hotels → total ₹65,600 → compliance FAIL (5 days < 7) → re-search 22 Aug (₹34,900) → compliant, ₹17,900 under budget.

8.4 What the loop costs and three loop shapes

  • The model is stateless, so every step re-sends goal, tool schemas and all prior steps: cost grows super-linearly (≈ quadratic), and doubling steps more than doubles cost.
  • The context window is the hard wall; manage it by truncating observations, summarizing superseded steps and keeping only the last N in full (context engineering).
  • ReAct: one thought, one action; cheapest and easiest to debug, but can wander.
  • Plan-and-Execute: plan up front, parallel and predictable, but the plan predates the evidence; replan on failure.
  • Reflection: draft → critique → revise; better written output at 2–3× tokens.

8.5 Retrieval as a tool, memory and multi-agent design

  • In an agent, retrieval is an optional tool: rewrite the query, retrieve repeatedly, skip it for live data (call the API), and re-retrieve to verify the draft.
  • Memory: conversation state (one thread), task state/scratchpad (one run; without it there is no loop), long-term memory (across sessions).
  • Multi-agent: when one agent has too many tools (14), a crowded context, a do-everything prompt and one failure domain, an orchestrator routes to specialist agents over shared state, with human approval. Handoffs lose context, so start with one agent.
  • Frameworks: Microsoft Agent Framework, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK (MCP-native), Google ADK (A2A), Pydantic AI, Strands/Mastra/Agno. Pick by stack; the loop is portable, the state store is not; protocols outlive SDKs.
  • Carry forward: RAG answers, agents finish; control flow defines an agent; the loop is small; RAG lives inside the agent; state is the hard part (checkpoints + human before irreversible steps).
